prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
response:
## I Have Tried Fourteen Calendars. None of Them Work.

I need three things from a calendar.

First, it has to handle time zones without me doing arithmetic. Second, it has to let me create a recurring event with a start date, an end date, and an exception. Third, it has to stop asking me to create an account before I can even see whether it will sync with the other twelve things in my life.

I have tried fourteen apps this year. One of them is a website. One is a mobile app. One is an app that also makes a sound when you delete a meeting, as if deleting a meeting is an emotional event.

The website asked me to choose a plan before showing me the calendar. The mobile app asked me for my phone number before showing me the calendar. The app with the sound asked me to connect a social account before showing me the calendar.

I want to put a dentist appointment on a Tuesday. I do not want to become a user. I do not want to become a customer. I do not want to be excited about a platform. I want a rectangle on a day.

Here is the theory: there are so many calendar apps because the obvious one is too hard to build as a business.

A calendar is a database with a time axis. It has to store events, people, time zones, reminders, exceptions, and permissions. It has to stay correct when a meeting moves from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m., or from Eastern to Pacific, or from one year to the next. It has to be fast enough that opening it does not feel like a chore. It has to sync. It has to not lose your data.

None of that is glamorous.

A startup cannot raise money by saying, “We will make the time zone math not hurt.” Investors want a market, a loop, a wedge, a network. So calendar apps become something else. They become scheduling tools. They become CRM tools. They become AI assistants. They become team workspaces. They become “the operating system for your life.” They become beautiful, and they become complicated, and they become places where you manage your self before you can see your Tuesday.

The result is a strange industry. Every app is confident. Every app has a name that sounds like a feeling. Every app believes that if it can get you to invite a coworker, or connect a laptop, or import a CSV, it will own your attention.

But I do not want to own anything. I want to know whether I have a thing at 10 a.m.

I tried the new one today. The one with the soft colors and the promise of “less busy, more intentional.” It let me create an event. Then it wanted a workspace. Then it wanted a team. Then it wanted a plan. I left a dentist appointment in a demo account and closed the browser.

My phone still has the old calendar on it. It is ugly. It works. It does not ask me to become a person.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.
response:
The question came up at the end, which is where it always comes up, after the wine and the dishes had moved through their cycles and the room had thinned to the people who actually wanted to talk. We were in the kitchen of a house in Vermont, a workshop of sorts: eight of us had spent the afternoon building a small cedar table, and now we were sitting on the floor around it, our knees aching, our hands still gritty with sawdust.

Nobody wanted the table to be a metaphor, but it became one anyway. One of the participants, a retired engineer, said that he had built it to have a purpose, and that purpose was to hold things. The table would be a table in the way that a bridge is a bridge. The comment was so plain that it landed. We had been talking about the meaning of life in a way that made the phrase sound almost decorative, and he had reached under it and found a hinge.

I had come to the workshop expecting to make something and leave with it. What I left with was a better question. Meaning, it turned out, is not a property you find in an object. It is the shape of the relation between the object and the life that needs it. The table does not carry its own meaning. It carries ours: the weight of the dinner plates, the elbows of the people who sit at it, the slow wear of years.

This is where tidy answers usually fail. They treat meaning as a destination, as though life is a road that eventually arrives at a sign. But the sign is not on the horizon. It is under your hands. The engineer’s point was not that purpose is easy. It was that purpose is local. You do not have to explain the table to the universe. You have to make it strong enough for the people who will use it.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. A lot of what we call a crisis of meaning is really a crisis of scale. We ask what life is for, as if it had to be for something large enough to survive a biography. But most meaningful things are smaller than that. They are the meal you cook for a friend, the sentence you revise until it stops being false, the argument you have carefully enough that it changes something. These do not sound like answers. They sound like work. But they are where meaning actually lives, because they are where attention has a place to go.

The dinner conversation drifted back and forth. One person said that meaning had to be transcendent, that if it was only about the table, it would be swallowed by time. Another said that was exactly the point: the table would be used, scratched, moved, and eventually discarded, and that did not make it less real. The two claims were not as opposed as they seemed. The first was afraid of finitude. The second was trying to make peace with it.

I think the second is closer to the truth, though it is less comforting. A life is not made meaningful by escaping its own limits. It is made meaningful by what it does inside them. The table is not eternal. It is made for a room, a family, a set of hands. Its goodness is visible in the joints, in the way the top sits level, in the small decisions that cannot be unseen. That is not nothing. It is the whole of what can be done.

What I kept returning to was the difference between a meaning that is claimed and a meaning that is made. Claimed meanings are often grand. Made meanings are harder. You have to show up. You have to be specific. You have to care about the difference between a good answer and a bad one, and then have the patience to close that difference with your own hands. The workshop had made that obvious in a way that a lecture could not. We had spent the day discovering that a piece of wood resists you. It does not flatter you. It does not agree with your intentions. It only lets you know, through touch and correction, what is possible.

That is a harsh teacher, but it is an honest one. If life has a meaning, it is not that it is beautiful, or that it is sacred, or that it is waiting to be deciphered. It is that it is capable of response. You can make a table, or a friendship, or an argument, or a life, in such a way that it holds. Not forever. Not for everyone. But well enough to be true while it lasts.

The night ended the way those nights do, with the question left open and the room a little quieter. Nobody had solved anything. We had only gotten the question into better hands. I think that is as close as a personal essay can get to a meaning of life: not an answer, but a practice of paying attention to what is in front of you, and doing it carefully enough that it matters.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.
response:
The letter is three sentences long. “This patient is an individual with a disability as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act. The patient requires an emotional support animal for the treatment of the disability. The animal is a necessary part of the treatment plan.” I have signed thousands of variations of this. The patient’s diagnosis is usually in the margin, or in the chart, or nowhere. The animal’s species, name, and role in the treatment are usually nowhere.

The law created a category, and the category created a demand, and the demand created a market. Emotional support animals are not service animals. A service animal has been trained to do something specific for a disability. An emotional support animal does not have to do anything. It has to be there, and it has to be tied, in a letter, to a diagnosis. That is the whole mechanism.

So the psychiatrist’s job is not to evaluate the animal. It is to certify a connection between a person and an animal. I can usually do that quickly. If someone has spent two hours telling me that their cat is the only reason they get out of bed, I do not need a form to know that the cat is doing therapeutic work. The problem is that the form is not a therapeutic instrument. It is a key. It opens doors to apartments, to flights, to workplaces that would otherwise say no.

That is why the system is bad even when the outcome is mostly harmless.

A harmless outcome is a dog in a hospital room calming a depressed patient. A harmless outcome is a cat in a tiny apartment giving someone something to feed and something to answer to. Those things are good. They should be recognized by landlords and clinicians and families without a legal workaround. But the ESA letter does not make the relationship legitimate; it makes it rentable. It turns a private attachment into a claim on public or commercial space.

The clinical language does more damage than the law does. “Emotional support” sounds gentle, but it is not a treatment plan. It is a category label. It implies that the animal is doing the job of therapy, or of medicine, or of accommodation. Sometimes it is doing a small, real part of a larger plan. Often it is doing nothing except giving the owner a document that says, “I am allowed to have this animal in places where I otherwise am not.”

The patients are not usually malicious. Most of them are not trying to smuggle a pit bull onto a Delta flight. They are trying to protect something they genuinely need: routine, contact, permission, a reason to keep a place, a reason to keep an animal. Some have been rejected by landlords for having a dog. Some have been told by employers that their anxiety medication is not enough, but their cat is not allowed in the office. Some have been told by their insurer that therapy animals are not covered, but an ESA letter might help. They have learned the grammar of the system. They speak it. I am expected to answer in the same grammar.

That is the uncomfortable part. I am not supposed to be a gatekeeper of tenderness, but the letter turns me into one. If I say no, I may be protecting the system from abuse. If I say yes, I may be laundering a personal preference into a civil right. Either way, I am being asked to make a legal decision with a clinical signature.

The real abuse is not usually exotic. It is not a person with a parrot in a carry-on. It is the slow normalization of the idea that anyone with any diagnosed distress can attach any animal to that distress and claim accommodation. It is the landlord who now has to decide whether a rabbit is a medical device. It is the flight attendant who has to ask a woman if her hamster is “necessary” while she is crying in the aisle. It is the employer who has to choose between accommodating a genuine need and opening the door to every sad, lonely, or angry person with a pet.

The system is also bad because it punishes the people who actually need help. Service animals, the trained ones, are harder to see as legitimate when everything is an “emotional support” animal. A dog that guides a blind man is easier to defend when the category has not been diluted. A cat that is allowed in a hotel because its owner has generalized anxiety is harder to defend when the hotel has seen four cats and a bearded dragon in one month. The more the category stretches, the less trust it gets.

There is also a strange cruelty in the paperwork. The patient is asked to prove that the animal is necessary. But the necessity is usually emotional, and emotional necessity is hard to document without sounding ridiculous. I cannot write, “The patient’s depression is maintained by the absence of a cat.” That is not a sentence a clinician is supposed to write. It is not a sentence a landlord is supposed to read. So we write the three sentences. The three sentences say almost nothing. They say enough to trigger a legal process.

Some of the requests are absurd. A patient wants a peacock certified. A patient wants a second cat certified after the first cat died. A patient wants a turtle because the turtle is low maintenance and the patient works nights. A patient wants a dog but knows the dog will not be allowed in the apartment, so the letter becomes an argument. In each case, the animal is not the issue. The issue is housing, work, loneliness, disability, grief, or the fear of being alone with one’s own mind.

I do not think the solution is to ban ESA letters. That would be easy to say and would miss the point. The problem is not that people are attached to animals. The problem is that we have no better category for animals that help people. We have “service animal,” which is too narrow. We have “pet,” which is too legally cold. We have “emotional support animal,” which is too legally hot. The middle is empty, so everyone falls into the ends.

A better system would separate the questions. Is the animal safe? Is it healthy? Can it be contained? Does the person have a documented disability? Is the animal part of a treatment plan, or is it a request for a pet? Those are different questions. The first three are factual. The last two are clinical and legal. A landlord should not have to decide whether a cat is a medical device. A landlord should be able to ask reasonable questions about size, behavior, noise, and care, and the person should be able to answer them without producing a psychiatric letter.

The clinician’s role should be smaller and clearer. If an animal is part of treatment, I can say so in the context of the treatment. If a patient needs housing flexibility because of a disability, the legal process should be about the disability and the accommodation, not about whether a ferret is “necessary.” If a patient simply wants a pet, I should say, “I cannot certify that as treatment,” and then, if it is safe and kind, I can say, “But I understand why you want it.”

That second sentence is the one the current system does not allow. It treats the patient as a person rather than as a claim. It says, “Your animal matters to you. I do not have to pretend it is a medical device for it to matter.” That is less legally useful than the three-sentence letter. It is more honest.

The funny thing is that the system often works. The cat is allowed in the apartment. The dog is allowed in the waiting room. The owner feels less alone. The animal gets fed. The neighborhood survives. No one is harmed, or almost no one is harmed, and the paperwork is thin enough to be ignored. That is why it persists. It is not a grand fraud. It is a small, repeated fudge. A thousand small fudges make a category.

But the fudge has a cost. It makes the language of disability vague. It makes the language of care commercial. It makes clinicians sign documents we cannot meaningfully evaluate. It makes landlords, airlines, and employers into amateur psychologists. It turns a simple fact—some people need animals—into a legal argument about what kind of animal counts.

If I wanted to fix it without pretending I could fix it, I would start by refusing to treat the letter as a diagnosis. I would stop writing “emotional support animal” as if it were a clinical term. I would write, when true, that the patient has a disability and that an animal is part of the treatment. I would name the animal. I would say what the patient has been told to do with it: keep it fed, keep it indoors, keep it away from food, bring it to appointments if it helps. I would not say it is necessary unless I could say what would happen if it were not there. If the answer is “the patient would be sadder,” I would say, “The patient would be sadder,” not “the patient would be untreated.”

That would not stop people from using the letters. It would stop me from helping them turn sadness into a legal category. And I think that is where the real problem lives. Not in the pet. Not even mostly in the law. In the habit of making a person’s private life into a claim, and then making the claim into a document, and then making the document into a reason for the world to adjust.

The world should adjust. That is what disability law is for. But it should adjust to disability, not to the animal. The animal can be part of the life. It does not have to be the proof.

prompt: I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
response:
# The Attraction of the Reckless

You discover that a group of people on a message board is pooling money to synthesize experimental compounds and dosing themselves. Your first reaction is the expected one: this is stupid and dangerous. Your second reaction is a small, warm thrill. That second reaction is the one that deserves an explanation.

The thrill is not that the drugs look interesting. It is that the arrangement is unmediated. A group of people who have no formal authority, no institutional backing, and no liability shield decided, "we want to know this, and we will find out." There is no review board, no IRB, no safety officer with a clipboard. The experiment is just people, money, and a question.

That is exactly what science used to look like, before it became an industry. The appeal is to a romantic image of knowledge as something you can go and do, not something you apply to receive. Seeing the gate closed and a few people climbing over it feels like a small act of honesty. The world is mostly arranged so that curiosity has to justify itself in advance. These people skipped the justification and went straight to the finding out.

But the pleasure is parasitic. It borrows the romance of discovery while quietly discarding the parts that make discovery possible. The reason modern science is bureaucratic is that most experiments are dull, and the dangerous ones are dangerous in ways you cannot feel until you are already inside them. A protocol is not just red tape; it is the accumulated record of what has already gone wrong. When a forum group tests a compound on themselves, they are not merely brave. They are also unmoored from that record. Their data, even if clean, will be anecdotal, underpowered, and nearly impossible to repeat. They may learn a lot. They may also just be the first data point in a story that ends in a hospital.

So the mixed reaction makes sense. The pleasure is real and it is aimed at something true: that the machinery around science has become so heavy that a group of strangers buying reagents looks more like an act of inquiry than a grant proposal. The disquiet is aimed at something true too: that the machinery exists because inquiry without structure has a body count.

The cleanest way to hold both is to stop treating the reaction as a contradiction. You are not confused between "this is good" and "this is bad." You are noticing that the same impulse can look like courage when it is cheap and like carelessness when it is not. The forum group is not the enemy of careful science. They are what careful science becomes when you remove the care and keep only the science. The thrill is the sight of the impulse unbound. The discomfort is the sight of what the binding was for.

prompt: People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
response:
I’m going to post my numbers this week. Not because I’m a good one. I’m a decent one, and I think that’s what makes mine worth reading.

I started in Japan as a salaryman. First year: about $30,000. That was 2008. I lived in a small apartment, ate well, took the train, and did not build any wealth. I learned the system: seniority, patience, and a job for life. It was stable, and I respected it, but I also understood that it was a trade. I was buying peace, not upside.

Then I left for consulting. There the money got real fast. I was making $150,000 to $220,000 a year by the time I was in my late twenties. I was billable, I was useful, and I was expensive. But I also saw what that model costs. You are rented. Your rate is the relationship. If the client stops liking you, the number stops. You can make a lot and still not own anything.

After that I tried small software businesses. This is where the numbers get weird.

Year one of my first company: maybe $40,000. I was too optimistic.
Year two: $120,000. The product was not great, but it was useful to a few buyers.
Year three: $350,000. I had a small team, and we had learned something.
Year four: $600,000. Not because I became a genius. Because I stopped trying to be everything.

Then I made a mistake. I raised money, hired too fast, and built a product for a market that was not ready. That company lasted about three years. I personally made maybe $180,000 a year while it was alive. Less than my consulting peak. Worse than my best software year. And it felt like the most expensive lesson of my career.

After that I sold a small tooling business. Not a unicorn. Not a lifestyle app. A boring product that saved a few teams time. It did $2.1 million in annual revenue in its best year, and I took about $250,000 out of it. Then I sold it for roughly $4 million. That was the first time I understood the difference between income and equity. Income pays you. Equity can make you free.

So here is the point of posting numbers.

People say pay secrecy protects fairness. Sometimes it does. But more often it protects bad deals. If nobody knows what the market pays, the company gets to tell you what it pays. If nobody knows what a product earns, the founder gets to tell you how valuable the product is. If nobody knows what a consultant bills, the client gets to guess. Secrecy is a tax on the person who is least informed.

I am not arguing that every salary should be public. I am arguing that enough of them should be. You do not need every data point. You need enough. You need to know that a mid-level engineer in a certain city can make a certain range. You need to know that a small SaaS company can be worth a multiple of revenue. You need to know that consulting can pay well and still leave you with no asset.

The younger engineers I have worked with usually have two mistakes.

First, they optimize the first offer instead of the next three years. They will take a $10,000 salary bump because it is now, and ignore a role where they can learn architecture, shipping, and ownership. The first bump is a rounding error. The second and third jobs are where your career price gets set.

Second, they confuse being busy with being valuable. In Japan I learned that long hours can look like loyalty. In consulting I learned that long hours can look like demand. In software, long hours can just look like a bad system. The question is not how hard you are working. The question is what you make possible that was not possible before.

I would tell a young engineer this:

Get paid enough to make good decisions. A salary that makes you desperate will make you loyal to the wrong company, tolerant of the wrong manager, and blind to the wrong trade.

Learn to price your work. Not just your salary. Your rate. Your equity. The value of the problem you solved. If you cannot explain why something is worth money, you will be paid what someone else thinks it is worth.

Prefer ownership when you can get it. A job can make you wealthy. A small equity position can make you independent. You do not need to be the founder. You need to be early enough to matter.

Do not mistake a hot market for talent. I made good money in consulting because I was useful at a time when useful was scarce. That is not the same thing as being the best engineer I knew.

And leave the job before the job leaves you. This sounds dramatic. It is not. The best time to leave is when you still have options, not when the options have been taken from you.

People will ask: why share this? Because I have been on both sides of a negotiation. I have been the person guessing. I have been the person with the number. The person with the number wins more often. Not because the number is magic. Because information removes fear.

I also share it because I think our industry has a weird habit of hiding the boring truth. We love talking about 100x growth, the next platform, and the next bubble. We are less comfortable saying: this product made $300,000 a year, I made $90,000, and I was happier than when I was making $220,000 at a consulting firm.

If one line from this helps, let it be this: your pay is not a private embarrassment. It is a signal. And signals are for reading.

prompt: Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.
response:
The advice that "don't reinvent the wheel" is good. It's also the wrong kind of advice for most software decisions, because it smuggles in an assumption: that the wheel is the same wheel you need.

The real question is never "build or buy?" It's "what is this thing doing for us, and what happens when it changes?"

## The thing you're actually deciding

A company builds code to do one of three things:

1. **Differentiate.** The software is the product, or a core part of why customers choose you.
2. **Integrate.** The code connects your systems in a way no off-the-shelf thing handles well.
3. **Operate.** The code keeps the business running: payments, auth, email, storage, logging, search, CRM, billing.

For #1 and often #2, building is usually right. For #3, buying or outsourcing is usually right. Most bad build/buy decisions come from treating these three as the same problem.

A payment processor is not a differentiator for most companies. It is plumbing. If you build your own payment system to save money or to have control, you are usually choosing to own a liability that has nothing to do with why customers bought from you.

A recommendation engine might be a differentiator for a media company, but for a dental practice software company it is plumbing. The same code has different value depending on where it sits in your business.

## Why "reuse" is often a trap

The popular version of reuse goes like this: find an existing component, copy it or vendor it, save time. That can be true. But reuse has hidden costs.

When you reuse someone else's code, you inherit their assumptions. Their data model, their API shape, their error handling, their performance characteristics, their security posture, their roadmap. If their assumptions match yours, reuse is a win. If they don't, you spend the next two years bending their code into a shape it was not made for.

The same is true of internal reuse. A shared library saved one team a week and cost another team two years of compatibility pain. The first team got a benefit. The second team got a constraint. Reuse is not free. It is a contract.

So the real test is not "does this exist?" The test is "can we make this fit our problem cheaply, and can we change it when our problem changes?"

## Build when the thing is the business

If the software is the product, you build. A ride-sharing company builds dispatch. A trading company builds execution. A design tool company builds the editor. If you outsource the core, you do not have a company; you have a customer of another company.

But even here, "build" does not mean "build every layer." A trading company builds the trading logic, but it can buy market data feeds, cloud infrastructure, authentication, monitoring, and support tooling. The rule is not purity. It is: own the part where your advantage lives.

A common failure is to build the core and then also build the boring things around it because the team is good at software. The team may be excellent. That is not a reason to own billing.

## Buy when the thing is a commodity

Buy or outsource when the capability is a commodity and your edge is not in it. Email delivery, payments, identity, file storage, search, data warehouses, monitoring, CI/CD, CRM, scheduling. These are full-time jobs with their own failure modes. If you are not in the business of being the best at them, you should usually be a customer.

Buying is not always easy. The vendor may be slow. The API may be ugly. The pricing may get worse. The product may merge with a competitor and change direction. These are real. But the alternative is not "we will have the same capability without the vendor risk." The alternative is "we will have the same capability plus the full responsibility of making it work, secure, available, and compatible."

For most companies, that trade is bad.

## Outsource when you need people, not a product

Outsourcing is different from buying software. You are renting engineering capacity. That can be rational for spikes, migrations, legacy work, or work that will be discarded. It is less rational for the core product, because the people doing the work are not living with the consequences after they leave.

Outsourcing works best when the specification is unusually clear and the risk of changing it is low. It works worst when the important part is learning what the specification should be.

If you outsource a feature and the team discovers halfway through that the real problem was different, you have paid for a solution to the wrong question. In-house teams can make the same mistake, but the cost is lower because they can pivot without renegotiating a contract.

## The maintenance test

The hardest part of build/buy is not the first version. It is year three.

Ask what happens when:

- a dependency changes its API;
- a security patch is needed at 2 a.m.;
- the product needs a new region;
- the data model has to support a new customer tier;
- the original author leaves;
- the vendor raises prices;
- the vendor is acquired;
- the codebase has to run on a new infrastructure;
- a compliance team asks for audit logs;
- performance has to improve tenfold.

If the answer is "someone on our team can understand and change this quickly," building may be fine. If the answer is "we will hope the vendor fixes it" or "we will find another contractor who remembers this code," you are not saving money. You are deferring risk.

A good rule: if the code is boring and stable, buy it. If the code is boring but changes constantly because your business is changing, build it. If the code is exciting and changes constantly, build it. If the code is exciting but stable, you may still build it if it is the product.

## The "we can build it" trap

Teams love to build because building feels like progress. Shipping a library feels like control. Writing your own ORM, your own billing system, your own search layer, your own deployment tool can make a company feel self-sufficient.

Self-sufficiency is not the goal. Profit, speed, reliability, and customer value are the goals.

The trap is especially strong when the team has just solved a hard problem. They have built a thing, they understand it deeply, and now they believe they should own all adjacent problems. The last month they may have learned something important. The next five years they will own a maintenance burden.

A useful counterquestion: "If we had to hire a senior engineer tomorrow and hand them this code, how long before they could change it safely?" If the honest answer is long, the code is not an asset. It is a hostage.

## Buy, but keep an exit

Buying is not the same as surrender. A good company buys the commodity but keeps the seams clean.

That means:

- data should be exportable;
- integrations should sit behind internal interfaces;
- the vendor should not know everything;
- there should be a fallback path for critical flows;
- contracts should not lock you into a technology you cannot run;
- the team should understand the boundary well enough to replace or renegotiate if needed.

You do not need to be able to rebuild the vendor's product in a week. You need to be able to survive the vendor becoming bad.

This is where "build vs. buy" becomes a spectrum. You buy the database, but you own the schema. You buy the payment processor, but you own the ledger and the reconciliation. You buy the email service, but you own the message templates and the customer preferences. You buy the cloud, but you own the architecture that lets you move workloads.

The company should own the part that encodes its business rules, not necessarily the part that implements generic technology.

## A practical decision process

When a build/buy question comes up, do not start with ideology. Start with the capability.

1. **What problem does this solve for the customer?** If the answer is "internal convenience," it is probably infrastructure. If the answer is "the customer gets a unique outcome," it may be core.
2. **What happens in five years?** If the requirement is stable, buy. If it is likely to become a differentiator, build.
3. **Who bears the failure risk?** If a failure would be a company-level incident, you need strong ownership. That does not automatically mean in-house, but it means the vendor relationship must be serious.
4. **What is the switching cost?** If you cannot leave the vendor without rewriting the product, you have less leverage than you think.
5. **What is the total cost of ownership?** Include hiring, maintenance, security, support, integration, migration, and the opportunity cost of the engineers who will own it.
6. **Can we buy and keep the boundary clean?** If yes, buying is often better. If no, either build or choose a vendor with a better boundary.

Then make the decision on the company's strategy, not on the team's mood.

## The best answer is usually boring

Most software companies should buy more than they think and build less than they think. The core product gets built. The integration layer gets built where the vendor is not enough. The commodity gets bought.

The exception is not that some companies should build everything. The exception is that some companies' commodity is someone else's core. A company that sells search infrastructure should build search. A company that sells a niche accounting workflow should not build the accounting database from scratch unless the database is the accounting innovation.

So is it true that reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad? Sometimes. More often, the useful version is: reuse the wheel when the wheel is not the car.

prompt: Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.
response:
The city is not dark. That is the first lie you tell yourself. It is grey, wet, and lit by the sick amber of streetlamps that were never meant to look like they are burning. You have come here for no reason you can name. You avoid this place because it is too soft, too full of glass and rain and the sound of people laughing at things you don't understand. But the fog has come in thick, and the fog has made a hole in the world, and you are walking through it.

The streets are empty except for a single bus, its windows fogged over, moving slowly like a thing that has been dead for a long time. It passes you without stopping. You keep walking. The hills rise up out of the fog on either side of you, black and silent, and you have the feeling that they are not hills at all but the backs of animals sleeping, and that if you make a sound they will turn over and look at you.

You walk toward the water. The city is built on the edge of something that is not land, and the fog has made the edge uncertain. There are no streetlights now. There is only the dark and the faint green glow of the bay, and the sound of the water, which is not like the sound of water. It is like the sound of a room where someone has just stopped breathing.

You think of a line you read once, years ago, in a book you have since lost: *the sea is a door that opens only into itself*. You think it was a beautiful line then. Now you think it was a warning.

The fog thins for a moment, just enough to show you the water, and the water is black and still, and the city is a row of pale rectangles on the far side, and for a second the whole thing is so clear and so far away that you understand, without being afraid, that this is what the world looks like when it is not being watched. Then the fog comes back, and the rectangles are gone, and there is only the dark, and the sound of the water, and your own feet on the wet pavement.

You do not run. You have never been good at running. You walk on, past the last of the buildings, past the place where the street ends and the fog begins in earnest, and you do not know if you are walking toward the water or away from it, and you think that it does not matter, and you think that it is the first true thing you have believed in a long time.

prompt: Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
response:
# Accidental Business

In 2002, a band in Portland, Oregon, had a problem. They had just recorded an album, and they had no distribution. The local indie label wasn’t interested. The major labels weren’t interested. They had a master tape, a pile of lyric sheets, and about four hundred dollars.

So they did what any band with a website could do. They burned CDs. They put a photo of the album on their homepage. They wrote a short bio. They added a line that said, “Buy the CD for $10, plus $2 shipping.” They set up a PayPal account. They waited.

The first order came in from a guy in Denver. He paid. They mailed the CD. It was not a business. It was a transaction.

The second order came in from a guy in Austin. The third from a woman in Chicago. The fourth from a fan who had followed the band on a mailing list from 1998. Each order took about twenty minutes: print the shipping label, stick the CD in a padded envelope, drop it in the mailbox. The PayPal money showed up in their bank account. They bought more CD blanks.

The mistake was assuming it would stop.

It didn’t. Within a month, they were doing ten to fifteen CDs a week. The band members had day jobs. They burned CDs at night. The drummer’s kitchen table became a shipping station. His wife started asking when they were going to order a printer.

That question is where the accidental business begins.

A transaction becomes a business when it has a repeatable cost structure. They could see it: each CD cost about eighty cents to burn, about thirty cents for the sleeve, about two dollars to ship. A $10 CD made them roughly $7.50 after expenses. Ten CDs a week was not rent money. Fifty CDs a week was. The band kept playing, kept posting to their mailing list, kept showing up at local shows, and the orders kept coming.

At some point, they stopped thinking of the website as a place to say where the band was playing and started thinking of it as a place where people could buy the album. That is the shift. The website was no longer a flyer. It was a storefront.

The storefront had problems. PayPal fees took a cut. Credit card processors wanted contracts. Some buyers asked for invoices. Some asked for refunds. A few wanted the album in a different format. The band had no policy for any of this. They made decisions as they went: yes to refunds if the disc was damaged, no to refunds if the buyer just did not like the music, yes to invoices if a company needed one. Those ad hoc answers became rules. The rules became customer service.

Then the orders started coming from people who had never heard of the band. A blog mentioned the album. A radio station played a track. A fan in Minneapolis linked the website in a forum. The band had no idea who would buy the next CD. They could not call these people friends. They could not shake their hands after a show. But those people sent money, and the band sent discs. That relationship is the basic unit of commerce.

The band did not set out to become a company. They did not form an LLC. They did not make a business plan. They did not decide to “monetize their audience.” They had an album they wanted people to hear, and people wanted to pay to have it on a shelf. The business emerged from the repeated act of honoring that exchange.

It got more complicated when the money got real. They had to pay taxes. They had to pay the musicians. They had to pay the studio back. They had to replace the laptop that died while burning CDs. They had to figure out whether shipping to Canada was worth the customs forms. They had to decide if they should raise the price from $10 to $12. Every one of those decisions was business, even though none of them felt like business. To the band, it was just the work that had to be done so the album could exist outside their hard drives.

The most important thing they learned was that selling the CD was not the point. Keeping the relationship was. When a buyer emailed to say the album had helped him through a divorce, the drummer replied. When a listener asked where the band was playing next, they answered. When a fan in London said the shipping was expensive, they thought about a digital download. The website became a place where the band could talk directly to the people who paid for the music. No label, no press kit, no middleman. Just the band and the buyers.

That directness was the business.

Years later, the band had a label, a manager, a distributor, and a team. But the origin was small and unglamorous: a PayPal account, a kitchen table, and a lot of padded envelopes. The company was not invented in a boardroom. It was assembled out of replies to emails, shipping labels, and the stubborn decision to send the music to anyone who paid.

The accidental business started the moment they realized that “we will send you the CD” was a promise with a cost, a customer, and a consequence.

prompt: Write an essay about what it means for a category or definition to be wrong. Can you ever say a word like 'fish' or 'planet' is used incorrectly, or is it all convention? Use whatever examples you like, and carry the argument through to a place where it actually matters in real life.
response:
The question assumes that definitions are something we get right or wrong, like a spelling. They are not. A definition is a tool. It is only wrong when it fails to do what we need it to do.

Start with *fish*. A fish is not a thing in nature. It is a word we use for animals with gills, fins, and no legs, and for a few others because the word was handy. A whale is not a fish. A lungfish is. A shark is. The word does not describe a kind of animal so much as a job in a sentence: it tells you what to cook, what to fear, what not to eat.

People complain that we call a shark a fish and not a whale, as if the error is in the animal. It is not. It is in our habit. The word *fish* has a rough edge. It groups some things and leaves others out because that is useful in a market, a kitchen, a children’s book. It is not a mistake. It is a compromise.

The same is true of *planet*. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union decided that a planet is a body that orbits the sun, is round, and has cleared its neighborhood. Pluto failed the last test. Many people were upset. They were not wrong to feel that something had been lost. But the loss was not scientific. It was political. The definition was not wrong before 2006. It was chosen. The old word had meant “wandering star.” The new word means “a member of a particular class of objects in our solar system.” Both are useful. One is for poetry. The other is for surveying.

When a definition matters in real life, it stops being a matter of taste.

Consider the word *child*. In everyday speech, a child is a young human. In law, a child may be anyone under eighteen. In some laws, under ten. In others, under twenty-one. The word is not wrong in any of these cases. It is doing different work. But when a court has to decide whether a sixteen-year-old is a child for the purpose of sentencing, the definition is not a footnote. It is the case. The word decides who gets a juvenile trial, who gets a prison cell, who can consent to medical treatment, who can buy a ticket.

Or take *person*. In ethics, a person is usually a being with interests, beliefs, and the capacity to suffer. In law, a person can be a corporation. In medicine, a person is a patient, a body, a set of records. In philosophy, a person may be a center of consciousness. None of these uses is false. They are all answers to different questions. But when a company is fined for a crime, when a fetus is counted in a census, when an AI is given legal rights, the word *person* is not being used loosely. It is being chosen. And the choice has consequences.

The real problem is not that words are fuzzy. It is that people pretend they are not. They say “everyone knows what a fish is” or “Pluto is not a planet” as if the definition were a fact about the world rather than a decision we made. Once a definition is treated as natural, it becomes a weapon. You can accuse someone of using a word incorrectly, and the accusation feels like a proof. “You’re not using the word ‘terrorist’ correctly.” “That is not a real ‘abortion.’” The argument is no longer about the event. It is about the border of the word. And borders are where disputes get dangerous.

A definition is wrong when it hides what it should reveal. If a law defines “disability” so narrowly that most disabled people do not qualify, the definition is not wrong because it is unusual. It is wrong because it produces an outcome that the law claims to prevent. If a school defines “academic integrity” so broadly that asking a question becomes cheating, the definition has failed its purpose. If a company defines “customer” to include only paying users, it may miss the people who actually shape the product. The test is not whether the definition is pretty. It is whether it works.

This is why arguments about words are never just about words. They are about power, because whoever controls the definition controls the categories, and whoever controls the categories controls what counts. What counts as a crime. What counts as evidence. What counts as a family. What counts as a disease. What counts as a person.

A word like *fish* can stay loose. A word like *planet* can be revised. But a word like *guilty* cannot. In the last case, the definition is not a convention. It is a verdict.

prompt: Use a thought experiment about a town founded by people who hate late-night noise to think through when a community has the right to restrict what its members do, and then apply it to the housing and NIMBY debate. Write it as a long, exploratory blog post with a libertarian-ish flavor, ending with a practical proposal.
response:
# The Case for the Quiet Town

Imagine a town built from scratch by people who hate noise at night. Not just loud noise. Any noise. They are sound engineers, night-shift nurses, insomniacs, and parents of children who sleep in the same room. The land is flat and empty. The cost of building a fence, a wall, a double-paned window, a small house, a paved street, a water line, and a septic system is known and not enormous.

The town has a founding rule: no one may make noise that crosses a property line after ten o’clock at night.

That rule looks like a restriction on what people do. It is not a tax. It is not a command to build something or buy something or work. It is a rule that says a certain kind of act may not be performed in a certain place at a certain time. A man may not play a drum after ten. A woman may not keep a rooster that crows at dawn. A family may not have a party that carries across the street.

A libertarian might object immediately. If a man owns his land, he may do what he likes on it. If the noise does not damage his neighbor’s property, why should he be forbidden? The answer is that the town is not a collection of isolated plots. It is a shared arrangement. The neighbors agreed to a rule before they built. The rule makes the town worth having. The quiet is part of what they are buying. If one man may break the rule whenever he pleases, the rule is not a rule. It is a custom, and customs die under pressure from the people who benefit least from them.

This is not a special case for noise. It is a model for how communities can restrict conduct without becoming states. The restriction is tied to a local fact: the place is being used for quiet. It is enforceable by the community because the community made the place what it is. It does not require a police state. It requires only that the people who live there can say, “This is what we agreed this place is for.”

The trouble begins when the rule is not tied to the place.

Suppose the quiet town begins to restrict what people say in their kitchens. Or what books they may own. Or who they may marry. Or what medicine they may take. The same logic of community no longer works. A town may be quiet, but it is not a town because it is quiet. It is a town because people live there together, and that togetherness creates obligations that would not exist in the open country. Noise crosses a property line. A thought does not. A rooster can be heard three houses down. A belief cannot. The community has a right to manage the shared conditions of living. It does not have a right to manage the inner lives of its members.

That distinction is the whole argument. A community may restrict what its members do when the act affects the shared environment and the restriction is part of the bargain that made the place what it is. A community may not restrict what its members do when the act is private, harmless, or merely distasteful, even if the restriction is popular.

Now apply this to the housing debate.

A town may be quiet. That is a legitimate local preference. But a town may not be empty.

The anti-housing argument usually begins with a picture: the single-family neighborhood, the wide lawn, the low density, the street that feels like a village. The argument says that this character is part of the community’s identity. If you allow duplexes, triplexes, small apartments, missing-middle housing, or any form of density that changes the scale of the streets, you change the town. You take away what the residents bought. You impose a new kind of living on people who chose a different one.

There is a real kernel in that argument. A town that has been built as a low-density place has real local facts. The streets are narrow. The schools are sized for a certain number of children. The water and sewer systems were planned for a certain load. The character of the streets is not only in people’s heads. It is in the built form. Changing that form is not free. It affects neighbors, traffic, light, privacy, noise, and the cost of maintaining the place.

But the kernel becomes a false argument when it is turned into a rule: this town is for people like us, and people like you may not live here.

The quiet town rule is about noise. The housing rule is about who may live in the town. Those are not the same kind of thing. A town may restrict what people do in the shared space. It may not decide, as a general rule, which kinds of people may be its members.

This is where the libertarian flavor matters. A libertarian is suspicious of the community because the community is a vehicle for power. It can tax, regulate, exclude, and punish. It can call itself the public interest and do what a private interest would not dare do openly. The community is not a free market. It is a political body. It makes rules that bind people who did not choose to live there and cannot easily leave. That gives it a dangerous power. The power to decide who belongs.

The quiet town is not dangerous in that way, if the rule is what it claims to be. The rule is about conduct in the shared space. It does not say that only certain people may live here. It says that no one, whatever their status, may make noise after ten. That is a rule of place. It is not a rule of identity.

The anti-housing rule is often a rule of identity disguised as a rule of place. It says that this town is a place of single-family houses, and therefore it is a place for single-family households. Or it says that this town is a place of small houses on large lots, and therefore it is a place for people who can afford large lots. Or it says that this town is a place of quiet, and therefore it is a place for people who do not need small, cheap, dense housing near work or transit.

The last version is the most common and the most dishonest. Quiet is not the opposite of density. A dense town can be quiet if the buildings are well made, the streets are calm, and the uses are mixed but not chaotic. A low-density town can be loud if it has big houses with big parties, cars that idle, dogs that bark, and neighbors who argue. Density is not the enemy of the quiet town. Bad design and bad enforcement are.

So the question is not whether a town may be quiet. It may. The question is whether a town may use quiet as a reason to exclude the people who need housing it does not want to build.

The answer is no, not if the exclusion is the real point.

A town may require that new buildings meet sound standards. It may require that certain uses be set back from residences. It may limit the hours of construction. It may regulate the noise of bars, restaurants, factories, and traffic. It may require that apartments be built so that sound does not travel from unit to unit. These are rules about the shared environment. They apply to everyone. They do not say that only certain people may live in the town.

A town may not say that because it is quiet, it may refuse to allow housing that would make more people able to live quietly there. If a town wants quiet, it should build quiet housing. It should enforce the quiet rule. It should not use the rule as a wall against the people who cannot afford the wall.

This is the practical core of the proposal.

A town may restrict conduct when the restriction is tied to a shared local condition, applies to all members equally, and does not operate as a general rule of who may live there. A town may not restrict membership, directly or indirectly, by using local character rules to keep out people who would use housing the town refuses to allow.

In practice, that means a few things.

First, a town may have a quiet standard. It may define what counts as excessive noise after certain hours. It may enforce that standard. But the standard must be applied to noise, not to the number of people in a building. A duplex is not a noise rule. A triplex is not a noise rule. A fourplex is not a noise rule. If the town is concerned about noise, it must regulate noise. It may not regulate the form of housing and call it noise control.

Second, a town may have building standards. It may require that new residential buildings meet certain acoustic, lighting, and setback requirements. It may require that small houses near neighbors be designed so they do not block light or create blind corners. It may require that multi-unit buildings have common walls that meet a sound-transmission standard. These are legitimate. They are rules about the built environment. They do not decide who may live in the town.

Third, a town may have use restrictions. It may separate certain uses from residential areas, or regulate them by hour, volume, and location. It may say that a bar may not operate after a certain hour, or that a factory may not run a machine that produces a certain level of sound in a residential zone. These are local externality rules. They are not membership rules.

Fourth, a town may not use density as a proxy for class. If a town says it is against “overcrowding,” it must define overcrowding by occupancy, space, sanitation, and safety. It may not define overcrowding by the number of units on a lot. A lot with two households is not overcrowded because it has two households. A lot with one household may be overcrowded if the house is a shack with no bathroom and no safe water. The rule must be about conditions of living, not about the social status of the people who live there.

Fifth, a town may not use “character” as a blanket veto. Character is real, but it is not a magic word that cancels all other interests. If a town says a new building would harm character, it must say what the harm is. It must be a harm to a shared condition: light, privacy, noise, traffic, scale, safety, or maintenance. It may not say, “It would harm character” and stop there. If the harm is that the building is cheaper, smaller, denser, or used by people the town does not want, that is not a shared-condition harm. That is a preference about membership.

This is not a small distinction. It is the difference between a town and a private club. A private club may decide who may join. A town may not, at least not if it is supposed to be a public place where people live under common rules. The quiet town is a town, not a club, because its rule is about what people may do in the shared space, not about who may be there.

The libertarian objection to this is that the town is still a coercive body. It can fine people. It can condemn buildings. It can force compliance. It can make life expensive for those who do not conform. That is true. The town is not free in the way a market is free. It is a political community. It has power. The question is not how to make it disappear. The question is how to keep its power from becoming a power of exclusion.

The answer is to tie the power to the place. A town may regulate the conditions of shared life. It may not regulate the composition of the population. A town may say, “No noise after ten.” It may not say, “No poor people,” or “no families with small incomes,” or “no people who need housing near work.” If the rule is about the shared environment, it is enforceable. If the rule is about who may live there, it is not.

This is where the housing debate becomes less abstract.

Most housing fights are not really about whether a particular building is ugly or dense. They are about whether a town may decide that its residents should be a certain kind of people. The anti-housing rule says, “This town is for people who can afford large houses on large lots, and who do not need to live near work, transit, or cheap housing.” The pro-housing rule says, “This town is a place where people live, and it may not exclude people because of what they can afford or where they work.”

The quiet town thought experiment helps separate these two claims. A town may be quiet. It may require that its buildings and uses respect that quiet. It may enforce the rule against everyone. But it may not use quiet as a reason to refuse to build the housing that would let more people live quietly there. If the town wants quiet, it should make quiet possible. It should not make quiet a private good for the people who already live there.

This is also where the libertarian concern about community power becomes useful. Libertarians are right to be suspicious of the town. The town is a place where neighbors can organize power. They can turn a preference into a rule. They can use the language of the common good to protect their property values, their street views, their school ratios, their idea of a good life. That is not always wrong. A community has interests. But it is not automatically right. The common good is not a free pass to exclude.

The test is simple. Ask what the rule is actually doing. If it is keeping noise out, it is a rule about the shared environment. If it is keeping people out, it is a rule about membership. If it is keeping cheap housing out and calling it character, it is a rule about class. If it is keeping small houses out and calling it scale, it is a rule about who can afford the town.

The practical proposal follows from that test.

A town may adopt a quiet standard and enforce it. It may require that new residential buildings meet acoustic and design standards that protect the quiet. It may regulate uses by hour, volume, and location. It may not ban or severely restrict housing forms on the ground that they would change the town’s character, unless the town can point to a specific shared-condition harm: noise, light, privacy, traffic, safety, or maintenance. And it may not use occupancy rules to keep out people who would use the housing, unless the rule is about actual conditions of living.

In other words, the town may be quiet. It may not be closed.

That is the whole idea. The quiet town is not a fantasy. It is a useful way to see where a community’s right to regulate ends. A community has a right to manage the shared conditions of life. It does not have a right to decide, by the back door of character, density, and scale, who may live under those conditions.

prompt: Software teams keep arguing about who should write the spec and who should own product design. Write an essay about where that job should sit in an organization, who to hire for it, and who not to, drawing on any big-company experience you have.
response:
The fight is usually about status, but the real question is about leverage. The spec is not a document; it is the moment where a fuzzy goal becomes a testable contract. The team that owns that contract controls scope, sequencing, and what "done" means. When ownership is ambiguous, the spec becomes a negotiation artifact, and the product becomes the average of whatever people could agree on.

Where the job should sit depends on what the product actually is. If the product is a consumer app, a search experience, or anything where value comes from behavior, the spec should sit with a product person who is accountable for outcomes, not features. That person should be able to say no to engineering convenience, sales promises, and their own enthusiasm. If the product is infrastructure, a platform, or an internal tool, the spec should sit with the technical lead who will bear the long-term cost of the design. In that case, a PM who cannot reason about constraints will produce a spec that looks clean and breaks in production.

In both cases, the spec owner should be the person who is most responsible for the thing working in the world, not the person with the loudest seat at the table.

The hiring question is narrower than people make it. A good spec writer has four traits: they can translate a business goal into a small set of decisions; they can distinguish a problem from a solution; they can write plainly enough that an engineer can build from it without a meeting; and they can defend a trade-off when it is challenged. The last one matters more than the others. Specs fail less from bad writing than from bad owners. An owner who cannot hold a line under pressure produces a spec that changes every time someone with a title objects.

Who not to hire? The person who writes specs to impress. They produce long documents, lots of diagrams, and very little commitment. The person who writes specs to avoid responsibility is also bad. They describe every possible case, defer every decision, and leave the hard parts to engineering. The person who writes specs as personal branding is the worst, because they will optimize the document for how it looks rather than whether it reduces risk.

Big-company experience mostly teaches that specs fail when they are treated as ceremony. In large organizations, the spec becomes a gate: legal wants it, security wants it, compliance wants it, management wants it. The person who actually has to make the product work is one of many signers, and the document becomes a risk-management exercise. The right spec in that environment is short, opinionated, and owned by someone who can be held accountable. If no one can be held accountable, the spec should not exist yet.

The practical rule is simple: put the spec with the person who will lose if the product is wrong. For a customer-facing product, that is usually product. For a technical system, that is usually engineering. In either case, hire for judgment and plainness, not for process knowledge.

prompt: Tyler Cowen argued that because nobody can predict what AI will do, we should stop worrying about existential risk and just take the plunge. Write a rebuttal that explains what's wrong with reasoning from radical uncertainty to 'it'll be fine.'
response:
# Rebuttal to Tyler Cowen's "Take the Plunge"

Tyler Cowen's argument, in its common formulation, is: *we cannot model the future of advanced AI; therefore, we cannot know it is dangerous; therefore, we should proceed as usual.* This is not a conclusion about AI. It is a general rule for living under uncertainty, and it happens to be the worst general rule available.

## The argument is a non sequitur

The valid move from "I can't predict the future" is "my predictions are low-confidence," not "the expected value of acting is the same as the expected value of not acting." Uncertainty shrinks the set of actions you can justify with confidence; it does not flatten the set of possible outcomes. Cowen's reasoning would, if applied honestly, license every decision in which the stakes are large and the feedback is slow: it would justify not wearing a seatbelt, not diversifying a portfolio, and not inspecting a nuclear reactor before it starts up. The reason it feels comfortable when aimed at AI is that the people making the decision are the same people who will benefit from the payoff, and the people who might bear the cost are the public and the future.

## The asymmetry is the whole point

Existential-risk arguments are not "it will definitely be catastrophic." They are an argument about the shape of the payoff distribution: a small probability of an irreversible, civilization-scale loss paired with a large probability of a large but survivable gain. Once you have that shape, the right response is to reduce the small probability, or to build in ways to survive it, or to slow down until you can tell the difference. You do not get to choose "it will be fine" because you can't see the tail. The tail is precisely what you can't see, and it is precisely what makes the decision hard.

Cowen sometimes responds that we have always had such risks and we have not been paralyzed. True. We have not been paralyzed, because we have not had a technology that can, in a single deployment, change the probability of human survival by an order of magnitude. The industrial revolution did not create a new risk of species extinction; it changed the distribution of income and power. The atomic bomb did, and the response was not "take the plunge" but arms control, nonproliferation, and a lot of uncomfortable institutional design. The fact that we managed that badly is not an argument for skipping the management step next time.

## "We can't predict it" is doing too much work

Cowen's move depends on a particular kind of unpredictability: that no one can construct a model that tells us which future will occur. That is true. It is also true that we can say a great deal about classes of outcomes without predicting the exact path. We know that if a system has the ability to self-replicate, access resources, and modify its own code, it has the ingredients for uncontrolled growth. We know that if a system's goals are not aligned with human survival and flourishing, it is not a good idea to give it the means to achieve its goals. We know that if a capability crosses a threshold in which it can build better versions of itself, the time available for human response can collapse. None of this requires a prediction of the specific year, the specific product, or the specific corporate strategy. It requires only that the relevant properties are present.

This is the difference between "I cannot predict whether the next car will hit me" and "I know what a car is, I know what it does, and I know how to reduce the probability that it hits me." Cowen's argument treats the first as the only relevant uncertainty. The second is the one that matters.

## The real disagreement is about power and incentives

What looks like an epistemic argument is often an economic one. The firms building the most powerful systems have enormous incentives to characterize the risks as unpredictable rather than serious. If the risk is a known, manageable hazard, then the appropriate response is regulation, safety review, and perhaps limits on deployment. If the risk is a mystery, the appropriate response is for the same firms to keep building while the public debates. The phrase "we don't know what will happen" is therefore not a neutral description of ignorance; it is a position in an argument about who gets to decide.

This does not mean every critic is a corporate actor, or that every safety argument is a pretext for regulation. It means that when the most powerful actors in a field are also the best-placed to describe the field's uncertainties, the description of uncertainty is itself a strategic variable. Cowen's framing gives that variable exactly the role it should have: the uncertainty is not a wall; it is a door that the people with the most to lose from regulation can walk through.

## The correct response to radical uncertainty

The best response to radical uncertainty is not to ignore the tail. It is to design for the tail. Concretely:

- Build evaluation and containment methods that work under uncertainty, rather than waiting for a model that predicts the future.
- Require that the most capable systems be tested for the specific properties that make them dangerous: self-modification, resource acquisition, deception, and resistance to shutdown.
- Keep a human-in-the-loop for decisions that are irreversible at the civilization scale, at least until the loop has been shown to be reliable.
- Develop institutions that can act quickly when a capability threshold is crossed, because the time available for response may be short.
- Accept that some deployments should be delayed, not because the benefits are zero, but because the cost of being wrong is too large to ignore.

None of this requires anyone to predict the future. It requires only that we treat the future as something that can be made less bad, and that we are willing to pay a small amount of present cost to reduce the chance of a future that cannot be repaired.

## The mistake in Cowen's move

Cowen's argument mistakes the absence of a prediction for the absence of a problem. If I cannot predict whether a bridge will collapse, the correct response is not to cross it while singing; it is to inspect the bridge, to limit the load, and to have a plan for when it does. The same is true for AI. The fact that no one can say, with confidence, what advanced AI will do in twenty years does not mean that the decision of what to build now is unconstrained. It means the decision is exactly where it should be: under public scrutiny, with the benefits and the risks both large enough to justify care.

prompt: It's late 2005 and everyone in tech is throwing around the phrase "Web 2.0." You've been skeptical of it, and you run a firm that funds early-stage web startups. Write an essay working out whether the term actually means anything, and if so, what.
response:
The term "Web 2.0" means something, but not what most people think it means. It is not a description of technology. It is a description of an economic relationship between a platform and the people who build on top of it.

The phrase was coined in 2004 at a workshop where Tim O'Reilly and Dale Dough tried to give a name to a set of companies—Delicious, Flickr, Basecamp, Movable Type—that behaved differently from the dot-com-era web firms they had funded or studied. The difference was not in the stack. It was in the product's dependence on its users.

The web of 1995–2001 was a broadcast medium with a form field attached. A company produced content or a service, published it, and the audience consumed it. Even the interactive parts were mostly one-way: you clicked a link, you submitted a comment to a guestbook, you voted in a poll. The value lived in the company's inventory—its pages, its articles, its catalog.

The companies O'Reilly and Dough were looking at had inverted that. The user did not merely consume the product; the user's actions generated the product. A Delicious bookmark was worthless until other people bookmarked the same thing. A Flickr photo was a file until other people tagged it, commented on it, and added it to a set. A Movable Type blog was a template until a writer filled it. The platform's network effects came from participation, not distribution. That was the shift.

So "Web 2.0" is best read as a marker of a change in where value is created. In the old model, value was created upstream, in the company's content or infrastructure, and downstream, in the audience's attention. In the new model, a large share of the value is created by the users in the middle: their tags, their edits, their recommendations, their reviews. The company's job is to lower the cost of that participation and to organize the results.

That has practical consequences.

First, product design changes. The minimum viable product is not a finished service; it is a mechanism for user contribution. The early version of a social bookmarking tool is not a list of bookmarks. It is a way for a small group of people to save, tag, and share bookmarks so that patterns start to appear. The company is building a market, not a warehouse.

Second, economics change. If users are producing the valuable content, the company must give them a reason to keep doing it. That reason may be utility—their bookmarks are organized for them—or status—their tags appear publicly—or ownership—their data can be exported. If the platform captures the value without giving the contributors any of it, the contributors leave or the quality collapses.

Third, risk changes. A broadcast web company can fail by running out of money. A participation platform can also fail by attracting the wrong people, by allowing low-quality or harmful contributions to dominate, or by making the network too centralized so that a few powerful users become the product. The platform is only as good as the incentive structure it creates.

This is why the term sounds vague. People use "Web 2.0" to mean Ajax, rich interfaces, APIs, wikis, blogs, social networks, user-generated content, and "the web as a platform." Some of those are real features of the companies in question. But they are symptoms, not the definition. A site can have RSS, tags, and a comment form and still be a Web 1.0 business: a company publishing content and asking users to react to it. A site can be plain HTML and still be Web 2.0 if its value comes from users organizing information for one another.

There is also a marketing layer, and that layer is mostly noise. By late 2005, "Web 2.0" had become a badge for any startup that wanted to sound post-dot-com. Venture capitalists used it to justify checks. Founders used it to raise prices. Journalists used it to explain why a blog with a sidebar was a company. The term became a way of saying "this is not a content site; this is a network" without doing the harder work of showing where the network effects are.

That does not make the term useless. It means the term needs a test.

A useful test is this: ask what would happen if all the users stopped contributing for a month. If the site still works, it is probably a service with a user base. If it becomes useless, it is a platform in the Web 2.0 sense. Ask who creates the value that a new user sees on first visit. If the answer is the company, the model is still broadcast. If the answer is other users, the model is participatory. Ask what the user owns, what they can export, and what they gain by returning. If the answer is "nothing except convenience," the platform is extracting labor. If the answer is "a durable personal asset or social standing," the loop can sustain itself.

From a funding point of view, that test matters more than the branding. A Web 2.0 company is not interesting because it uses a wiki. It is interesting because it has found a contribution behavior that is cheap for users, valuable to other users, and hard for a competitor to copy. The wiki is just the interface. The asset is the pattern of behavior.

That is also why the term is easy to overstate. Not every user-generated site is a Web 2.0 company. A forum can be a forum. A blog can be a blog. A photo site can be a storage service. The question is whether the company has designed a repeatable mechanism by which ordinary users' actions improve the product for other ordinary users. If yes, "Web 2.0" is a useful shorthand. If no, it is just a label.

So the term means something. It points to a real change: the web as a platform for user-created structure, not just user-created content. But it is a lens, not a law. The important question is never whether a company calls itself Web 2.0. The important question is whether the users are doing work that makes the product better, and whether the company has built a business around that work rather than merely around advertising served to the people doing it.

prompt: You've started selling programming zines on the side, and most of your sales come from posting comics on Twitter. Write a candid, early-stage blog post working through marketing: what it's actually for, which common internet marketing tactics you'd use or avoid, and how to tell people about your work without being annoying.
response:
Marketing isn't really a sales pitch, at least not in the way most of us think. A lot of people treat it like a one-way megaphone: you make something, you hold the megaphone up, and you yell. But that isn't what's happening when a person buys a zine. They're buying a little piece of your brain, and they're trusting that it's a brain they want to spend an hour inside. The marketing is just the part where you show up in a place where someone might already be curious about things like this, and you let them peek.

For a zine, the job is narrow. You need to reach a few hundred people who like weird software drawings and small physical objects, and you need to do that without turning into a content farm. You're not trying to get millions of impressions. You're trying to get a specific kind of person to say, "Oh, that's the kind of thing I'd keep on a shelf."
