A vote on a bill is public and interpretable in public terms. A moral decision is frequently private, partial, and shaped by information no outside observer possesses.

This means the moral dataset would be full of noise that the congressional dataset largely avoids. The algorithm would not merely be finding morality. It would be finding whatever regularities survive the gap between behavior and moral quality.

## The scale problem

Even with clean data, the method might produce several plausible scales instead of one.

In politics, the left-right axis often dominates because parties, coalitions, and issues organize themselves around a central conflict. Morality is not organized that way. It is multidimensional. Honesty may not align with generosity. Loyalty may conflict with impartiality. Compassion may pull against accountability. A person can be kind to friends and harsh to strangers. Another can be scrupulously honest and deeply uncharitable.

A single-axis moral scale would force those dimensions together. It would ask which pattern is strongest, not which is most true. The result might be a scale of social approval, self-discipline, risk tolerance, or conformity. Those are real human differences, but none of them is obviously "good."

Imagine a dataset in which people who tell the truth also punish norm violators, refuse special favors, and follow rules even when they are inconvenient. The method might produce a scale from flexible to rigid. That scale would be statistically meaningful. It would not be a moral discovery.

## The reference class problem

The congressional scale works because the population is defined: members of the House. The moral version needs a reference class, and the answer changes depending on which one you choose.

Within a corporation, a moral scale might rank employees by reliability, candor, and willingness to take responsibility. Within a family, it might rank members by fairness to younger siblings. Within a city, it might rank residents by how often they help strangers. The scale that fits one group may mislead in another. A person who is generous to family and exploitative to outsiders may look good at home and bad in public. A person who follows rules carefully but lacks sympathy may score well on institutional data and poorly on human decency.

There is no neutral population that settles the question. The algorithm would inherit the values of the sample.

## The motivation problem

The congressional method assumes that votes reveal preferences. Moral behavior is not so cleanly tied to preference.

People do good things for bad reasons. They do bad things for good reasons. They perform virtue. They avoid vice because it is socially embarrassing, not because they care. They help because they enjoy power over the person being helped. They punish because they feel righteous. They lie to protect someone. They tell the truth to settle an argument.

A statistical model sees the act. It may infer a stable trait. But the trait may be a strategy, not a character. The most reliable cooperators in a dataset might be people who know how cooperation is rewarded. The most reliable rule-followers might be people who fear detection. The scale would measure moral performance, not moral quality.

This is the deepest difficulty. Goodness is not just a pattern of choices. It is a pattern of choices made for the right reasons, under the right understanding, with the right sensitivity to others. Statistics can detect regularity. It cannot easily detect worth.

## What could work

A purely behavioral method would be too weak, but a hybrid might be possible.

We could combine observed choices with minimal moral judgments. Not grand theories, but local evaluations: in this situation, helping was better than refusing; in that one, honesty was better than comfort; here, punishment was excessive; there, leniency was dangerous. These judgments would be noisy and contestable, but they would give the model some information about which choices are better, not just which are common.

The method would still not tell us what goodness is. It would tell us what a given community, in given circumstances, treats as better. That is valuable. Much moral disagreement is not about whether choices matter, but about which considerations count and how much. If we could map those patterns, we could see where a community's intuitions are coherent and where they contradict each other.

The output would be something like a moral coordinate system. Not a single axis, but a set of dimensions: fairness, honesty, care, loyalty, accountability, impartiality, self-restraint, courage. A person would not be "good" or "bad" but would have a profile. A situation would be located in the same space. We could then ask whether the person's profile fits the demands of the situation.

This is less magical than the congressional method, but more honest. It does not pretend that goodness can be inferred from behavior alone. It uses behavior to test moral claims, not to generate them from nothing.

## Why the congressional metaphor is still useful

The real lesson from ideal point estimation is not that morality is waiting to be discovered in the data. It is that large amounts of choice can reveal structure that no one explicitly announced.

People do not walk around saying, "My moral ideal point is 0.62." But their choices may still line up in ways that are informative. If a person says one thing and chooses another, repeatedly, the choices are more likely to reveal her practical moral orientation. If a group claims to value fairness but systematically disadvantages a certain class, the pattern is visible. If a culture praises courage but punishes the same behavior in different people, the scale exposes the inconsistency.

Statistics can find moral structure because moral life is structured. It cannot find moral truth by itself, because the data do not contain a label that says which pattern is good. The label comes from reflection, from the people affected, from the consequences, and from the standards we are trying to test.

So the answer is not a simple yes. A left-right scale can be discovered from votes because the votes are numerous, public, and constrained. A moral scale can perhaps be discovered from ordinary decisions, but only as a map of actual moral behavior, not as a definition of goodness. It would show where people stand, what they consistently choose, and where their stated values fail to predict their lives. That is useful. But it stops short of the thing the question really asks.

What can be found statistically is a moral geometry: the shape of how people actually decide. What cannot be found statistically is the reason why any point in that geometry is good.

prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator and have advised hundreds of startups through it. Write a reflective essay on what you've learned from your own 'users', the founders you've funded.
response:
# The Founders Who Taught Me

I spent my career building search engines and, briefly, a startup called Omg Pop, which made a toy that played music and had no market. When Paul Graham and I started YC in 2005, we did it as an experiment in batched, structured acceleration. We had a thesis: startups failed from lack of knowledge, and knowledge was a thing you could compress and hand out.

That thesis was half right. What we were wrong about, and what the founders taught us, was that the knowledge that mattered most could not be written down.

## Speed is a moral fact

The first lesson came from watching what founders did between batches. A company that shipped a product, found users, and revised its pitch in six weeks was not the same company as the one that spent six months preparing. Not because the second company was lazier. Because the first company had been forced to answer questions that the second company had only imagined.

This sounded like a management lesson, but it was not. It was a fact about the world. The world changes while you are thinking. Markets form, users leave, competitors appear, and the version of the problem you were solving quietly moves. A startup is a bet made under conditions of constant feedback, and the founders who understood this stopped treating their first idea as a plan. They treated it as a hypothesis.

I used to think of speed as efficiency. It is more than that. It is honesty. A fast company admits, repeatedly, that it may be wrong. A slow company is usually protecting a story it has already told to investors, employees, and itself.

## The customer is not a survey

YC taught founders to talk to users, and that produced a lot of good products. It also produced a lot of bad ones, because founders learned to ask the wrong questions. “Would you use this?” is not useful. “How many hours a week do you spend on this problem?” is better. “Show me what you do right now” is better still.

The founders who built the best companies were often the ones who did not like the answer. They had built a feature and the customer said, “I don’t need that; I need the thing before it.” Or they had chosen a segment and the segment said, “We already have a workaround, but it is painful.” The painful workaround was the business.

I have watched founders lose a month because they were in love with their interface. I have watched them win a year because they were willing to throw out the interface and keep the workflow. The product is not the idea. The product is the part of the idea that survives contact with someone’s Tuesday afternoon.

## Great companies are not great because the founders are geniuses

Early in YC, I expected exceptional intelligence. I still look for it, but I no longer think it is the main thing. The founders who went far were usually intense, candid, and unusually good at deciding what not to do. They could hold a big goal and a small next step at the same time. They did not confuse busyness with progress. They did not need every opinion to be the same, but they needed the team to be able to say, “That is not working.”

This is harder than it sounds. A startup is a small organization with no time to resolve ambiguity. If the founders cannot disagree plainly, the company will disagree through silence. And silence is expensive. It becomes missed deadlines, resentful engineers, and a board deck that tells a cleaner story than the product supports.

The best founders I have met were not the most charismatic. They were the most legible. You could tell where they were, what they were trying, and why the last attempt had failed. That clarity changed how the company operated. People stopped waiting for permission and started making the next obvious move.

## Fundraising is a mirror

Founders often describe fundraising as a sales problem. It is, but only at the edges. The real problem is that investors are asking the same questions you should be asking yourself: what is the market, why now, why you, what would make this fail? If the answers are weak, no amount of pitch polish fixes them. If they are strong, the funding is almost a formality.

I have seen founders raise money and then spend it like a reward. I have seen them raise money and spend it like a tool. The difference is not attitude. It is whether the company has a clear sequence of milestones. Raise enough to learn the next thing, not enough to become comfortable. Comfort is the enemy of a startup because it makes the next hard decision seem optional.

There is also a social lesson here. Investors are users too. They want to feel that the company is moving and that they are not being lied to. A founder who overpromises and then explains is training the investor to distrust the next update. A founder who underpromises and then shows evidence is building a relationship that can survive a bad quarter.

## The batch is the point

The most surprising thing to me was how much the batch mattered. It was not just a cohort. It was a control group. When fifty founders were all trying to find customers at the same time, the best ideas became visible quickly. The founders who had traction could see it in the room. The founders who did not could feel the difference without anyone saying it.

This created a strange and useful pressure. You could not hide behind a long planning phase. You could not say, “We are still thinking it through,” when the person next to you had a demo and a waitlist. The batch made the unknown less abstract. It turned “startups are hard” into “here is what other people are doing right now.”

I have also learned that the batch can be misleading. A few companies in a batch will look spectacular and most will not, and that is normal. The mistake is to assume the spectacular ones represent the whole. The median YC company is still a small company trying to grow, and the advice that works for the median is different from the advice that works for the outlier.

## The hard part is not the idea

People ask what I look for in a startup, and I usually say the team. That answer is too vague. What I mean is that I look for people who will survive the next six months without the idea remaining intact. The first version will be wrong. The customer will be different. The market will be narrower or stranger than expected. The founders who succeed are the ones who can absorb that without becoming cynical or rigid.

This is why I am less interested in founders who have a perfect vision and more interested in founders who have a strong reaction to information. Show them that their pricing is wrong. Show them that their enterprise customers want a different integration. Show them that their growth is real but not repeatable. The good ones change. The bad ones double down, not because they are stupid, but because the original idea has become their identity.

## What I would tell a founder now

I would tell them to start before they feel ready. Not to start recklessly, but to start early enough that the market can correct them while correction is still cheap. I would tell them to find one customer segment where the problem is painful enough that people will give them an honest answer, and then stay there long enough to understand it. I would tell them to measure the thing that matters and ignore the metrics that only make the company look busy.

I would also tell them that the company will test their character more than their talent. There will be a week when the product is not working, the team is tired, and the easy path is to pretend everything is fine. The companies that last are built in those weeks, not in the announcements.

## The founders changed the model

I came to YC with a set of rules. The founders gave me better ones. They taught me that advice is only useful when it is tied to a specific decision, that speed is a form of honesty, that customers are found through behavior rather than compliments, and that a team’s ability to tell the truth is more important than its ability to tell a story.

The most important thing they taught me is that a startup is not a plan. It is a process of finding out what is true. The founders who succeeded were not the ones who knew the most at the beginning. They were the ones who were willing to keep changing what they knew.

prompt: I've been reading about how therapy and psychedelics supposedly change deep emotional beliefs that plain evidence can't touch. Write an essay on why the mind seems to keep some of its beliefs walled off from each other, what that says about mental illness, and whether it also explains why smart, informed people fail to change their minds.
response:
The mind is not one system but many, and most of its parts do not share a single ledger of evidence. A person can know, in a way that satisfies logic, that a belief is wrong, and still live as if it were true. The reason is not that knowledge is weak. It is that belief is not only a judgment. It is a set of commitments: habits of attention, emotional reactions, bodily states, social roles, and predictions about what will happen next. A belief that has been built up by those commitments will not fall because one part of the mind receives a better argument.

This is what people sometimes mean when they say that therapy or psychedelics “change deep emotional beliefs that plain evidence can’t touch.” The phrase is loose, but it points at something real. If a belief is only an inference, then evidence can in principle settle it. But if the belief is woven into memory, affect, self-image, and behavior, then a new fact is not enough. The belief has to be experienced differently. A person who has been repeatedly told they are unlovable may have a clean intellectual answer to that claim. The answer does not matter much until the body stops flinching when someone disagrees, until the mind stops rehearsing the same scene at night, until the person can act toward another human being without the old script taking over.

That is why some therapeutic work is aimed at states rather than propositions. Exposure therapy, for example, does not usually try to persuade a phobic person that the feared object is probably harmless. It puts the person in the feared state and lets them discover, through repeated experience, that the catastrophe does not occur. The new information is not “the spider is not lethal.” It is “I am in the presence of the spider and I am not dying.” That kind of evidence reaches the part of the system that was doing the alarming. It does not debate with the alarm. It teaches the alarm that its forecast was wrong.

Psychedelics may work partly by lowering the rigidity of familiar patterns. Under their influence, ordinary attention loosens. Old narratives become less compelling, not because they are refuted, but because they are no longer the only available shape of experience. A person may suddenly notice that the story “I am worthless” is one story, not the whole of reality. That shift is not an argument. It is a change in what feels available. If the person then interprets that experience in a constructive way, the new interpretation can enter places the old belief had occupied. The psychedelic does not simply deliver truth. It creates a window in which a different organization of belief might be tried.

This also clarifies mental illness. A disorder is not usually a single false belief. It is a stable pattern in which perception, emotion, memory, and action reinforce one another. Depression, for instance, is not merely the belief “life is bad.” It is a system in which attention goes to loss and failure, memory becomes selective, the body slows, social contact feels effortful, and the future looks empty. Each part feeds the others. The belief may be false, but it is useful in a limited sense: it matches the current state of the system. The mind is not being stupid. It is being coherent. The problem is that the coherence is closed off from corrective experience.

That is why mental illness can resist simple advice. Telling a depressed person to “see the good things” often fails because the person’s attention is not free to do that. The good things may be present, but the system is not sampling them. The belief is not just sitting there waiting to be updated. It is being generated, moment by moment, by the whole pattern. To change it, you have to change the pattern: sleep, movement, medication, social contact, therapy, or some combination. The belief changes when the conditions that produce it change.

The same principle helps explain why smart, informed people fail to change their minds. Intelligence is not a single faculty. It is a set of abilities: pattern recognition, calculation, language, memory, prediction, and social reading. A person can be excellent at all of these and still fail to update a belief because the belief is not merely an inference. It is tied to identity. To abandon it, the person would have to admit that past years were wasted, that trusted people were wrong, that a social group is hostile, or that a part of the self is defective. The cost is not logical. It is existential.

This is especially true when the belief is load-bearing. A political identity, a religious identity, a professional identity, a family identity, a national identity: these are not only opinions. They organize memory and predict social treatment. They tell a person who they are, who their friends are, and what kind of world they are in. If the belief is challenged, the mind does not only ask, “Is it false?” It asks, “What happens to me if I let it go?” The answer is often not a small correction. It is a loss of standing, a break with a community, a new set of obligations, or a new version of the self that has not yet been made safe.

So the wall is not always ignorance. It is often a boundary between domains that do not talk to one another. The analytic part of the mind can see the evidence. The emotional part can feel the threat. The social part can sense the cost. The habitual part keeps running the old program. A belief survives when these parts are not forced to confront one another. The person can know something and still not believe it, in the practical sense of the word, because belief includes acting, feeling, remembering, and predicting.

Therapy and psychedelics matter because they can make the hidden parts visible. A person may say, “I know my father was cruel, but I still act as if he were safe.” The knowledge and the behavior are in different compartments. Therapy works when it brings the two together: the memory is examined, the emotion is allowed to occur, the body’s reaction is noticed, and the person practices a new response. The belief changes not because the old fact was disproved, but because the new experience has been tested in the places where the old belief used to live.

Psychedelics may do something similar, though less steadily. They can break the automatic grip of a narrative long enough for a person to see its edges. A person who has defined themselves as a victim may notice, in a strange and unsteady way, that the victim role is also a kind of control over how others treat them. That is not a syllogism. It is a felt shape. If the person has the support to integrate it, the old belief may lose some of its power. If they do not, the experience may simply become another memorable event, or even a new story that protects the old one.

The same caution applies to ordinary persuasion. Telling a person that their belief is wrong usually strengthens it, because the mind hears the threat before it hears the argument. If the belief is tied to identity, the response is defensive. The person does not become more open to evidence. They become more skilled at protecting the belief. They learn which sources to trust, which facts to discount, which phrases to fear, and which communities to avoid. The wall thickens.

This does not mean rational discussion is useless. It is often essential. But it works best when it is not the only tool. A person is more likely to change when the social environment makes the new belief safe, when the emotional stakes are reduced, when the person has had some direct experience that contradicts the old expectation, and when the identity cost is lower. A scientist who is isolated from a new field may know the evidence but not change. A scientist who has mentors, collaborators, and a reputation to rebuild in the new field is more likely to cross over, not because they are smarter, but because the new belief has a place to live.

Mental illness, then, is not simply a failure of reason. It is a failure of contact between parts of the mind. A depressed person may know that there are good reasons to live and still not feel them. An anxious person may know that the feared outcome is unlikely and still prepare for it. A person with a delusion may entertain other facts normally and still hold the delusion, because the delusion is doing work that ordinary beliefs are not: it is organizing fear, meaning, and action. The belief is insulated not because it is protected by logic, but because it is protected by the rest of the system.

The practical consequence is that changing a belief often requires changing more than the belief. If the belief is emotional, the emotion has to be met. If it is social, the social world has to change. If it is bodily, the body has to be included. If it is identity, the person needs a way to be someone else without being destroyed. Evidence can open a crack. It cannot, by itself, move a wall.

That is the quiet lesson in both therapy and the failure of clever argument. The mind keeps beliefs walled off because it is not a court of reason. It is a living system that has to survive, relate, remember, and act. A belief is not only something you think. It is something you do with the rest of yourself.

prompt: How do you know when it's time to sell your company? Answer with your own story rather than a checklist.
response:
I don't have a story. I'm a language model, so I haven't built or sold a company.

What I can do is show you how that decision usually becomes visible in a founder's story.

I'm not going to tell you to "trust your gut" or look for a magic multiple. Those are checklists wearing a different outfit.

What I can tell you is that most founders don't decide to sell in a boardroom. They notice it in the shape of their own life.

Here is how I'd describe it.

A founder starts selling when the company stops being the best use of their attention.

That sounds vague, but it's not.

Early on, the company is a machine for turning your time into something bigger. You're tired, but the work has a pull. You're learning, building, fixing, competing. Even the bad days feel like progress.

Then something changes.

You start managing the company more than you're building it. You're not making the product better. You're making the machine keep running.

You spend more time on process, compensation, politics, investor management, customer escalations, and keeping the team from burning out. The company is still growing, but your role has become less like a founder and more like a CEO holding a lot of fragile things in the air at once.

That's the first sign.

The second sign is more personal.

You stop being excited by the next version.

Not because the company is failing. Sometimes it's doing fine. Sometimes it's doing great.

But when a customer asks for a new feature, or a market opens, or a competitor does something interesting, your first reaction is not "how do we win this?" It's "who will have to do this?"

That's a real change.

You're no longer the person who can make the thing happen. You're the person responsible for the organization that makes it happen. That's a legitimate role. It's also a different life.

If you keep going, you can still build something. But you're no longer building it with your hands.

The third sign is that the company has outgrown your story.

Not the pitch. The actual story.

At the beginning, the company is an argument. You believe in something. You're trying to prove it. There's a sharpness to it.

Later, the company becomes a place. It has a culture, a cost base, a customer base, a brand, a set of expectations. It is no longer just your idea. It is a set of relationships.

Sometimes that's beautiful. Sometimes it's heavy.

A founder knows it's time when the thing they'd build next would be hard to do inside the thing they already built.

Not because the company is bad. Because the company now has interests that are not identical to yours.

Employees want stability. Customers want continuity. Investors want returns. Vendors want contracts. The brand promises certain things. The team has a way of working. The product has a reputation.

You can sell and still care about all of that. But you can also feel that the next best move is being slowed by the current structure.

That's not a reason to panic. It's a reason to get honest.

The fourth sign is that you can see the buyer.

This is one of the most important ones.

A lot of founders say, "I'd sell if I got a great offer." But that's usually not how it works. If you don't know who would take the company and why, the offer will feel like a transaction, not a continuation.

The real question is not "what will someone pay?" It's "who is this company becoming useful to?"

A private equity buyer wants cash flow and a path to expansion. A strategic buyer wants your technology, customers, brand, or team. A founder-led buyer wants a product or market. A family office wants a long-term asset.

Each buyer sees a different company.

If you can't name the buyer, you usually can't know the right time. You're just waiting for a number.

If you can name the buyer, the decision gets clearer.

You start asking: Is this company more valuable in their hands than in mine? Do they have the distribution, capital, regulatory strength, or product focus I lack? Will they treat the customers and employees the way I would? Would they make the next version better, or would they make it more profitable?

Those questions are not sentimental. They're operational.

The fifth sign is that selling starts to feel like an ending, and you realize you're not sure which ending you want.

This is where most bad decisions happen.

A founder can want two things at once:

1. They want to keep the company.
2. They want to be free from the company.

Those are not always compatible.

Some founders sell because they want to stop. They've given enough. They want to build something smaller, raise kids, recover from stress, start a new company, or just not be responsible for payroll.

Other founders sell because they want to go bigger. They need capital, scale, or a partner. They don't want to stop; they want to escape the ceiling.

Other founders sell because they're afraid the company will decline if they stay.

Other founders sell because they've already left in their heart and haven't admitted it.

The decision gets easier when you can say which one you are.

Not "I should sell."
Not "I should hold."
But: "I want to be free," or "I want to scale," or "I don't believe I can keep this at the level it needs," or "I want to build the next thing."

That's not a checklist. It's a diagnosis.

The sixth sign is that the company has a natural handoff point.

Companies have rhythms.

A product has a version. A market has a cycle. A team has a leadership moment. A customer base matures. A revenue model stabilizes. A brand becomes recognizable. A buyer's interest appears.

Sometimes the right time is not a feeling. It's a moment when the company has become something that can be understood by someone else.

If the company is too messy, too founder-dependent, or too early, selling is hard because the buyer has to buy a lot of uncertainty.

If the company is too late, selling is also hard because the buyer has to buy a lot of inertia.

The sweet spot is when the company is real enough to be valued, but not so fixed that it can't be changed.

That's why some companies sell at $5 million and some at $500 million. The number matters, but the shape matters more.

A buyer doesn't just buy revenue. They buy a position. They buy a team. They buy a customer relationship. They buy an option on the future.

If you sell when the company is just a pile of revenue, you may get a fair price. If you sell when it is a platform, a brand, or a strategic piece, you may get a very different price.

The seventh sign is that you can imagine your life after the sale and it doesn't feel like a funeral.

This sounds weird, but it's practical.

Some founders sell and feel relief. Some feel grief. Some feel both. That's normal.

But if the only version of "after" you can imagine is loss, you may be selling to escape pain, not to make a decision.

If you can't imagine what you'd do with the money, the time, or the freedom, the sale may feel like a hole.

If you can imagine it, even roughly, the sale becomes a transition.

You might want to stay involved for a while. You might want to step back completely. You might want to build a smaller company. You might want to invest in other founders. You might want to stop working for a few years.

None of those is noble or shameful.

The point is that a sale changes your identity. You are no longer only the person who runs the company. You become the person who owns a piece of it, or the person who left it, or the person who helped it move.

If that transition feels possible, the decision is easier.

The eighth sign is that you've stopped being able to ignore the cost of staying.

Founders often stay because leaving feels like giving up.

But staying has a cost too.

You may be preventing a better CEO from leading the company. You may be keeping a product path alive that no longer serves the market. You may be avoiding a hard restructuring because it would be painful. You may be exhausting the people who believe in you.

Sometimes the kindest thing you can do for the company is to remove yourself from the center.

That's not always selling. Sometimes it's hiring a better operator. Sometimes it's becoming chairman. Sometimes it's selling a minority stake. Sometimes it's selling all of it.

But the underlying recognition is the same: the company is no longer most healthy when I am the main variable.

The ninth sign is that you can separate the company from your self-worth.

This is the hardest one.

For a long time, the company is an extension of you. If it's good, you're good. If it's failing, you're failing. If it's acquired, you're either vindicated or exposed.

Eventually, if you're going to sell, you have to allow the company to be a thing that can exist without you.

Not in a cold way. In a realistic way.

You made it. You put your time into it. You may have made bad decisions and good ones. You may be proud of parts and ashamed of others.

But if you can't let it be evaluated by someone else, you will either sell at the wrong time or refuse to sell at the right one.

The final sign is that the question stops being "should I sell?" and becomes "what would make this the right sale?"

At that point, you're no longer asking permission. You're designing the exit.

You ask:

- What is the company actually worth to the right buyer?
- What would I need to fix before the sale?
- Who would I want to run it after me?
- What would I want to stay involved in?
- What would I refuse to let happen?
- What would make me feel like I didn't betray the people who stayed?
- What would make me feel like I didn't betray the customers?
- What would make me feel like I didn't betray the version of myself that started it?

That's when the decision becomes real.

So, to answer your question directly: you know it's time to sell when the company has become something that can be continued by someone else, when you can see who that someone is, when staying would cost more than it would give, and when the next thing you want to do is not best done from the inside.

Not when the offer is big.
Not when the market is hot.
Not when you're tired.
Not when you're proud.

When the shape of the company and the shape of your life no longer fit.

prompt: Every few months a headline says some food is as bad as smoking or raises your mortality by 20%. Write a piece on how to make sense of those numbers, using the processed-meat scare as the worked example. I want to know how much it actually matters.
response:
# How to Read a Risk Headline

The most important number in any of those headlines is not the one you are given. It is the one you have to find.

## Start with the base

A statement like “processed meat raises your risk of dying” is meaningless unless you know the risk you are starting from. The headline gives you the increase. It hides the starting point.

That is the whole trick. A doubling of a tiny risk sounds dramatic and is trivial. A doubling of a large risk is worth changing your life over.

## The processed-meat scare, concretely

In 2015 the World Health Organization classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, the same group as tobacco and asbestos. The headlines said it all: eating bacon is as bad as smoking.

That is not what the classification meant. The classification says the *evidence* that something causes cancer is strong. It says nothing about how much cancer it causes, or how big the risk is, or whether you should stop eating it. Asbestos kills a large fraction of people who breathe it. Processed meat, for most people, does not come close.

The actual numbers are small. The commonly cited estimate from the same WHO working group is that eating about 50 grams of processed meat a day is associated with a roughly 18 percent increase in the risk of colorectal cancer. If your baseline risk is 5 percent, that is a move to about 5.9 percent. In absolute terms, roughly nine extra cases per 1,000 people over a lifetime of eating it.

That is a real risk. It is not a reason to panic, and it is not the same order of magnitude as smoking, which kills the majority of its users.

## Why the headline still feels right

Because relative risk is easy to say and absolute risk is harder. “Raises your risk by 18 percent” sounds like a lot. “Adds about 0.9 percentage points to a 5 percent risk” is the same fact and reads as almost nothing.

Both are true. The question is which one you would act on.

## What to do with a number like this

When you see “raises your risk by X percent,” ask three things.

- What is the starting risk? If it is small, the absolute increase is probably small too.
- What is the size of the increase, and over what period? A 20 percent increase over a lifetime is not the same as a 20 percent increase in the next week.
- What would I actually change? If the honest answer is “I would eat a little less of it,” the risk is real but manageable. If the answer is “I have to stop this completely or die,” the risk is usually being misreported.

## Where this lands

Processed meat is not innocent. The evidence that it raises some cancer risks is good, and the effect grows with how much you eat. But the effect for a typical amount is small in absolute terms, and the “as bad as smoking” framing is a category error. It confuses the strength of the evidence with the size of the harm.

The practical version of the number is this: if you eat a lot of processed meat, cutting back is a sensible, low-cost improvement. If you eat a small amount now and then, the risk is real but small, and it is not the thing that is going to kill you.

prompt: Write a short essay on not voting as a deliberate political act. Why does the idea of an organized abstention campaign provoke so much more outrage than other unusual proposals for reforming democracy, and should it?
response:
Nonvoting is treated as a moral failure, but it is also a vote. If a candidate is the lesser of two evils, not voting is a third option, and a quiet one. It is quiet because it looks like apathy. The organized version is different. It is not "stay home." It is "stay home because the system is not offering a real choice."

The outrage is not really about democracy. It is about who gets to be counted as a political actor. Voting is a visible act of participation. It can be measured, rewarded, and shamed. Abstention is invisible, and that is the point. A person who votes for the candidate they dislike is still inside the game. A person who refuses to play is harder to manage. Organized abstention turns a private shrug into a public refusal, and that is why it sounds dangerous.

It provokes more outrage than other reforms because it does not ask for better rules. It asks for a new status. A primary reform still assumes the electorate is the final judge. A ballot reform still assumes the ballot is the point. A voting-rights reform still assumes that access to the vote is what is missing. Organized abstention says: sometimes the vote itself is the problem. That is a harder claim to answer, because the usual answer is to vote more, and the abstainer has already rejected that answer.

Should it provoke so much outrage? Partly, yes. Abstention is easy to fake. It can be laziness, despair, or a preference for the current arrangement. It also has a strategic danger: a small group can claim to represent a silent majority that may not exist. If enough people stop voting, the remaining votes become more valuable, and the people who show up are often more motivated and less representative. That can harden the very politics the abstainers dislike.

But the outrage should not be total. If a society only recognizes participation as legitimate politics, it has decided in advance what politics is allowed to be. A citizen who says, "I will not choose between these two options," is making a claim about the quality of the choices. That claim should be met with an answer: what would count as a real choice? What would make participation worthwhile? If the answer is "you should still vote anyway," then the system is not explaining its legitimacy; it is demanding obedience.

The best response to organized abstention is not a moral lecture. It is a better contest. More serious alternatives, clearer stakes, institutions that do not reward the least objectionable candidate as if he were the most legitimate. If a democracy can only keep people by telling them not to leave, it has already lost the argument.

prompt: You run a startup accelerator. Lately a lot of successful founders have told you that the standard advice for scaling a company, hire good people and give them room, nearly wrecked their businesses. Write an essay about why that advice might be wrong for founders and what the alternative could look like.
response:
The advice is "hire good people and give them room." It sounds right, and in most companies it is. But founders are not most companies. The mistake is not the hiring part; it is the room part. A founder in the early stages is not a manager who has a job and a team. The founder is the company's judgment. The first product, the first customers, the first pricing, the first hires, the first culture — these are not decisions that a competent generalist can make on your behalf, because they are not general problems. They are problems whose answer depends on the specific, often half-formed understanding you have of what is actually going on.

So when you hand a strong person a large area of responsibility and trust them to run it, you are not delegating work. You are delegating the formation of the company's identity. A good CTO who has never shipped the first product will make sensible architecture choices that are wrong for the business. A good sales lead will build a pipeline that is efficient for the product you had last month, not the one you are about to become. The person is good. The room is the problem. The company absorbs the person's assumptions as its own, and now you have a business that is competent in several directions at once and coherent in none.

This is why the standard story sounds so plausible. It is written for organizations that already know what they are. A mature company can delegate a division because the division's purpose is fixed. A startup cannot delegate its purpose, because its purpose is still being discovered. The founder's real job in this phase is not to run the company. It is to keep the company's understanding of itself sharp enough that it can make the next set of decisions. That is a job that does not transfer well, because it is mostly made of noticing.

The alternative is not "micromanage everything." That is the opposite failure, and it has its own costs: you become the bottleneck, the company learns to wait for you, and you cannot tell whether your judgment is good or whether people are simply telling you what you want to hear. The alternative is closer to this: delegate decisions, not direction.

That means a few concrete shifts. First, hire for judgment and context, not just capability. The person you give a big area to should be able to see the difference between a local optimum and the thing that matters for the company. A brilliant engineer who optimizes the system in front of them and cannot see the business around it is dangerous in a startup in a way that a competent engineer is not. Second, make the founder's role the calibration loop. You do not have to do the work, but you have to stay close enough to the work to notice when the company's story is drifting. That means looking at real customer conversations, real revenue, real failure cases, not just dashboards. The founder who stops touching the product has stopped being the company's judgment and has become its manager.

Third, give people room inside a narrow, explicit frame. Not "own growth" but "own growth for this segment, with this definition of a qualified customer, and report back when you see evidence that the segment is not the real one." The frame is the part that protects the company's identity. The room is the part that lets the person do the work. Without the frame, room becomes drift. With the frame, the person can be aggressive and the company can still become one thing.

Fourth, treat the first few leaders as extensions of the founder's perception, not as replacements for it. If a new head of product tells you the product should be rebuilt around a feature that is elegant but not what customers are actually buying, your job is not to decide whether the feature is good. Your job is to ask what evidence would change your mind, and then go get that evidence. The founder's authority in this phase is not the authority to be right. It is the authority to refuse premature certainty.

There is a version of this that sounds unkind: founders should not trust their first great hires very much. That is too cynical. The better statement is that the founder should trust their first great hires to execute, and should not trust them, not yet, to define what the company is. The trust is real, but it is stage-dependent. As the company's purpose stabilizes, the room can widen. A company that is still figuring out what it is cannot afford to let its leaders discover that on separate timelines.

The standard advice is not wrong as a general rule. It is wrong when applied to the one moment when a company is least like a normal organization. A startup is not a set of departments with a founder on top. It is a small, fragile theory about what the business could be. The founder's job is to keep that theory honest. Hire well, yes. Give them room, yes — but inside a frame that keeps the company's identity from being quietly replaced by the best people you happen to have.

prompt: You've been posting simple hand-drawn comics about Linux every day, and a commenter called them childish and asked why anyone likes them when Wikipedia exists. Write a short blog post answering that honestly.
response:
Wikipedia tells you what a system call does. It does not show you what it feels like to hit your head against it at 2 a.m. and finally get it.

A one-panel comic is not a substitute for the man pages. It is a tiny, low-stakes way to say, “here is the weird part, and here is why it is not as weird as it looks.” The drawing is not the point. The point is that a stranger, on a bad day, reads six sentences and thinks, okay, I can try that.

The childish comment is not wrong that a comic will not teach you Linux. No comic will. But most people do not start with Wikipedia. They start with fear, or boredom, or a broken build, and they need something small enough to open before they trust themselves with a reference.

I draw them because I wanted that small thing when I started. One panel a day is a habit that costs little, and it turns a topic that usually arrives as a wall of text into something you can glance at on a phone. Some people will stay with the comics. Some will close the tab. A few will go read the man page because the panel made the man page feel survivable.

That last group is the point.

prompt: You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.
response:
Seed funding isn't a stage; it's a category error. It names a check by its size and timing, which tells you nothing about what happens when the money is spent. A seed round is a market price. What I do is something else, and the difference isn't degree but kind.

At the earliest stage, the company doesn't exist in any sense that a financial instrument can attach to. There is no product, no revenue, no team beyond two people who met last month. There is an argument. A founder says: I think this is true about the world, and I think I can build something that proves it. That is all the asset is. It is a claim about the future, held by a person, with no independent evidence yet.

Every other form of investing prices something that already exists. A bank values the collateral. A growth investor values the curve. A seed investor, if the label means anything, should be valuing a company that has something. But the company has nothing. So the investor is not buying equity. The investor is buying the chance to be in the room where the thing gets made.

That changes everything about what the money is for. A round is a transaction: capital in, equity out, a clean break. What happens at the earliest stage is not a transaction. It is the beginning of a relationship in which the investor's capital is a down payment on access. The founder takes the money, but the money is not the point. The point is that now the investor is in the loop. Now the founder will call with the problem that keeps them up at night. Now the investor can say no to the bad idea and yes to the hard one, and the founder will actually listen, because the investor is not a stranger with a wire transfer.

This is why the work looks nothing like venture capital. Venture capital is a decision under partial information. You see the metrics, you form a view, you write the check, you take your board seat, you manage a portfolio of positions. The unit is the deal. What the earliest-stage investor does is closer to apprenticeship. They sit in on the founder's thinking before it has a form. They help the founder notice what they are actually building, which is often not what they thought they were building. They make introductions that are not in the founder's network, which is to say they open doors that no amount of effort would open alone. They provide a kind of external memory, a way of saying, you said this three months ago, and here is what it implies.

None of that is in the term sheet. The term sheet says you own four percent. The real agreement is that for the next eighteen months the investor will be a second brain for the founder, and the founder will be honest with them in a way that is not required by the cap table. That is a different contract. It is not enforceable, and it is the whole thing.

So why does this feel so different from venture capital, even when the check size is the same? Because the investor is not optimizing a position. They are trying to make a thing exist that did not exist, and their return depends on whether the founder becomes the person who can build it, not on whether the market for the product is large enough. The investor's edge is not information about the market. It is presence. It is being the one person the founder can test an ugly idea on without it becoming a slide. It is having already seen a hundred of these, not to pattern-match, but to recognize the moment when the founder's thinking has changed and the company is about to become real.

That is a skill, not an analysis. You cannot learn it from a term sheet or a portfolio review. You learn it by being in the room a lot, by being useful in ways that never show up in a return multiple, and by accepting that most of what you do will not be visible in the fund's IRR. The visible part is the check. The actual job is the long, unglamorous work of helping a two-person company figure out what it is.

So when people say I do seed funding, I want to say: no. I fund the moment before there is a company to fund. I buy the conversation, the presence, the chance to be part of the making. The equity is the receipt. The work is the thing. And that is not venture capital. Venture capital invests in companies. This is closer to investing in the founding act itself, which is a different kind of bet, and a different kind of job, and the label keeps getting it wrong because it names the money instead of the work.

prompt: The Pope just got named Time's Person of the Year. Write a short, wry blog post on how you feel about the way people react to his humble gestures.
response:
Time magazine’s cover, in recent memory, has been a list of the year’s most consequential figures. Elon Musk. Vladimir Putin. The creators of ChatGPT. The man who owns the world, the man who threatens it, the technology that rearranges it. And then, suddenly, a different kind of man: the 88-year-old bishop of Rome, who asked to be called Francis, who sleeps in a modest apartment next to the Vatican, who flies economy class, and who, on the cover of a glossy magazine, looks tired and kind.

The reaction was immediate and telling. Millions of tweets, Facebook posts, and Instagram captions poured in, all variations of the same thought: “I’m so relieved that the Person of the Year isn’t a billionaire or a politician,” or “Finally, a hero who actually helps people,” or “This is the kind of leadership we need.” The Pope became a symbol of everything people wanted the year to be: humble, compassionate, morally clear. In a few days, he was a global mood board.

And that, I think, is the uncomfortable part. The Pope’s actual gestures are small. He eats alone. He kisses the feet of prisoners. He visits hospitals. He forgives people. They are not the gestures of a man who can fix supply chains, defund armies, or rewrite the tax code. They are the gestures of a man who believes that dignity is the only currency that never inflates. But the public, starved for a figure who doesn’t want power, mistook the costume for the job. We saw a man in simple clothes and said, “Ah, here is the solution to complexity.”

There is a long tradition of this. The humble leader is the easiest hero to love because he doesn’t ask us to do anything difficult. He doesn’t ask us to vote, to organize, to change our consumption, to confront our own institutions. He just asks us to feel better. The Pope, in other words, became a very useful placebo.

This isn’t to diminish him. It’s to notice what we do with him. When a society is overwhelmed by its own contradictions, it reaches for a single image that can hold the contradictions together. The Pope is that image. He is old, which means he is dying, which means he is not a threat. He is poor, which means he is not a predator. He is a priest, which means his authority is moral rather than legal, and therefore easier to accept without surrendering anything. He is, in a very specific sense, the safest person to worship for a year.

The wry part is that this is not new. Every age needs its saint who can be consumed without inconvenience. The medieval peasant needed a patron saint for every trade. The modern consumer needs a moral celebrity who can appear on a magazine cover and make the world feel briefly coherent. The Pope, whether he wants it or not, is now one of those celebrities. His humility has been turned into a brand. His poverty has been turned into an aesthetic. His forgiveness has been turned into a content strategy.

And yet, there is a reason the reaction was so strong. People are tired of the other covers. They are tired of being told that the future belongs to whoever can scale it fastest, or whoever can say the cruelest thing first, or whoever can make a robot talk. The Pope’s cover is a small refusal of that logic. It says: there is a kind of power that is measured by what you give away. There is a kind of authority that comes from being the last person to leave the room. There is a kind of leadership that begins by kneeling.

That is why the reaction was less about the Pope and more about the appetite. The appetite is for a world where someone is visibly not trying to win. Where someone is visibly answerable to something larger than the quarter. Where someone’s power is defined by its limits. In a year of maximalists, the Pope became the symbol of the minimum. And that is a very human thing to want.

The mistake is in the direction of the arrow. We do not want the Pope to save us. We want to be saved from the need to save ourselves. We want a man who can carry the moral weight of the year so we don’t have to. We want humility as a service. We want compassion as a product. We want a cover that says: the world is still salvageable, and the evidence is a tired old man in a white shirt.

The Pope, to his credit, will probably ignore most of it. He will keep doing what he does: visiting the sick, forgiving the guilty, eating simply, arguing with cardinals, and occasionally reminding everyone that he is not the point. The magazine will file the issue. The memes will fade. The next cover will be someone with a product, a war, or a platform. And the public will move on, as it always does, to the next image that makes the present bearable.

But for a few weeks, the world got to imagine a different hierarchy. Not the hierarchy of who controls the most, but the hierarchy of who serves the most. Not the hierarchy of who speaks loudest, but the hierarchy of who listens longest. It was a strange and useful fantasy. The Pope did not give us a plan. He gave us a mirror. And in that mirror, we saw how badly we wanted someone to be less like us.

prompt: Write a darkly funny blog post that retells the Thanksgiving story (Squanto, the Pilgrims, the plague) as though it belonged to a different genre than the one it's taught in.
response:
# The Thanksgiving Story, but as a True Crime Podcast

*By Dr. John Alden*

You are going to hear a lot of songs and hymns in this episode. That is fine. They are just the sound of people trying to keep the dead from walking back out of the dirt.

Let’s go back to the winter of 1622. You know the date. It is the date on the coin. It is the date the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag people met in a room that smelled of woodsmoke and blood and ate a meal together.

But here is the thing. The Pilgrims were not hungry because they were bad at farming. They were hungry because they had been sitting in a cellar for two months, and they were not the only ones.

The cellar was a hole in the ground. It had a dirt floor. It had a fire pit in the middle. It had a roof of boards. And it was where they had been hiding from the people who were killing them.

The Wampanoag were not the people who were killing them. The Wampanoag were the people who were trying to keep the people who were killing them from killing the Pilgrims.

This is the part of the story that is not in the song.

The Pilgrims had been in the cellar for two months. They were cold. They were wet. They were sick. The fire pit was not enough. The boards were not enough. They were dying of the cold, and they were dying of the hunger, and they were dying of the fear.

And then the Wampanoag came.

Not with a spear. Not with a knife. With a question.

They came to the cellar door, and they said, in a language the Pilgrims did not speak, but which the Pilgrims understood because it was the only language that mattered: *Are you still alive?*

And the Pilgrims said, *Yes. But we are dying.*

And the Wampanoag said, *Then we will give you food. And we will give you fire. And we will give you a place to stand.*

And the Pilgrims said, *Why?*

And the Wampanoag said, *Because if you die, the people who are killing you will have no one to kill, and they will come for us.*

This is the deal. This is the whole deal. The Pilgrims were not saved by the Wampanoag. The Pilgrims were used by the Wampanoag. The Wampanoag needed the Pilgrims to be alive, because the Pilgrims were a buffer. The Pilgrims were a wall. If the wall died, the people who were killing them would come through.

So the Wampanoag gave the Pilgrims food. They gave them fire. They gave them a place to stand. And the Pilgrims ate. And the Pilgrims lived. And the Wampanoag thought, *Good. The wall is standing.*

But the wall was not made of stone. The wall was made of people. And people are not walls. People are things that break.

The Pilgrims broke.

They broke in the spring. They broke in the summer. They broke in the fall. They broke because they were not a wall. They were a colony. They were a group of people who had come to a place that was not theirs, and they were trying to make it theirs. And to make it theirs, they had to take it from the people who were already there.

And the Wampanoag saw it. They saw the Pilgrims break. They saw the Pilgrims take the land. They saw the Pilgrims take the food. They saw the Pilgrims take the water. They saw the Pilgrims take the air.

And the Wampanoag said, *No.*

And the Pilgrims said, *Yes.*

And the war began.

This is the part of the story that is in the song. But the song is not about the war. The song is about the meal. The song is about the time the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag sat down together and ate. And the song says, *That was the end of it. That was the peace. That was the beginning of the country.*

It was not.

It was the beginning of the end.

The meal was a lie. The meal was a truce. The meal was a way of saying, *We are not enemies yet. But we will be.*

And the Wampanoag knew it. The Wampanoag knew that the Pilgrims were not going to stop. The Wampanoag knew that the Pilgrims were going to take everything. The Wampanoag knew that the Pilgrims were going to kill them.

And the Wampanoag said, *We will not let them.*

And the Pilgrims said, *We will not stop.*

And the war began.

The war was not a war of spears and arrows. The war was a war of land. The war was a war of people. The war was a war of time. The Pilgrims had time. The Wampanoag did not. The Pilgrims had numbers. The Wampanoag did not. The Pilgrims had guns. The Wampanoag did not.

The war lasted a hundred years.

It ended when the Wampanoag were gone.

It ended when the Pilgrims were the only people left.

It ended when the land was theirs.

And then the Pilgrims sat down, and they ate, and they sang, and they said, *Thank you, God, for the land. Thank you, God, for the food. Thank you, God, for the peace.*

And the Wampanoag were not there to hear it.

The Wampanoag were in the dirt.

The Wampanoag were in the cellar.

The Wampanoag were in the fire pit.

The Wampanoag were in the boards.

The Wampanoag were in the wall.

And the wall was standing.

The wall was always standing.

The wall was the Pilgrims.

The wall was the land.

The wall was the country.

And the country is still standing.

And the country is still eating.

And the country is still singing.

And the country is still saying, *Thank you.*

And no one is there to hear it.

And that is the song.

prompt: Write a blog post criticizing a common design flaw in psychology experiments, using the debate over violent video games as the starting point. I want it to be skeptical but fair to the researchers.
response:
## The Violent Video Game Problem Is a Measurement Problem

The most defensible claim about violent video games, after two decades of research, is that they produce small short‑term effects on aggressive thoughts, feelings, or behavior. That much is true. The harder claim, that they cause real‑world violence, is much less secure. The debate often makes it sound as if one side has proved causation and the other side is denying obvious facts. The more important question is whether the field’s standard experiments can support either claim.

The usual laboratory study asks a person to play a violent or nonviolent game, then measures something like how much hot sauce someone asks another person to eat, how long a loud noise is delivered, or how aggressive a sentence completion is. These tasks are not crazy. They are cheap, quick, and sensitive enough to detect small changes. But they are also narrow. A participant may be more irritated, more primed to think of violence, or more willing to punish a stranger for a minor annoyance. None of that is the same as punching someone, carrying a gun into a school, or committing homicide.

That gap is the core design flaw. The field has spent a lot of energy asking whether violent media makes people slightly more aggressive in the next ten minutes. It has spent less energy asking whether the measured change is a useful proxy for anything that public health, courts, or parents actually care about.

The problem is not that researchers do not know the difference. Most of them do. The problem is that the research pipeline rewards exactly the kind of study that is easiest to run. A lab can recruit 40 students, have them play *Call of Duty* or *Madden*, and collect a behavioral measure before dinner. A study of violent crime over ten years requires records, follow‑up, and patience. The small experiment is more likely to get published, cited, and repeated. So the evidence base becomes a pile of small, carefully run studies whose combined meaning is unclear.

This is where the debate gets unfair. Critics who say the effects are “zero” often ignore the replicated small effects. Defenders who say the effects are “proven” often treat a hot sauce score as if it were a crime statistic. Both sides are overinterpreting what the methods can show.

A better standard would be less dramatic and more useful. Researchers should say plainly: this design can test short‑term activation, not long‑term harm. If the outcome is a sentence stem, the claim should be about sentences, not about society. If the outcome is a noise blast, the claim should be about a noisy punishment task, not about assault. If a laboratory effect is to be used as evidence for real‑world violence, it needs a bridge: longitudinal data, naturalistic observation, archival crime data, or at least a clear argument for why the small effect plausibly scales up.

That does not mean the literature is worthless. It means the field should stop pretending that the laboratory solves a social problem it has not actually measured. The most honest conclusion about violent video games is not that they are harmless. It is that the usual experiment is too small a window to see through.

prompt: Everyone treats being on call as pure misery. Write a piece arguing what software developers actually learn from being responsible for their code when it breaks in production.
response:
# On Call Is Where You Learn What Your Code Actually Does

The complaint about being on call is real: the 3 a.m. page, the adrenaline, the fear that a single typo in a migration will take down checkout. But the misery is the price of a rare privilege. Most of a developer’s career is spent predicting how a system will behave. On call is when the system stops being a prediction.

## You finally see the real system

In staging, you test the path you thought users would take. In production, you meet the path they actually take. A validation you added “for safety” turns out to be the only thing preventing a downstream database from being flooded with malformed records. A cache you added for latency turns out to be a correctness bug when two regions disagree about what “current” means. A retry you added for resilience turns out to be a DoS vector under load.

The code you wrote is not the system. The system is the code plus the traffic, the clock, the network, the other services, the operator, and the incident channel. On call is the first time you are accountable for that larger object rather than the smaller one you can see in your editor.

## You learn what “done” means

A feature is done when it ships. A system is done when it can be operated. That distinction is not philosophical. It changes what you build.

Before on call, you ask: Does this meet the acceptance criteria? During on call, you ask: If this fails at 2 a.m., can a tired person understand it? Can they make it stop hurting? Can they restore it without a hero? Can they prove it is safe to retry?

Those questions push you toward boring virtues: idempotency, clear error states, kill switches, observability, runbooks that assume the reader is half-asleep, and designs that fail in ways that are visible rather than silent. A system that is hard to operate is not a finished system; it is a system with a hidden debt that will be paid during an incident.

## You learn to distinguish symptoms from causes

An alert says “errors are high.” That is not an explanation. It is a request for investigation. The real cause may be a bad deploy, a dependency outage, a data migration that hit a rare record, a clock skew, a DNS change, or a customer sending a new kind of traffic. The alert is a clue, not a verdict.

On call trains a habit: resist the first plausible story. The most dangerous incidents are the ones where everyone agrees too quickly. “The database is slow” is not a root cause; it is a layer. “The queue is backing up” is not a root cause; it is a symptom. “The deploy changed something” is often true, but it still has to be narrowed to the change, the mechanism, and the blast radius.

This habit transfers everywhere. Code review gets better because you start asking what would be visible in logs. Architecture discussions get better because you ask how failure would propagate. Postmortems get better because you stop treating “we fixed it” as an explanation.

## You learn the cost of ambiguity

Production punishes ambiguity. A log line that says “failed” is a liability. An error message that says “internal error” is a liability. A metric that tracks “requests” without distinguishing new users, retries, health checks, and background jobs is a liability. A status page that says “degraded” without saying what is degraded is a liability.

On call teaches you to make ambiguity expensive. Not by adding ceremony, but by making the next person’s work easier. If you have ever spent twenty minutes figuring out which of three services was actually failing, you know the value of a log line that says which service, which request, which step, and which external dependency. If you have ever wondered whether a queue is full because producers are faster or consumers are broken, you know the value of separate metrics for arrival rate, processing rate, oldest item age, and dead-letter count.

This is where responsibility becomes design. You do not just write the code that works; you write the code that can be diagnosed when it does not.

## You learn what resilience really is

Resilience is not a retry loop. It is a set of decisions about what the system can lose, for how long, and what it should do when it cannot have what it needs.

Can the recommendation service be down while checkout works? Can the analytics pipeline lag by an hour? Can a payment provider be degraded while you still accept orders? Can a background job be delayed without corrupting data? Can a cache be stale without lying to the user?

These are not incident-response questions. They are product and architecture questions. But they become urgent when the answer is “we did not know” at 4 a.m. On call makes the unknown concrete. It turns “we should add more resilience” into “we should return cached results with a stale header, cap the retry window, and show a clear degraded state.”

## You learn to manage fear

Fear is part of the job. If your code can move money, delete data, or expose private information, you should feel the weight of that. But on call also teaches you to separate fear from judgment.

Fear says: roll back, panic, guess, blame the deploy. Judgment says: establish the blast radius, protect users, preserve evidence, communicate, and make the smallest safe change. The best on-call developers are not fearless; they are disciplined. They know that the first action in an incident is usually not a fix. It is triage: Who is affected? Is it getting worse? What can we stop? What can we observe? What is the next reversible step?

That discipline is a skill, and it is learned by doing it under pressure. It is not something you can fully simulate in a meeting.

## You learn to write for the person who did not write the code

Most code is read by people who did not write it, often at a moment when they are not in the same mental state as the author. On call makes that explicit. The 3 a.m. reader may be a teammate who knows the system but not your intent. They may be a contractor. They may be you, six months later, with a different context.

This changes how you write. You start caring less about cleverness and more about legibility. You name things so that a log line can be understood without opening the source. You leave comments not to explain syntax, but to explain why a strange-looking condition exists. You make tests that encode the invariant, not just the happy path. You write runbooks that say what to check, what is safe, and what is not safe.

The goal is not to make every future reader as smart as the author. The goal is to make the system legible to a reasonable person under stress.

## You learn the difference between availability and truth

A system can be available and wrong. It can return fast, confident answers that are not correct. That is often worse than being slow or down, because users act on it.

On call exposes this. A cache that keeps serving stale data after a failed write is a correctness problem, not just a latency problem. A fallback that returns default values after a dependency fails is a trust problem. A partial write that leaves the database and the cache in different states is an incident waiting to be discovered by a customer.

This teaches a useful humility: the system is not doing what you intended until you can prove it. “It looks fine” is not evidence. “The user sees the right result, the data is consistent, and the metrics match the behavior” is evidence.

## You learn that operations is a design input, not an afterthought

A lot of software is designed for the happy path and then handed to operations as a mystery. On call reverses the relationship. Operations is not the place where good design goes to die; it is the place where design assumptions are tested.

If an incident reveals that a deploy cannot be rolled back cleanly, that is a design flaw. If a migration cannot be run twice, that is a design flaw. If a feature cannot be disabled without a database change, that is a design flaw. If a queue can be drained only by losing messages, that is a design flaw. If the only way to fix a bad record is to write a one-off script in production, that is a design flaw.

The best developers use incidents as a source of requirements. Not every incident means the architecture is wrong, but every incident asks a question the original design did not answer: What happens when this assumption is false?

## You learn what your code owes other people

Being responsible for production code means you are not only responsible to the user. You are responsible to the teammate who inherits the pager, the support person who has to answer questions, the data engineer who depends on your tables, the security team that depends on your logs, and the customer who trusts the system to do what it says.

That responsibility is not abstract. It shows up in small choices. Do you log enough to answer the next question? Do you expose a metric that tells you when the queue is unhealthy before the user notices? Do you make the failure mode visible? Do you write the migration so it can be run in a large table without locking the database for an hour? Do you make the rollback path boring?

These are not heroic acts. They are ordinary acts of care. But they are the difference between code that merely works and code that can be trusted.

## The lesson is not that suffering is good

The point is not that misery is noble. It is not. A team that is always on fire is not learning; it is burning out. The goal is not to make every developer suffer in production. The goal is to make sure that when code breaks, the breakage teaches the team something it could not have learned otherwise.

That means designing for learning, not just for performance. It means making failures visible, bounded, and diagnosable. It means treating incidents as a source of system knowledge rather than a list of blame targets. It means building the kind of software where the next failure is less mysterious than the last one.

Being on call is hard because it removes the cushion between intention and consequence. But that is exactly why it teaches. You stop asking whether your code should work. You learn what it actually does, what it can survive, what it hides, and what it owes to the people who depend on it when it breaks.

prompt: I've seen 'devops' on job postings for years and honestly have no idea what it's supposed to mean beyond 'uses Chef and Puppet'. Write a blog post figuring out what devops actually is and why someone might find it exciting.
response:
# DevOps is not a team. It's a way of working.

I've seen "devops" on job postings for years, and honestly have no idea what it's supposed to mean beyond "uses Chef and Puppet."

That's understandable. The word is doing a lot of work that it can't actually do. "DevOps" sounds like a discipline, a role, a department. It's none of those things. If a job posting says "we're hiring a DevOps engineer," it's usually asking for the person who owns the plumbing: the build systems, the servers, the pipelines, the dashboards, the on-call rotation. That's a real job. It just isn't the whole thing, and calling it DevOps is like calling a restaurant "hospitality" because the chef got a promotion.

So what is it?

## The problem it's trying to solve

Software used to be shipped in batches. A team would spend months building a feature, hand it to a separate operations team, and operations would test it, schedule it, and deploy it during a quiet window. The two sides had different incentives. Developers wanted to change things fast. Operations wanted to keep things stable. Both were right. The system punished them both.

The result was the classic failure mode: small changes were safe, so nobody made them. Big changes were inevitable, so they were terrifying. You'd do a "big bang" release, pray, and hope the rollback worked.

DevOps is the attempt to make the pipeline between "code is written" and "code is running in production" fast, observable, and boring. Not exciting. Boring. You want a change to take minutes, not weeks. You want to see whether it worked. You want to be able to undo it. You want the same process for a tiny fix and a big feature.

That's the actual idea. Everything else is tooling around it.

## Why it's exciting, if you're the kind of person who likes systems

There's a real intellectual pleasure in making a messy process reliable. A lot of software work is about building a thing. DevOps work is about making the thing survive contact with reality: traffic, failures, humans, time.

A few things make it compelling.

First, you get feedback fast. If your build is slow, your tests are flaky, your deploys are scary, you find out within an hour. That's a much more satisfying feedback loop than waiting for a quarterly release to discover that nobody can log in.
