Second, you're close to the real system. You see what actually happens when users hit the service. You see the failure modes that unit tests never predicted. You learn how infrastructure behaves under load, under misconfiguration, under human error. That knowledge is hard to get from inside a single application.

Third, it forces you to think about failure as a normal state. Not "what if something breaks?" as a hypothetical, but "what happens when this disk dies, when this dependency is slow, when this deploy is half-finished?" You design for it. You rehearse it. You make the recovery path as well understood as the happy path.

Fourth, the work is concrete. A good pipeline can be inspected. A good alert has a runbook. A good incident has a timeline. You can point at the thing and say whether it works. That's rare in a lot of technical roles, where the output is a model, a document, or an opinion.

There's also a strange satisfaction in making something less interesting. The goal is to reduce surprise. Fewer 2 a.m. pages. Fewer "it worked on my machine" arguments. Fewer heroic manual fixes. If you're the person who likes order, that's a good place to be.

## Why it disappoints people

DevOps also attracts people who want to be the person who gets to say no. The role can become a gate: "I control the servers, so you can't deploy without me." That's the opposite of the goal. The point is to remove the gate, not to staff it with a better gatekeeper.

It can also become a tooling obsession. People collect automation the way some people collect cameras. Every new platform, every new agent, every new dashboard, every new "shift-left" initiative. The tools are useful when they reduce the cost of doing the right thing. They're harmful when the work becomes maintaining the tools that were supposed to make the work easier.

And it can be lonely. The person who owns the pipeline is often the only person who knows why the pipeline works. If that person leaves, the organization learns the hard way that the automation was really just a set of scripts with strong opinions.

So if you're evaluating a DevOps job, look for the shape of the work, not the adjective. A good posting will mention reducing lead time, improving reliability, making deploys routine, improving observability, reducing incident response time. It will talk about outcomes. A weak posting will list technologies and assume that using them constitutes the work.

## What it is, finally

DevOps is a set of practices for making software delivery a continuous, observable, recoverable process instead of a scheduled, risky event. It's not a toolchain. It's not a team. It's not a philosophy. It's a way of organizing work so that changes are small, feedback is fast, and failure is manageable.

If that sounds dry, it is. But for some people, dry is the point. The excitement isn't in the ceremony. It's in the system working when it's supposed to work, and failing in a way you can understand when it isn't.

prompt: Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.
response:
There is a particular kind of shame that does not come from doing a bad thing, but from having a bad thing done to you and not being able to prove it. You have the memory. The other person has the record.

The first reason for silence is not cowardice. It is that the event often does not fit the shape of the story you will need later. A comment at a meeting. A joke that landed differently depending on who was in the room. A promise made privately and a door closed publicly. At the time, your mind is trying to survive, not to build a case. You learn quickly that the details you remember most vividly are the ones that are hardest to verify. The details that would help a case file are the ones that blur first.

So you stop telling people. Not all at once, but in increments. You stop telling your close friends, because you can feel the story becoming a burden on them. You stop telling new acquaintances, because you do not want to explain yourself before you have earned the right. You stop telling anyone, because each retelling changes the story slightly, and the changes feel like lies even when they are only the ordinary drift of memory.

Then there is the second reason, the one nobody mentions in a meeting: you are afraid of being the reason something good stops. If you were a junior colleague, maybe you are afraid of losing a mentor. If you were a woman in a small field, maybe you are afraid of being the woman who made a department unfriendly to women. If you were the only person of your gender or race in the room, the cost of speaking is not just personal; it is institutional. You are being asked to pay for a problem you did not create.

This is where media coverage usually arrives, and this is where it makes things worse. The standard story wants a clean arc: a person is harmed, the person speaks, the truth emerges, the system corrects itself. That arc is satisfying, and it is also a trap. It implies that the only failure between harm and correction is silence. It implies that if you have not yet spoken, you are still complicit, still protecting the powerful person, still part of the problem.

A person who has been silent for years can read that and think: they already decided the story. They need a version of me that will fit.

The media does this in small, technical ways. It asks for the first incident, as if the first incident is the most important one. It asks for the moment you decided to speak, as if the decision is a single clean event rather than a long negotiation with your own fear. It wants a photograph, a title, a job description, something that makes the human being legible to a stranger. It wants the powerful person’s name before it wants the survivor’s name, because the name is the story. And it wants a response, because a response is news.

Each of these asks has a purpose. But taken together, they turn a person’s life into a format. You are no longer deciding whether to tell the truth. You are deciding whether your truth will be allowed to remain complicated.

Most harassment is complicated. It is not one act with one meaning. It is a pattern, and patterns are hard to prove. It is often ambiguous on purpose, because ambiguity is cheaper than denial. The person who did the harm can say they were joking, that you were overreacting, that you are being dramatic, that you have always been like that. The ambiguity is not a bug. It is the method.

When a journalist asks for the clean version, the complicated version goes away. Not because it is false, but because it will not be believed. A story that says “it was never one terrible moment, it was a hundred small ones, and I was not sure I had the right to name them” is a harder story to run. It does not have a villain’s face in the headline. It does not let the reader finish feeling righteous.

There is another problem: the story is not only about you. It is about everyone who was in the room and said nothing. The journalist may not say this directly, but the article will be read by them. They will see their own silence described as the background condition of the abuse. They will feel indicted, and they will defend themselves. Some will come forward. Some will deny. Some will say they did not know. The person who was harassed will then be responsible for managing the emotional fallout of a story that was never really about her.

This is why silence can last. Not because the person has no story, but because the cost of the story is paid in advance. The person must imagine the interview, the questions, the corrections, the response, the second article, the third article, the way her name will be attached to the powerful person’s name in search results for the rest of her professional life. She must imagine her family reading it. Her old colleagues reading it. Her future employers reading it. She must imagine that the person who harmed her will use her silence against her, and then use her speech against her, and then use her credibility against her, because she was once uncertain, once polite, once afraid.

The media makes this worse because it often treats the story as a public good in a way that the person did not choose. The public good language is not always false. Sometimes speaking does help other people. Sometimes it changes a department, a firm, a field. But when the public good is presented as the only legitimate reason to speak, it quietly replaces the person’s own reasons. It says: your fear is not a reason. Your exhaustion is not a reason. Your desire to keep your life small and private is not a reason. Only the greater good counts.

That is a heavy thing to ask of someone who has already been asked to carry the emotional labor of a workplace that should have protected her.

I think about this because I have watched people I respect become unable to tell their own story after it was told for them. The article came out with a paragraph about their childhood, a sentence about their office, a quote that made them sound braver than they felt. Then the comments. Then the reply from the other party. Then the follow-up. By the end, the person was no longer the subject of the story. She was a footnote to a debate about evidence, tone, timing, and who had the right to be believed.

The silence that follows is not the same as the silence that came before. The first silence was private. It was a choice made in the dark, with no audience. The second silence is public. It is a reaction to being made visible under conditions you did not choose. It is not shame, exactly. It is the exhaustion of being a case.

A better story might be slower. It might not have a headline. It might begin with the question: why did no one else act? It might treat the silence not as the obstacle to justice but as evidence of a system that made silence rational. It might ask the institution what it knew, when it knew it, and what it did. It might resist the need for the survivor to perform certainty, because certainty is not what trauma leaves behind. It might allow the person to say, “I do not know if this is enough to prove,” and still take the story seriously.

This is not a call for no journalism. It is a call for journalism that understands what it is doing. A person who has been silent for years is not holding out for the perfect moment. She is waiting to see whether the world will let the truth be uneven, inconvenient, and unfinished. Most of the time, it will not. It will want a winner and a loser, a quote and a response, a lesson and a byline. And so she will stay quiet, not because the story is not true, but because the only version of the story she is offered would require her to become a stranger to herself.

The tragedy is not that she was harmed. That is already done. The tragedy is that the system which harmed her is also the system that decides whether her account of it will be received as truth or as spectacle. And until that changes, silence will look like consent.

prompt: Write a blog post encouraging engineers to tell a colleague's manager when that colleague does great work, especially as a way to support people from underrepresented groups. Cover when it matters, how to do it well, and what can go wrong.
response:
# Give Credit Where It's Due

When an engineer on your team does something good, tell their manager. Not because the engineer asked you to, and not because you're a people pleaser. Because the way managers form opinions about people is broken in a specific, predictable way, and you have information that corrects it.

## Why It Matters More Than You Think

Most managers have too many direct reports to watch everything. They see your team's output, but they see *your* team's output through your framing. If you say "we shipped the migration," the manager files "they shipped the migration." If you say "Priya caught a race condition in the scheduler that would have corrupted three days of data, and she wrote the fix herself," the manager files "Priya caught a race condition..." Those two sentences go into different places in the manager's head. The first is a fact about a project. The second is evidence about a person.

People from underrepresented groups are especially likely to work in teams where their contributions are filtered through someone else's summary. They're more likely to be the only person in the room, more likely to have their ideas attributed to whoever spoke first, and more likely to be evaluated on how they land with a group that hasn't spent years calibrating to their communication style. Every time a manager's opinion of them is formed from secondhand description rather than observation, the description is doing more work than it should. Your one sentence can put the actual evidence in the record.

This isn't only about protecting people from underrepresented groups, though it matters there most. It's about making evaluation run on what people actually did. If you only tell managers about your star engineer, you've built a system where the people you notice become the people who get promoted. You notice what's in front of you. You are not a neutral camera.

## When It Matters Most

A manager's opinion of someone is most plastic when the manager has the least direct data. That's new hires, people who joined a reorg, people in adjacent teams, and anyone whose work is visible to you but not to them. If you've worked with someone for two years and their manager has watched them in every 1:1, your testimony is a nice confirmation. If you've worked with them for three weeks and their manager has seen them once in a staff meeting, your testimony is the data.

It also matters most when the work is the kind that doesn't show up in a ticket system. A careful code review that prevented a bad design from getting built. A debugging session where someone taught a junior engineer how to think about a class of bug. A design doc that quietly resolved a conflict between two teams. A production incident where someone stayed calm and found the cause in an hour. These are real contributions. They are also exactly the contributions that vanish when someone else writes the summary.

And it matters when the person is about to be evaluated. Promotion season, performance review season, and the weeks after a big release are when a manager is actively assembling a picture of someone. If the picture is mostly "they were reliable" and "they hit their goals," that picture is thin. If it includes two or three concrete examples of judgment, it's a different picture.

## How to Do It Well

Lead with the specific thing they did, not with an adjective. "Priya caught a race condition in the scheduler" is useful. "Priya is a great engineer" is a claim you'd have to defend and the manager can't do much with. The first sentence is evidence. The second is a verdict.

Attach the consequence. The manager needs to know why the thing mattered. "She caught a race condition that would have corrupted three days of data" tells the manager what was at stake. "She caught a bug" does not. You don't need to be precise about the dollar figure. You need to be clear about what would have gone wrong and what the alternative was.

Separate the person from the project. If you say "the team did a great job on the migration," you have not told the manager anything about Priya. If you say "the team did the migration, and Priya owned the trickiest part," you have told the manager something they can use. This is not about stealing credit from the team. It's about making visible the parts of the work that required a particular person's judgment.

Say it to the right person. If you have a working relationship with the manager, a short note or a line in a 1:1 is enough. If you don't, a brief email with the specific example is fine. You don't need to schedule a meeting. You don't need to make it a formal endorsement. "I wanted to flag that Priya did X on the project we worked on last month, because it's not obvious from the ticket history and I think it's worth your knowing." That's the whole thing.

Do it more than once. One note is a data point. Three notes over a quarter are a pattern. If someone consistently does good work on your team, your manager should hear it from you at intervals, not just when something dramatic happens. The dramatic things are memorable. The steady, excellent work is what actually builds a career, and it's the work people forget to mention.

## What Can Go Wrong

You can overshoot. If you turn every interaction into a testimonial, you stop being a useful colleague and start being a fan. The manager will discount you. The person you're praising will feel awkward. The right frequency is roughly: when you've seen something genuinely good, mention it. Not every day. Not every pull request. When the work was good in a way that matters and that the manager probably doesn't know about.

You can make it about you. "I was really impressed by how Priya handled the design review" is fine, but it's weaker than "Priya handled the design review in a way that resolved the conflict between the two teams." The manager doesn't need to know how you felt. They need to know what the person did. Your feelings are the reason you're writing; they aren't the content.

You can create a problem for the person by being the only one who praises them. If you are the only voice in the building saying good things about someone, you've made them dependent on your testimony, and you've put yourself in a position where the person has to manage your opinion as part of managing their career. That's not a healthy dynamic. The goal is for the person to be known for their work, not for being someone's favorite collaborator. If you find yourself being the sole source of good news about someone, check whether that's because the work is invisible or because you've become a gatekeeper.

You can accidentally do the thing you're trying to prevent. If you say "Priya is the only one on that team who really understands the system," you've made a point about her, but you've also made a point about everyone else, and you've framed her in a way that makes her the exception rather than a colleague. You can give someone credit for something without turning the rest of the team into a backdrop.

And you can tell the wrong manager at the wrong time. If a manager is in the middle of a reorg, or is already forming a negative view of someone for reasons you don't know about, your well-meaning note lands in a context you can't see. That doesn't mean you shouldn't speak up. It means you should be honest about what you're doing: you're reporting what you observed, not making a case. "I wanted you to know that X happened" is different from "you should promote Priya." The first is information. The second is a recommendation, and it's not your job unless you're asked.

## The Part That's Easy to Forget

The person you're talking about probably doesn't know you told their manager. That's fine. You don't need to announce it, and you don't need their permission, though if you're close with them and it's a big claim, a heads-up is kind. The point is that the manager now has a fact. Whether the person benefits from it is downstream of that.

This is not a substitute for fixing the bigger problems. If your organization's promotion process is a black box, telling a manager one true thing about one engineer will not fix it. If the people who decide who gets promoted are not in the rooms where the work happens, your note is a bandage. If the culture is one where credit is a scarce resource that people hoard, your honesty is a small counterweight against a strong current.

But it's not nothing. It's the difference between a manager's opinion of someone being formed from what that person performed in the two meetings they attended, and being formed from what they actually did. It's the difference between "they seem fine" and "here is a specific thing they did that required judgment and went well." It's cheap. It's a sentence. And for the people whose contributions are most likely to get summarized away, a sentence from a colleague who was in the room is often the only record that exists.

prompt: There's a stereotype that the left thinks problems are social and fixable while the right thinks they're biological and fixed. Write an essay arguing about whether that gets things backwards.
response:
# The Left, the Right, and the Problem with Problems

There is a tidy way to say what divides American politics, and it is wrong. The left thinks problems are social and therefore fixable. The right thinks they are biological and therefore fixed. The left sees a sick child and asks who failed to provide; the right sees the child’s temperament and says some children are simply harder. The left blames the zip code; the right blames the DNA.

That is not what either side actually believes, and the error matters because it lets each side dismiss the other’s concerns as either naïve or cruel.

## What the right actually says

The right does not usually say human beings are fixed. It says institutions, incentives, and cultures are. The complaint is not that poor people are born poor. It is that a particular set of rules—welfare offices, school districts, zoning codes, court procedures—produces predictable bad results. Change the rules and the results change. That is a social claim. It is about arrangements, not genes.

The right is also suspicious of the left’s preferred fixes, but the suspicion is aimed at the mechanism, not at the existence of the problem. A conservative can agree that a neighborhood is dangerous and still oppose the particular program the left proposes. The argument is not “the neighborhood cannot be improved.” It is “this improvement will not work, will cost too much, or will create worse problems.” That is a contest over cause and effect. It is not a claim that human life is sealed shut.

Where the right does sound biological, it is usually in a weaker form: people differ, and differences persist. Some children are easier to raise. Some people respond better to structure than to encouragement. Some skills are hard to teach. Those are real observations, and they do not imply that everything is determined. They imply that policy should be humble, that outcomes will be uneven, and that the state should not promise what it cannot deliver.

## What the left actually says

The left is not the pure social-constructionist it is made out to be. Most leftists accept that people differ. They also accept that some differences are durable. The claim is not that environment can remake a person at will. The claim is that large patterns in achievement, health, and poverty are produced by large patterns in opportunity, and that those patterns are not what they appear to be.

A leftist can say, “this student is struggling” and also say, “the school under-resourced him, the clinic missed the asthma, the family lost the house, and the test was written for a different kind of knowledge.” That is not a denial of individual variation. It is a claim about the shape of the evidence. When a whole group fails at the same task at the same time, the explanation is more likely to be in the conditions than in the people.

The left’s error is not that it thinks biology is irrelevant. It is that it often treats the social explanation as sufficient, as though once the social causes are named the problem is close to solved. It overstates the power of policy. It underweights persistence, taste, local knowledge, and the fact that people are not clay.

## Where the stereotype gets things backwards

The stereotype flips the real positions. The right is the side that is most willing to say a problem is institutional and therefore changeable. The left is the side that is most willing to say a problem is structural and therefore hard to change quickly.

The right says: this agency is incompetent, this court is slow, this incentive is corrupt. Fix the institution. The left says: the economy is rigged, the labor market is broken, the legal system is stacked. These are not small malfunctions. They are features of the whole. The right’s problems are local and fixable. The left’s problems are large and resistant.

That is the opposite of the usual slogan. The slogan says the left believes in social plasticity and the right believes in biological fate. The reality is that the right often believes in the plasticity of rules and the left often believes in the rigidity of systems.

## Why the error is useful

The stereotype is useful because it lets each side avoid the hard question. If the right is biologically deterministic, then its skepticism of policy is just prejudice. If the left is socially naïve, then its programs are just wishful thinking. Both dismissals are easy. Both are mostly wrong.

The actual disagreement is narrower and less comfortable. It is about what counts as a real cause, what a good policy can change, and how much variation in outcomes should be expected. The right thinks too many leftists underestimate the persistence of differences and the limits of central planning. The left thinks too many rightists mistake the persistence of a problem for the permanence of a cause.

Neither side is arguing from genes to excuses. Both are arguing from evidence to prediction. The evidence is disputed, the predictions are bad, and the politics is loud. That is a normal argument about a hard subject. It does not need a caricature.

prompt: I've just finished Infinite Jest and I'm still puzzled. Write a long, funny, opinionated review for people who've read it (spoilers fine) that tries to say what the book is actually about and how its structure relates to that.
response:
The footnotes are the only sane people in the book, and they are in the basement.

The novel is about the moment when entertainment stops being a thing you do to pass time and becomes the architecture of the state. It is about what happens when the audience is no longer an audience. The carols are a preview, not a metaphor. They are the actual mechanism: a product so perfectly tuned to the viewer that it delivers a lethal dose of its own success. The carols kill because they are so good. That is the whole book in one sentence, and if that does not trouble you, you are already in the carol.

The rest of the novel is a long way of asking who is still in the room when the screen goes black.

The structure is not a gimmick. It is the argument. The present day is not linear, not because Pynchon wanted to be difficult, but because that is what a society looks like when it has optimized for attention. The narrative keeps interrupting itself the way the world keeps interrupting you: an ad, a memory, a drug, a piece of trivia, a new story, the same story with a better hook. The text refuses to let you settle because the people in it have no place to settle. The timeline is a symptom. The footnotes are the only place where time behaves.

The footnotes matter because they are where the book is actually read. They are slow, exact, historical, and often funnier than the main text. They are also where the novel’s real intelligence lives. The main text is the fever. The footnotes are the doctor in the hallway, writing the chart. When Pynchon drops a footnote about a seventeenth-century painter, a Roman emperor, a drug trial, or a piece of theater, he is not showing off. He is giving you the only stable ground the novel offers. The body of the book says: everything is happening now. The footnote says: here is what happened before, and here is how it got here.

The novel’s deepest joke is that the future is a footnote.

The carol is the product. The rest of the book is the aftermath. But the aftermath has no center, because the carol has not happened yet. The novel keeps circling around the moment of total absorption without letting you sit in it. That is not lazy. That is the point. If Pynchon had given you the carol, you would have had a spectacle. Instead you get the culture that needs it: the addicts, the athletes, the parents, the bureaucrats, the children, the therapists, the fans, the men who keep saying they are going to do something and then do not. The book is about a world that has already become the carol, except that the carol is the one thing it cannot quite show you.

This is where the book gets mean.

The people in Infinite Jest are not stupid. They are usually intelligent, articulate, and self-aware. They can talk about their problems in detail. They know what is wrong with them. They can name the drug, the habit, the institution, the parent, the failure. Knowledge does not help. In fact, knowledge is part of the problem, because the novel’s world has turned everything into information. The Enfield Du Maurier drug is not just a narcotic. It is a technology of escape with a brand name. The tennis academy is not just a school. It is a machine for producing winners. The WPA is not just a government office. It is a system for turning citizens into consumers of their own misery. The carol is not just a film. It is the final product of all of it.

The WPA is one of the book’s great comic devices, and one of its great terrors. The people working there are trying to help a nation that has become a customer. They are not sadists. They are mostly exhausted professionals doing their jobs in a bureaucracy that has learned to monetize despair. The WPA meetings are funny because they are so ordinary. They have forms, slogans, coffee, bad jokes, and the unshakable confidence that the correct procedure will solve a problem that is not procedural. That is the actual comedy of the book. Not the drugs, not the sex, not the tennis, but the way institutions keep running while the world inside them becomes increasingly unmanageable.

The family plot is the human core.

The Incandenza family is a house that has become a performance. James is the son who is expected to be a genius and cannot stop trying to be one. Claire is the mother who has turned love into a set of rules. Orin is the father who left and left the whole family with a problem it cannot solve. Milo is the little brother who is already learning how to be a consumer, a performer, and a patient. The family is not a normal family. It is a laboratory where the novel tests what happens when a person is treated as a project. James’s tragedy is not that he is weak. It is that he is too responsive. He is a character in the worst sense: someone who has become a shape for other people to fill.

The novel is funny because it takes the absurd seriously.

Pynchon writes about drug dealers, tennis coaches, government employees, actors, addicts, children, and dying people with the same deadpan precision. He does not moralize. He accumulates. A scene can begin with a man trying to get high and end with a discussion of eighteenth-century theater, and the connection is not decorative. The connection is that the man is not really having a private experience. He is being processed by a culture that has already packaged the experience. The comedy comes from the gap between what the character thinks is happening and what is actually happening. The character thinks he is choosing. The system thinks he is selecting. The book thinks both are true, and that is why it is funny.

The tennis plot is not a subplot. It is the book’s theory of meritocracy.

The tennis academy is a place where children are sorted by talent, will, and usefulness. It is also a place where the adult world learns what it has made. The boys are not just athletes. They are products. Their pain, their ambition, their bodies, and their failures are all material. The novel does not need to tell you that the academy is corrupt. It just lets you watch the machinery. The players train, compete, injure themselves, get promoted, get benched, get sold. The adults talk about the future, the nation, the team, the next generation, and the next sponsor. The tennis is the clearest version of the book’s central bargain: you will be rewarded if you can become the thing the system wants you to become.

The carol is the bargain taken to its limit.

A tennis academy can say it is producing winners. A drug can say it is producing relief. A government office can say it is producing stability. A family can say it is producing a child. The carol says: I will produce the viewer. It will know you better than you know yourself. It will know when to make you laugh, when to make you cry, when to make you want to turn it off, and how to keep you from turning it off. It is not evil because it is malicious. It is terrifying because it is successful. The carol is not the villain. The carol is the result.

This is why the book is so hard to put down and so hard to explain.

It is hard to put down because it is good at the thing it is describing. It knows how to hold you. It knows when to give you a joke, a memory, a piece of trivia, a sudden turn, a long footnote, a strange historical image, a sentence that lands like a punch. It knows how to make you want to keep going. That is the book’s great discomfort: it practices the very skill it is warning about. You are not just reading a novel about attention. You are being kept in attention. Pynchon is not innocent. He is a craftsman, and the craft is part of the argument.

It is hard to explain because the book refuses the explanatory stance.

If you say it is about addiction, it says: yes, and also institutions. If you say it is about technology, it says: yes, and also the family. If you say it is about the carol, it says: yes, but the carol is not the point; the carol is the destination. If you say it is a satire, it says: yes, and the satire is not laughing at the world from outside. It is laughing at the world from inside, which is much funnier and much worse.

The footnotes are where the satire becomes philosophy.

The main text is the culture. The footnotes are the archive. They give the novel its sense that the present is not a blank. Everything that looks new has a history, and everything that looks new is a variation. The carol is new, but it is also the descendant of every trick, every sermon, every opera, every drug, every government program, every parent who told a child a story to keep them still. The footnotes remind you that the future has a past. The main text makes you feel like there is no past, only the next stimulus.

The book’s last image is not the carol. It is the people who will watch it.

That is the real horror. Not the machine, but the readiness. The novel ends not by showing you the perfect entertainment, but by showing you a world that has become available for it. The people in it are not zombies. They are more frightening than zombies, because they are still capable of speech, desire, affection, and self-justification. They can talk. They can plan. They can love each other in the narrow way available to them. They can also sit down and press the button. That is the thing Infinite Jest will not let you forget: the carol does not need to break the world. The world has already arranged itself for the carol.

The book is also a joke about the reader.

You are not outside the text. You are inside it. The footnotes tell you things you did not ask for. The narrative keeps giving you more. The novel knows that you will want to understand it, and it turns that desire into another kind of consumption. You can read it as a puzzle, a prophecy, a satire, a family story, a drug story, a tennis story, a government story, a film story. Each of those is true. None of them is enough. The book is not asking you to solve it. It is asking whether you can keep reading when the reading itself has become the thing you are trying to escape.

That is the real question.

Not: what is Infinite Jest about? But: what happens when the only available life is the next thing? The carol is the final form, but the final form is not the beginning. The beginning is the man who takes the drug because he cannot stand the present. The mother who makes a game of love because the real thing is too dangerous. The child who learns early that his value is his performance. The government employee who fills out the form because the form is all that is left. The tennis player who runs because stopping is unbearable. The reader who turns the page because the page is where the world has become manageable.

The book is funny because it sees the joke in every one of them. It is tragic because the joke is true.

The carol is the end of the joke. The footnotes are the only place the joke is not happening. That is why they feel like the real book. They are where Pynchon steps out of the fever and says, with enormous precision: this is where we came from, and this is how the present got its shape. The main text is the world. The footnotes are the map. The carol is the place where the map and the world become the same thing.

So what is the book actually about?

It is about a civilization that has made itself into a spectator. It is about the people who think they are still living inside the spectacle. It is about the institutions that keep the spectacle running. It is about the family that cannot stop performing. It is about the drug that tells you the present is too much. It is about the film that will tell you the present is exactly enough. It is about the footnote, which is the last place where a person can say: wait, this is not the whole story.

The carol is the future. The footnotes are the past. The novel is the present, and the present is the part that will not sit still.

prompt: Suppose a city wanted to become the next Silicon Valley. Is that even possible, and if so what would it really take? Write an essay working out what actually causes a technology hub to form.
response:
A city cannot decide to become a technology hub any more than a lake can decide to become a geyser. The difference between the two is not intent, but structure. A geyser sits above a reservoir of hot water that a fault channel feeds from below. If you dig a pipe where there is no reservoir, you get a dry hole. Silicon Valley is a reservoir. It formed because several hard-to-fake conditions happened to overlap in one place, and once they did, the rest followed. A city that wants the next Valley is really asking whether it can build the reservoir, or only the pipe.

The first thing to understand is that a technology hub is not a cluster of companies. It is a market for a specific kind of talent, plus a market for patient capital, plus a dense network of people who can absorb and transmit technical knowledge faster than the normal channels. Companies move. Capital follows. But the talent market and the knowledge network are the substrate. If a city gets a few anchor firms and no substrate, it gets a campus, not a valley. If it gets the substrate and no anchors, it gets a place where startups are cheap to start and hard to scale. The hub forms when the substrate and the anchors reinforce each other.

So what makes the substrate?

**1. A deep supply of people who can do the work and want to be where the work is**

The obvious answer is universities. It is also too simple. A university produces graduates; a hub needs a continuous flow of people who are technically skilled, professionally ambitious, and willing to take the risk of working in something unproven. That last part matters. A city can have excellent engineers and still have no startup culture if the local career logic says the safe move is to join a stable employer, a utility, a hospital, a bank, or a government agency. The hub needs people for whom “I could be wrong, but the upside is large” is a normal professional state.

That is why the classic Silicon Valley story is not just Stanford. It is Stanford plus a local labor market where being a founder, an engineer, a product person, or a technical operator is a respectable path. The region also benefited from military electronics, aerospace, and a culture in which technical people were not a small elite apart from commerce. They were inside the commercial system. The result was a pool of people who could build, sell, manage, and raise money without having to import every function from outside.

A city that wants to replicate this cannot simply import a university program. It needs a labor market that makes technical risk-taking a normal option. That means employers who hire and promote people with startup experience, investors who understand what they are buying, lawyers and accountants who know the forms, and enough working examples that a twenty-six-year-old can imagine a life in which she builds a company, fails, and still has a career.

**2. Capital that is local enough to know the people and patient enough to survive uncertainty**

Venture capital is not just money. It is a local institution for deciding which uncertain technical projects deserve resources before the market is sure. A hub needs investors who can sit in a room, hear a bad idea, recognize a good founder, and still say yes. It needs investors who can make a second check when the first one has not yet produced a press release. It needs enough capital that the best local founders are not forced to leave immediately, but not so much that the market becomes a casino where the only question is who can raise the largest round.

The capital has to be connected to the people. An out-of-town fund can write a check, but it usually needs a local bridge: an operator, an engineer, a former founder, a university lab, a corporate R&D group, a law firm, an accountant, a landlord, a service provider. That bridge is what makes the investment legible. A city can attract one big fund, but the fund will not create a hub by itself. It will create a pipeline of deals that may or may not belong to the city.

This is also why “venture capital” alone is not enough. Early-stage companies need many kinds of support: small checks, angel money, corporate pilots, government procurement, research grants, and sometimes boring debt. A hub that depends only on venture capital becomes fragile. It booms when the venture market is hot and collapses when it cools. A more durable ecosystem has capital at many horizons.

**3. Knowledge spillovers: the reason proximity matters**

The most important advantage of a physical hub is that it shortens the distance between a problem and the people who have already solved a similar problem. In a dispersed economy, a founder learns by reading papers, attending conferences, calling consultants, and hiring people from far away. In a dense hub, she learns by walking into a coffee shop, talking to a former colleague, seeing a competitor’s product, hiring a designer who just left another startup, or discovering that the person who can fix her infrastructure problem lives forty minutes away.

This is not romantic. It is information economics. Technical knowledge is sticky. Much of it is not in the published literature. It is in tacit judgment: what works, what does not, what the customer actually wants, what the regulator will tolerate, what the board will accept, what the codebase will survive. A hub makes that knowledge transferable because it puts the carriers of the knowledge near each other.

The spillover works in both directions. Startups learn from each other. Companies learn from startups. Universities learn from companies. Investors learn from operators. Service providers learn what is needed. A city with only one large employer does not get this. A city with many large employers in the same sector may get some of it, but the strongest version comes when the employers are diverse enough that people can move across them without losing their skills.

This is one reason defense and aerospace mattered to the original Valley. They were not just employers. They were training grounds. They produced people who understood complex systems, procurement, reliability, and the interface between engineering and management. When those people moved into electronics, software, and later the internet, they brought a kind of institutional memory. A modern city cannot simply copy the defense industry, but it can look for sectors that produce transferable technical judgment: semiconductors, biotech, advanced manufacturing, cybersecurity, energy systems, logistics, aerospace, robotics, data infrastructure, financial technology, health technology. The sector matters less than the fact that the sector produces people who can work across functions and move between organizations.

**4. A legal and institutional environment that makes the experiment cheap to run**

A startup is a legal experiment. It needs a way to divide ownership, hire people, protect ideas, take money, sell shares, issue equity, comply with regulations, and, if necessary, die without dragging the founders into ruin. The United States had several advantages in the twentieth century: corporate law, limited liability, securities regulation that permitted private investment, relatively flexible labor markets, and a legal culture that treated commercial risk as normal. Silicon Valley added local specialization: lawyers who understood equity, venture terms, patents, corporate governance, and the particular anxieties of technical founders.

A city that wants to become a hub does not necessarily need to rewrite its national law, but it needs to remove local friction. Zoning that makes it hard to find office space or housing. Licensing that delays a new employer. Tax rules that punish small firms. Procurement rules that exclude startups. University policies that make it difficult for faculty and students to spin out companies. Immigration rules that make it hard to hire or retain technical people. These are not minor details. They change the cost of trying.

The deeper point is that the institution must be legible. A founder should be able to answer basic questions without becoming an expert in every agency: How do I incorporate? How do I hire? How do I take investment? How do I protect intellectual property? How do I sell? How do I shut down? If the answer is “ask around, it depends, and be careful,” the city has raised the cost of experimentation. If the answer is “here is the form, here is the lawyer, here is the precedent,” the city has lowered it.

**5. A corporate base that can absorb talent and create demand**

A common mistake is to imagine a hub as a place where everyone starts companies. That is not how it works. The healthy ecosystem has a mix of startups, scale-ups, large companies, research labs, service firms, and public institutions. The large companies matter because they create demand, pay for infrastructure, hire people who may later found companies, and provide a place for technical people to work when they are not ready to take startup risk.

Intel, Apple, Cisco, NVIDIA, Google, and others were not just symbols. They were employers, buyers, suppliers, and talent magnets. They also changed what was possible locally. A company like Apple creates demand for design, supply chain, software, manufacturing, retail, and services. A company like NVIDIA creates demand for systems engineering, software, cloud infrastructure, and research. A company like Cisco creates demand for networking, security, and enterprise software. A city that attracts one large anchor may get a regional economy. A city that attracts several anchors in related but distinct fields may get a hub.

This is where the “Silicon Valley” model is often misunderstood. The Valley did not become the Valley because a government designated it. It became the Valley because firms, universities, investors, and workers made the same place the center of a particular set of problems. If a city wants to become the next hub, it should ask what problems it is uniquely positioned to solve. Not “What can we become?” but “What can we do better than anywhere else?”

**6. A culture of failure that is real, not advertised**

Cities love to say they celebrate failure. Most do not. What a hub needs is not a celebration of failure, but a low social penalty for a failed attempt that was honest and competent. A founder who tried, learned, and closed the company should still be hireable. An engineer who left a failed startup should not be treated as a suspect. An investor who wrote a bad check should still be able to write a good one. A university lab that produced a company that did not scale should still be considered productive.

This culture is not a slogan. It is a pattern of repeated outcomes. If every failed startup becomes a scandal, a lawsuit, a betrayal, or a moral lesson about recklessness, people will not try. If failures are common and mostly boring, people will try. The original Valley had a rough version of this. It was not generous to everyone. It was ruthless. But it did not require that a failed founder be professionally dead. That is the difference between a culture that punishes error and a culture that prices risk.

**7. Infrastructure that matches the work**

A technology hub needs physical infrastructure, but not the romantic version: a river, a park, a waterfront, a bike lane. It needs the unglamorous kind. Reliable power. Fast networks. Data centers or access to them. Laboratory space. Clean rooms, where relevant. Manufacturing floor space. Housing near the work. Transit or road capacity that does not make the daily commute a punishment. Childcare, schools, and public services good enough that families can live there.

This is where many tech-city plans fail. They focus on the flagship: the innovation district, the maker space, the incubator, the conference center. They forget that a company is not a logo on a building. It is a set of people who need to live, eat, commute, hire, and pay taxes. If the housing market is broken, the labor market is broken. If the power grid is unreliable, the data center is not a data center. If the schools are weak, the senior engineer will not move her family. If the transit system cannot carry the workforce, the company cannot hire from a radius.

The infrastructure question is also a question of scale. A small city can have a strong niche: one biotech campus, one advanced manufacturing cluster, one cybersecurity center, one agricultural technology hub. A large city can support several hubs. A region can support a full ecosystem if its cities are connected. The mistake is to compare a city of two hundred thousand to a metropolitan region of millions and conclude that the small city is failing. It may simply be the wrong unit.

**8. The role of government: useful, limited, and often counterproductive**

Government can help a technology hub form, but it cannot command one into existence. The useful roles are narrow: maintain rule of law, enforce contracts, keep the power and network infrastructure reliable, fund basic research, support education, make it possible for people to move and work, and reduce arbitrary barriers to entry. Government can also help by being a customer. Procurement can create early demand for software, sensors, cybersecurity, logistics platforms, health technology, or energy systems. But procurement is a tool, not a strategy. A city that buys local technology because it is local, rather than because it is good, will not create a hub. It will create a supplier of bad products.

The dangerous role is selection. A city that picks a single “innovation sector” and pours money into it usually mistakes a label for a cause. “We will become the blockchain capital of the Midwest.” “We will become the AI city.” “We will become the next Austin.” These statements describe a hope, not a mechanism. The mechanism is the market: the flow of people, capital, knowledge, and demand. If the market is not there, the label will not create it. If the market is forming, the label may help a little by making the city more visible. If the market is absent, the label will mostly help consultants.

There is a better way to think about government’s role. Do not ask, “Which industry should we choose?” Ask, “Which conditions are missing that would make it easier for many private actors to choose this place?” Is there a university lab that can spin out companies? Is there a law firm that understands venture deals? Is there enough housing? Is there a sector with enough technical employers to create a labor market? Is there a local investor class? Is there a public institution that can fund early research without managing the startups? Those are questions about the substrate.

**9. Why some cities get one and others do not**

Some cities have the pieces but not the overlap. A city may have a great university and no venture capital. It produces graduates who leave. A city may have venture capital and no deep technical labor market. It becomes a place where investors look for deals elsewhere. A city may have a large employer and no startup culture. It becomes a company town. A city may have startup culture and no capital. It becomes a place where people build small businesses, not scalable companies. A city may have all of those and no housing. It becomes a place where the young come, the companies grow, and the young leave.

This is why “talent” is the wrong headline. The right headline is the circulation of talent. A hub needs people to arrive, stay long enough to build something, and leave in ways that spread the knowledge rather than drain it. The best hubs have a rotation: students become engineers, engineers become founders, founders become investors or operators, investors become board members, board members become mentors, and some of them start again. The worst places have a one-way door: people arrive, get trained, and leave for somewhere with more capital or more demand.

The history of American technology hubs shows that the center of gravity moves when the problems move. The early electronics and computing center was the Bay Area. The personal computer era spread to other places. The internet era created hubs around software, venture capital, and platform companies. The mobile era made design, hardware, and app distribution matter. The cloud era made data centers, networking, and enterprise software important. The current moment is different again: AI, semiconductors, energy, biotech, robotics, cybersecurity, and industrial software are all becoming central. A city does not need to become “the AI city” in the abstract. It needs to become a place where a particular set of AI-enabled problems can be solved with local talent, local capital, and local demand.

**10. What a city should actually do**

If a city wants to become a technology hub, the first task is diagnosis, not branding. It should map the existing substrate. Where are the technical employers? What do they pay? What do their employees do when they leave? Are there lawyers who understand venture deals? Are there investors who write local checks? Are there universities with labs that produce companies? Are there manufacturers, hospitals, utilities, logistics firms, financial institutions, or public agencies with problems that could be solved by new firms? Is there housing? Is there power? Is there a legal environment that makes it easy to form, fund, hire, sell, and close a company?

The second task is to lower the cost of one repeatable experiment: a small technical company that can be founded, staffed, funded, and either grown or closed without heroic luck. That sounds modest. It is not. Many cities cannot make that experiment routine. The founder cannot find a cofounder with complementary skills. The first investors do not understand the business. The first hires are hard to make. The first customers are too far away. The first office is too expensive. The first regulatory question takes six months. The first exit is impossible. If the routine experiment is too expensive, the city will not get a stream of companies. It may get a few outliers, but not a hub.

The third task is to support the institutions that make knowledge transferable. Universities are the obvious ones, but they are not the only ones. Professional associations, industry conferences, user groups, open-source communities, trade schools, community colleges, apprenticeship programs, and company labs all matter. A city where technical people meet only at work has a thin knowledge market. A city where they meet in labs, conferences, user groups, and alumni networks has a thicker one. The goal is not to create “networking events.” The goal is to create repeated, low-cost contact between people who have different pieces of the same problem.

The fourth task is to be selective about anchors. A city should not chase every anchor. It should look for firms that create local demand and local talent. A data center may create jobs, but not necessarily a startup ecosystem. A cloud provider may create demand for software, but only if local firms can serve it. A semiconductor fab may create advanced engineering jobs, but only if the city can support the supply chain and the skilled labor. A hospital system may create demand for health technology, but only if clinicians, engineers, investors, and regulators can work together. The question is not “Can we attract a famous company?” It is “If this company is here, does it make it easier for other companies to form and grow here?”

The fifth task is to accept that the hub may not look like Silicon Valley. A city with strong manufacturing may become a hub for robotics, industrial software, and advanced materials. A city with a large health system may become a hub for clinical AI, medical devices, and regulatory technology. A city with a military base may become a hub for cybersecurity, simulation, and autonomous systems. A city with a major university in agricultural sciences may become a hub for precision agriculture, biosensors, and supply chain software. A city with a port and logistics network may become a hub for freight software, supply chain security, and automation. The name matters less than the fact that the city becomes the place where a class of problems is solved.

prompt: Last week I wrote about funding structures that line up innovation with business, and the most common reply was 'isn't that what B Corps are for?' Write a follow-up post on why 'doing good' shouldn't be defined by tax status or labels.
response:
# Good Is Not a Tax Status

The question "Isn't that what B Corps are for?" comes up every time anyone proposes a funding structure that lines up innovation with a business. The implied objection is that good already has a category. If you want to be good, file the paperwork. Pay the fee. Put the logo on the website.

It is not that simple.

A label is a claim about the future. It says a company will keep a certain shape under pressure, that its mission will survive a downturn, a founder departure, a new board. That is a strong claim, and certification can test for it. A B Corp scorecard asks whether the mission is embedded in the bylaws, whether workers have a voice, whether the company publishes a social and environmental report. It is a real instrument.

But it is not the thing. It is a way of describing a company that has already made a choice. The choice comes first. The label follows.

## The mistake in the question

The reply "isn't that what B Corps are for?" treats the label as the mechanism. It assumes that once a company is certified, the incentive structure is in place, and the rest is bookkeeping.

Incentives are not created by a seal. They are created by who can say no.

A company is good at a problem when the people who can stop a bad decision have a reason to do so. Investors who expect a return on the mission. Customers who pay for the better version of the product. Workers who leave when the mission is quietly dropped. Suppliers who refuse to be the weak link. A board that has the legal and practical power to enforce what the company said it would do.

A B Corp can have all of that, or none of it. The certification process is a snapshot, and the company that passes it in 2025 is not guaranteed to be the same company in 2031. The scorecard is not a perpetual engine. It is a report card.

## Why the label gets substituted for the work

Labels are convenient. They let a funder, a customer, or a journalist skip the harder question: what does this company actually do when the cost of doing good is visible on the balance sheet?

A label answers a different question. It tells you that someone has reviewed the company against a set of criteria. It does not tell you what happens when a new CEO arrives, when a product line is unprofitable, when a regulator changes a rule, when the market rewards the cheaper option.

The hard question is structural. Where is the mission written into the rights of the people who control the company? Who is paid based on whether the mission is met? What happens to the company if it sells the mission to the customer base? Can the mission be amended, and if so, by whom, and with what evidence?

A label can point at those structures. It cannot install them.

## What a funder should actually ask

If a company says it is built around a mission, the useful questions are not about certification. They are about control and consequence.

- Who can block a decision that undermines the mission?
- What do the people who can block it gain or lose if the mission is compromised?
- Is the mission in the governing documents in a way that survives a change of control?
- Do customers, employees, or investors have a practical way to enforce what the company claims?
- What has the company already refused, and what did that cost?

These questions do not have a single yes or no answer. They describe the shape of the incentive system. A company can pass a certification and still have a weak structure. It can have no label and a strong one.

## Why this matters for funding

Funders get trapped by labels because labels are easy to compare. A portfolio of B Corps looks like a portfolio of companies that care about the mission. But a portfolio is only as good as the structures inside each company. If the mission is decorative, the fund is financing decoration.

The better test is whether the company's governance makes the mission expensive to abandon. A mission that can be dropped by a vote of three board members is not a mission. It is a preference. A mission that is written into the rights of workers, customers, and investors, and that has been enforced at least once, is a different animal.

That is what a funding structure should line up with. Not a label. The people who can say no, and the reasons they will.

## The short version

A B Corp is a useful signal. It tells you that a company has been measured against a standard. It does not tell you what the company will do when the standard stops being convenient.

Good is not a tax status. It is not a certification. It is a set of incentives that make it harder to do the wrong thing than to do the right one. Labels can describe that. They cannot create it.

prompt: Why do street drugs like ketamine and MDMA keep turning out to be better psychiatric treatments than what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose? I want a speculative blog post that tries a few explanations and says honestly where they might fail.
response:
# Why Street Drugs Keep Beating the Pharma Pipeline

There is a pattern that is hard to explain if you take the pharmaceutical industry at face value. Ketamine was synthesized in 1962 and has been used for decades as an anesthetic. It is cheap, easy to make, and has been one of the most common drugs in clubs and prisons for thirty years. Only in the last ten years has psychiatry recognized that it works for treatment-resistant depression, and even then mostly through its metabolite hydroxyketamine, not the original molecule. MDMA was a research chemical in the 1970s, became a party drug, got banned, and is now being tested for PTSD with results that look better than any FDA-approved antidepressant. Psilocybin was studied in the 1950s, banned, and is now being studied again for depression and end-of-life anxiety.

These are not obscure molecules. They are not new discoveries. They were available, used, and understood by non-scientists long before the industry gave them serious attention. So why does it keep looking like the street is ahead of the lab?

A few explanations are worth taking seriously. Some of them are probably true. Some of them probably fail when pressed.

## 1. The Incentive Structure Is Wrong

The most obvious explanation is that pharmaceutical companies are not organized to find the best treatments. They are organized to find treatments that can be sold profitably for long enough to recover research costs.

That creates several distortions.

A new molecule has to be defensible as intellectual property. Ketamine, MDMA, and psilocybin are either not patentable or already off-patent. A company cannot lock them up for twenty years. Even if a firm can patent a delivery method or a formulation, competitors can often make a cheaper version. So the commercial prize is smaller than it would be for a brand-new compound.

Chronic disease drugs are also favored over episodic treatments. An antidepressant taken daily for years is a better business model than a substance given in a few supervised sessions. That matters because several of these compounds work in ways that are not easily converted into a daily pill. Ketamine is often used at short intervals. MDMA is being tested in a small number of clinical sessions. Psilocybin is also being tested as an occasional experience, not a routine medication.

The industry is not stupid. It is just optimized for a particular kind of prize. It is better at making a slightly better version of something already accepted than at commercializing a molecule that is cheap, difficult to protect, and does not fit a monthly revenue model.

This explanation is strong, but it fails in one respect: if a drug really worked better than existing treatments, companies should still be able to make money from a branded formulation, a delivery system, or a diagnostic package. They have done that before with less exciting compounds. So pure disincentive cannot explain everything. It explains why these drugs are underinvested, but not why the street found them first.

## 2. Street Selection Is a Brutal but Real Trial

Drugs used on the street pass through a kind of test that academic research does not. A lot of people use them, in varied conditions, with varied expectations, and then report whether the effect feels real.

That is not science. It is worse than science in many ways. Placebo, social setting, novelty, and danger all contaminate the signal. A club drug experience is not a controlled experiment. But it is a large, decentralized, repeated test of whether a compound produces a noticeable change in mood, perception, or social bonding.

MDMA is a good example. It is not a general euphoric. Its effect is specific: it increases empathy, reduces fear, and makes emotional memory easier to approach without collapse. That is exactly the kind of effect that might help someone reprocess trauma. A user in a room at 3 a.m. may not be able to name the mechanism, but they can notice that the drug makes it possible to talk about something painful without shutting down. That observation is crude, but it is not nothing.

Ketamine is similar. People do not use it because it reliably fixes depression in the way a textbook would prefer. They use it because it can break a loop. A person stuck in rumination may find that, for a while, the usual mental machinery stops. That interruption may be enough to let them do something different. Whether that becomes a durable psychiatric treatment is another question, but the initial signal is not mystical. It is a pharmacological interruption of a pattern.

Psilocybin works differently, but the same broad logic applies. It is not a happy pill. It can be frightening. But it changes the texture of experience and can make familiar problems feel strange, movable, or less fixed. That is not a cure, but it is a kind of access.

This explanation has real force, but it also fails badly if taken too far. The street finds effects, not treatments. It does not distinguish between a compound that helps one person for a night and a compound that improves outcomes over months. It does not control for expectancy. It does not tell you the dose, the timing, the contraindications, or the risks. It can also amplify a useful effect until the setting becomes part of the drug’s reputation.

So the street is a good source of leads. It is a terrible source of clinical conclusions.

## 3. Psychiatry Has Been Trapped in a Narrow Model

Another explanation is that mainstream psychiatry spent decades looking for the wrong kind of drug. The dominant model was often framed around monoamines: if depression is caused by too little serotonin, then add serotonin. If anxiety is caused by a chemical imbalance, then calm the system.

That model produced useful drugs. It is not empty. But it also trained researchers to look for molecules that fit a narrow pharmacological profile. A drug that works by changing glutamate signaling, or by temporarily destabilizing fixed emotional patterns, or by making traumatic memory easier to approach, may not look like the drug the model says you need.

Ketamine is a good case. It is an NMDA receptor antagonist. It is not a serotonin booster. It does not look like an antidepressant from the older monoamine perspective. But it can produce rapid changes, especially in people who have not responded to many other treatments. That suggests that at least some depression is not simply a matter of slow serotonin correction. It may involve stuck neural or cognitive states that need a different kind of intervention.

MDMA is another case. It is not an antidepressant in the usual sense. It is being studied for PTSD because it changes the conditions under which a person can encounter traumatic memory. It reduces fear and defensive avoidance while increasing emotional openness. That is not the same as adding serotonin. It is closer to changing the context in which memory can be processed.

Psilocybin is perhaps the clearest. It is a serotonergic hallucinogen, but its therapeutic promise is not that it makes people happy. It is that it may disrupt rigid patterns of thought and feeling, making it possible to reframe experience. That is a different therapeutic logic from a daily mood stabilizer.

This explanation is attractive because it fits the history. The industry and academic psychiatry did not ignore these molecules because no one knew they existed. They ignored them because the molecules did not fit the reigning model and the commercial system.

But this explanation also has a limit. If psychiatry had been more open, it still would have needed evidence. Openness is not a method. A drug can be theoretically interesting and still fail in trials. MDMA and ketamine have not been proven for every patient. Psilocybin is promising but not settled. The problem was not only that psychiatry looked in the wrong place. It was also that the commercial and regulatory systems made the right place expensive to enter.

## 4. The Setting Is Part of the Treatment, and the Street Knows That

A lot of these drugs are not inert chemicals delivered to a neutral body. Their effects depend heavily on context.

MDMA therapy is not just a pill. It is a pill plus emotional safety, trust, time, and guided reprocessing. Psilocybin is not just a dose. It is a dose plus music, expectation, preparation, and a setting that allows unusual experience to happen without immediate panic. Ketamine’s effects can vary with how it is administered, what happens after it wears off, and whether the person has any support for the change it produces.

This matters because the pharmaceutical model is built around a molecule. The molecule is the product. The patient takes it, the doctor adjusts the dose, and the effect is supposed to come from the drug itself. That model works well for many conditions. It works less well when the therapeutic effect is partly relational, partly experiential, and partly dependent on what the person does with the altered state.

The street understands this without theory. A bad drug experience can be worse than the problem it was meant to fix. A good one can be more than a chemical effect. People who use these drugs often talk about set and setting, intention, and aftermath. That is not scientific language, but it points to something real: these compounds may work partly by opening a window, and the value of the window depends on what happens through it.

This explanation is probably more true than the industry likes. It also makes these drugs harder to sell as ordinary medications. If the treatment is partly the session, the company has to sell a service, not just a pill. That is more complicated, less scalable, and less comfortable for a system that prefers a box on a shelf.

But the explanation can also be overstated. Context is not magic. If a drug only worked because someone was in a special room with a kind person, it would not keep showing effects across different studies and different populations. The chemical effect is real. The question is how much of the benefit comes from the molecule alone and how much comes from the molecule plus a structured human experience.

## 5. The Industry Is Not One Mind

It is tempting to say that “pharmaceutical companies” are a single actor that failed to find these drugs. That is too simple.

The industry is a set of firms with different portfolios, risk tolerances, and legal structures. Some are more interested in neuroscience. Some are more interested in psychiatry. Some have better discovery platforms than others. Some would like to own a psychedelic or rapid-acting treatment, but they may not have the right assets, the right partners, or the right regulatory strategy.

Regulation also matters. A company can choose not to invest in a compound if the legal and clinical path is expensive, uncertain, or politically awkward. MDMA was a controlled substance. Psilocybin was banned. Ketamine has a long history of abuse and nonmedical use. Each of those facts makes the development path harder, not because the drug is useless, but because the system has to be persuaded that the benefit is large enough to justify the complication.

This explanation is important because it avoids a cartoon. The industry is not a villain that deliberately hides good drugs. It is a collection of firms making bets under uncertainty. Some bets are not made because the expected return is too low, the risk is too high, or the route to approval is too messy.

But this explanation also has a failure point. If a treatment is genuinely better, the expected return should eventually become visible. Companies have followed less elegant compounds into difficult markets before. So regulatory difficulty may delay these drugs, but it does not fully explain why the street got there first. The street does not need a patent. It does not need a Phase III trial. It does not need a label. It only needs enough people to try a compound and notice that it changes something.

## 6. The Street Finds Compounds; Medicine Has to Make Them Safe

The deepest explanation may be that these two systems are doing different jobs.

The street finds compounds that change experience. Medicine has to determine whether that change is useful, repeatable, and safe enough to recommend.

That distinction matters. A drug can be powerful and still be dangerous. It can help some people and harm others. It can work in one condition and fail in another. It can produce a meaningful acute effect without producing a stable long-term benefit.

Ketamine is a good example of why the street lead does not automatically become a clean medical answer. It can help people quickly, but it also has risks: dissociation, blood pressure changes, bladder problems with repeated use, abuse potential, and uncertain long-term safety. The interesting question is not whether ketamine can produce a rapid antidepressant effect. It can. The question is which patients benefit, at what dose, by what route, with what monitoring, and for how long.

MDMA has a similar shape. It may be very useful for some people with PTSD, but it is not a general cure. It is not safe for everyone. It requires careful selection, preparation, and follow-up. Its value is not that it makes trauma disappear. It is that it may make it possible to approach trauma without being overwhelmed. That is a real therapeutic effect, but it is also a narrow one.

Psilocybin is the most complicated. It may produce profound changes in some people, but it is not a simple antidepressant. It can be frightening, disorienting, or destabilizing. The promising therapeutic claim is not that it is a happy drug. It is that, in the right conditions, it may help people break out of fixed patterns of thinking and feeling. That is a strong possibility, but it is also a claim that needs careful testing.

So the street is not ahead because it has better medicine. It is ahead because it is better at finding raw effects. Medicine has to do the harder, slower job: separating the useful effect from the noise, the risk, and the context that makes it appear.

## Where the Explanions Fail

None of these explanations is complete.

The incentive explanation says the industry does not want to make these drugs. That is partly true, but it cannot explain why no company has simply made a branded version and sold it. The answer is probably that the legal, regulatory, and reputational path is too costly, not that the commercial logic is absent.

The street-selection explanation says users found what researchers missed. That is true in a crude way, but the street is not a trial. It can mistake intensity for benefit, novelty for healing, and social support for pharmacology. It can also find a useful effect and then bury it under years of abuse, stigma, and bad outcomes.

The wrong-model explanation says psychiatry was looking for the wrong kind of drug. That is probably true for several of these cases, but it still does not explain the timing. If the model was wrong, other compounds with unusual mechanisms should have been found too. Some were. The problem is not that psychiatry only understood one model. It is that the system was slow to fund and approve molecules that did not fit the commercial and regulatory template.

The setting explanation says these drugs are not just pills. That is likely true, but it also makes them harder to treat as ordinary medications. If the treatment is partly a session, the industry has to build clinics, train people, and manage a service. That is less attractive than a pill, even if it is more effective.

The industry-is-not-one-mind explanation avoids blame, but it can become an excuse. Firms do not have to be a single mind to make predictable collective errors. When patents, reimbursement, liability, and regulation all push in the same direction, the result looks like a decision even if no one made it.

## The Most Honest Version

The most defensible explanation is a combination: these drugs are hard to commercialize, easy to use informally, and poorly fitted to the existing psychiatric model.

They are hard to commercialize because many of them are old, cheap, difficult to patent, or politically awkward.
