Schizophrenia, in its positive symptoms, seems to generate wants the person didn't have before: the conviction of being followed, the sense that the voice is a command. If preferences are what changed, the argument goes, we don't have a disease. We have a person with an unusual preference profile, and the right response is the same as for any preference — persuasion, incentives, a different environment.

That framing has a core insight, and I'll grant it. Part of what is called psychiatric illness is a learned or culturally shaped way of coping with a real, hard life. The economist is right that the preference is not arbitrary. It is tracking something.

But the argument collapses when it assumes that a preference that is "explainable" is therefore a "preference" in the ordinary sense, and that what is explainable is therefore not pathological. The mistake is in the first step. A preference is a stable, internally coherent ordering over outcomes, one that the agent can act on voluntarily, revise on reflection, and in principle give up without the rest of their psychological architecture coming apart. Most of what I treat in my practice is not that. It is a drive, a compulsion, a percept, a deficit — a force or an absence that has the phenomenology of a want but not the structure of one.

## What a preference actually is, and why the cases don't qualify

A genuine preference has three features. It is *volitional*: I can, for a time, choose not to act on it. It is *revisable*: if I am shown a better reason, I can update. It is *separable*: I can want a thing and not be it. I can want the drink and not be "a drink person."

An alcoholic, past a certain point, has none of these. The craving is not something he chooses; it arrives, and his capacity to act otherwise is genuinely impaired. Neuroimaging shows that in dependence, the salience of the drug and of drug cues is abnormally high relative to the salience of other rewards. That is not a matter of him having "decided" that whiskey is worth more than his liver. The valuation system is misfiring. If I tell him the consequences, he knows them — he has usually lived through them — and the knowing does not reduce the pull. A preference that cannot be acted against and cannot be argued with is not a preference. It is a drive with a target.

ADHD is worse for the preference story, because the "want" is not a want at all. What a person with ADHD experiences in a quiet, undemanding room is not a desire for stimulation in the way I desire a good meal. It is closer to a low-grade pain, a sense that something essential is being withheld. The motion, the risk, the next novel input — these are relief, not reward. The preference model requires that the person value the outcome; what is actually happening is that the person is in a state of aversive under-arousal and is doing what any organism does to escape aversion. Calling that a preference is like calling the flinching of a hand from a hot stove a preference for withdrawal. The withdrawal is real. It is not chosen.

Schizophrenia's positive symptoms are not wants either. A delusion is not a belief the person formed by weighing evidence; it is an experience that presents itself as given, with the phenomenological force of perception. "They are following me" does not feel like a hypothesis I happen to favor. It feels like the world. A hallucinated command is not a preference I've adopted. It is an intrusion I have to resist. To call these unusual preferences is to describe the wrong mental category. A preference is something you have; a delusion is something that happens to you, and the person is usually in pain about it, not pleased.

So the first error is taxonomic. The economist has taken a heterogeneous set of experiences — a misfiring valuation system, an aversive state that drives escape behavior, an involuntary percept — and forced them all into the single label "preference," and then argued that preferences are not diseases. The label does the whole work, and the label is false.

## The explainability trap

The second error is subtler, and it is where the argument actually feels persuasive. The economist's real point is this: these "illnesses" are not like a broken femur because they are *understandable*. The alcoholic is drinking because the drink works, because the life was unbearable, because the family drank. The ADHD kid is bouncing because the environment is hostile to a nervous system that needs input. The paranoid person is, in some cases, reacting to a world that is genuinely threatening or genuinely alienating. So we can *explain* them. And what can be explained, the argument continues, is not a malfunction; it is an adaptation, or a response, or a choice made under pressure. A femur cannot be explained away; a preference can, because preferences are the stuff of reasons.

But explainability is not the same as non-pathology. This is the load-bearing confusion.

Consider a person whose immune system has learned, over years of a brutal environment, to mount an exaggerated inflammatory response — an autoimmune condition. The response is *explainable*. It was shaped by real, recurrent threat. It serves, in a distorted way, a function the system once needed. And it is destroying the person's own joints. We do not say, because the response is understandable and was once adaptive, that the person has "unusual preferences" about their cartilage. We say the system is now producing harm to the organism, and we treat it. The fact that we can trace the response to a cause does not make the response correct.

The same structure appears in the psychiatric cases, and the fact that it appears is the whole point. The alcoholic's drinking is explainable — that is why it persists and why he cannot see it as optional. The ADHD kid's restlessness is explainable — that is why ordinary discipline reads as cruelty and fails. The paranoid person's conviction is, in some cases, a response to a real social rejection or a real violation. The explanation is not the opposite of the pathology. The explanation is *how the pathology got there and why it is so hard to reverse*. A condition that is well-explained by its causes is not thereby healthy; it is merely intelligible. And intelligible is the precondition for treatment, not the negation of illness.

A useful contrast makes this sharp. Take a person who has been through a genuine trauma and now has a phobia of a specific place. The fear is explainable, and in the moment of formation it was rational. We do not say the phobia is "just a preference for safety." We say the fear-response system is now over-generalizing, and we treat it. The explanation of the origin does not settle whether the current state is disordered. The question is whether the state is serving the person now, and whether it can be revised by the person's own reasons. A phobia answers no to both. So do the cases above.

## "Disease" is doing less work than the argument assumes

There is a third move in the economist's framing, often unstated: that to call something a disease is to locate a fault in the individual, and therefore to justify blame, coercion, or a medical model that ignores the social conditions that produced the state. The preference framing, by contrast, sounds kinder. It says: this person's preferences are a response to a life; meet the person where they are, change the incentives, fix the environment, and the "symptom" may not be a symptom at all.

Some of that is right, and I will not pretend otherwise. A large part of what is diagnosed as psychiatric illness is a sane response to insane conditions. A child in a violent home who is "hyperactive" and "defiant" is often a child who cannot be still and cannot be safe. A young man in a dehumanizing situation who becomes suspicious is not necessarily fabricating; he may be detecting real hostility that no one else will name. The preference framing is correct to insist that we stop treating the person as the thing that is wrong and start asking what the person is in. That is a real and important correction, and a good psychiatrist makes it constantly.

But the correction does not require the word "disease," and it is undermined by the word "preference." Calling the state a preference does not make it more humane; it makes it more *the person's*. A preference is something you own, something that is characteristically you, something for which you are in some sense responsible. If the alcoholism is a preference, then the alcoholic is, in the economist's own framework, a person who likes whiskey more than the rest of us do, and the appropriate response is the one we give to all strong preferences: persuasion, and a willingness to let the person have what they want. That is not kindness. That is a description that strips the person of the very thing they need, which is recognition that the state is not a free expression of who they are but something that has taken hold of them and is costing them their life.

The word "disease" — or better, "disorder," which is the more honest term — is not a blame instrument. It is a *location* instrument. It says: there is a state of this person's mind and body that is causing harm, that the person cannot simply will away, and that can be changed by interventions the person did not choose and cannot produce by effort alone. That is a factual claim about the structure of the state, not a moral one. And it is what makes treatment possible, because treatment is precisely the act of changing a state that the person cannot change from the inside. If the alcoholism is a preference, there is nothing to treat; there is only a person to be persuaded. If it is a disorder, there is a system to be worked on — the misfiring valuation, the aversive baseline, the involuntary percept — and there are things we can do to it that the person, alone, cannot.

This is not a semantic point. It is the difference between a stance in which the person is the problem and a stance in which the person is carrying something. The preference framing, whatever its intentions, lands on the first side. It makes the state the person's, and therefore makes the burden of change the person's, and therefore makes the failure to change the person's fault. The disorder framing does the opposite. It externalizes the state just enough to make it addressable, and it does so without denying that the state was shaped by the person's real life. Both things are true at once: the state was produced by conditions, and the state is now a thing in the person that causes harm and can be treated. The economist's framework can hold only the first of these, because a preference, by his definition, is not a thing that can be treated. It can only be held, or changed by the holder.

## What is actually going on, and why the distinction matters in the room

Let me say plainly what I think is going on in the three cases, because the general argument is easier to grant in the abstract than in the room.

Alcoholism is a disorder of valuation and of control. The person's reward system has been rewired so that the drug and its cues dominate what the person finds salient, and the systems that normally allow a person to do otherwise — to delay, to weigh, to walk away — are impaired. The person wants the drink in a way that is not a want. It is a demand the body makes, and the person's reasons are not strong enough to override it, which is exactly what a preference would allow. The person is not a whiskey-lover with a bad environment. The person is someone whose brain is now organized around the drug and is paying for it with the rest of their life.

ADHD is a disorder of arousal regulation and of the executive functions that let a person sustain attention and inhibit the next action. The restlessness is not a taste for motion. It is the behavior of a system that cannot hold the baseline. The person is not choosing stimulation over stillness; the person is in a state where stillness is aversive, and is doing what the state requires. The "preference" the economist sees is the escape behavior of a system in pain.

Schizophrenia's positive symptoms are not preferences but perceptual and belief intrusions. The conviction is not adopted; it is experienced as the world. The command is not wanted; it is resisted, often at great cost. A person in the grip of a persecutory delusion does not look like someone with an unusual but coherent set of wants. They look like someone to whom something is being done, and who is suffering about it.

In all three, the common fact is this: the state is causing harm, it is not freely held, it is not freely revisable, and it can be changed by interventions that act on the system rather than on the person's reasons. Those four facts are what "disorder" means. The economist's framework cannot accommodate any of them, because a preference, on his account, is freely held, freely revisable, causes harm only in the indirect way that all strong preferences can, and is changed by changing the person's reasons or their incentives. Every one of those clauses is false of the states I treat.

## Where the economist is right, and what I would concede

I will concede the real part of the argument, because it is real.

We have over-medicalized. We have taken states that are sane responses to bad conditions and filed them as individual pathology, and in doing so we have shifted the burden of change onto the person and off the world that made the state. We have done this with children, with the poor, with people in dehumanizing work, with people who have been abused. The preference framing is a correct protest against that. When a child is "hyperactive" because the home is a war zone, the right first answer is not a stimulant; it is a safe home, and the diagnosis that treats the child as the problem is a failure of imagination, not of medicine.

And we have under-explained. We have been too quick to say "this is a brain disease" when what is in front of us is a person whose mind is doing a rational, if costly, job in a hard situation. The explanation matters, because it changes what we owe. If the state is a response, we owe the person a different environment, not just a different molecule.

But none of that requires the word "preference," and the word is doing damage. The damage is this: a preference is the one mental state that is the person's in the fullest sense. It is what you value, what you are for, what you would choose if the pressure were off. To call the alcoholism a preference is to say the drinking is what the person is for, that it is the expression of their deepest ordering, that it is, in the end, up to them. That is not a humane description. It is a description that makes the person responsible for the thing that is destroying them, and it does so by using the most flattering word available — a preference, a taste, a value — to say what is actually a loss of control.

A person who is in pain and flinching is not expressing a preference. A person whose reward system has been hijacked is not expressing a preference. A person to whom the world is presenting itself as a threat is not, merely, holding an unusual opinion. These are states with a cause, a structure, a cost, and a treatability. They can be understood, and understanding them is how we treat them, and understanding them includes understanding the life that shaped them. But understanding a state is not the same as endorsing it, and locating a state in the person is not the same as making it the person's choice.

The economist wants to be kind, and the instinct is right. But the kindness he offers is the kindness of a framework that cannot see the thing in front of it. It sees a person with a preference and offers what we offer all people with preferences: reasons, incentives, and the freedom to have what they want. What the person needs is the recognition that what is in them is not what they want, that it is costing them their life, and that it can be changed by someone who sees it as a state to be worked on rather than a value to be respected. That recognition is not cold. It is the precondition for help.

prompt: Someone wrote to a famous songwriter saying she didn't know who she was and so couldn't make art. He told her she didn't need to know. Write an essay on whether self-knowledge matters for creative work, and how people actually come to know themselves.
response:
The songwriter’s reply is easy to respect and easy to mistake for the whole truth. Not knowing who you are does not stop a person from making a thing. A teenager with no stable self-concept can write a poem that lands. A person in the middle of a divorce can paint a room in a way that makes strangers cry. A musician can improvise a phrase that sounds like her, though she has no words for why.

But the reply also cuts off the part of the question that matters. If self-knowledge is not required to make art, it is still often required to keep making art, to choose what to make next, to survive the work, and to tell the difference between a good idea and a compulsion wearing a good idea’s clothes.

The confusion comes from treating “knowing who you are” as one thing. It is not. It is a bundle of different capacities, and creative work uses them unevenly.

One kind of self-knowledge is descriptive: I am bad at mornings, I get angry when I am hungry, I have been avoiding this subject for ten years, I am jealous of this particular kind of person, I am trying to prove something to my father. This kind is usually local, specific, and useful. It does not require a final portrait. It requires enough accuracy to stop being surprised.

Another kind is practical: what can I do, what do I want to do, what will I do when the first version is bad, what am I willing to give up, what do I need to keep doing in order to stay in the game. This kind is less about essence and more about stamina. Many people can describe themselves better than they can act on the description. The description may be true and still useless until it changes a decision.

A third kind is diagnostic: why does this subject keep coming back, why do I keep rewriting the same scene, why does this genre feel like home, why does success feel like danger, why do I stop when things start to work. This kind is the one that often matters most for a long creative life. It is not “I am a sensitive person.” It is “I am not interested in the subject; I am interested in the audience’s approval, and the subject is only the excuse I have for asking.”

A fourth kind is ethical: what do I owe the people in my life, what may I use, what is mine to tell, what am I pretending not to know, what do I want to be remembered for, what am I willing to lose if I say the true thing. This kind matters less for the first draft than for everything after it.

The reason people think they must know who they are before they can make art is that art feels like a confession. If the work is supposed to come from the self, then the self must already be available. But that is backwards. The self is not a finished object that stands behind the work. It is partly made by the work. You can know what you mean by writing badly. You can know what you are afraid of by making the thing and watching what happens when it exists. You can know what you can do by trying to do it badly enough that the habit stops helping.

This is why the famous songwriter’s advice is right at one level and dangerous at another. It is right because the block is often imaginary: a person will not begin because she feels she must first become a person. She will not write because she has not decided what she is “really” about. She will not make music because she has not found her “true voice.” The block is not the absence of self. The block is the belief that the self must be a completed answer before it can be a question.

It is dangerous because a person can spend years making work that is only a better and better version of a mistake. The mistake may be aesthetic: she thinks she wants to write novels when what she wants is to make short, sharp scenes. The mistake may be practical: she wants to be famous before she is ready to be seen. The mistake may be psychological: she is writing about grief because grief is the only subject that lets her feel important without having to be competent. The mistake may be ethical: she is taking material from other people and calling it discovery. The work may be good enough to be noticed. It may still be the wrong work for her, and the wrongness will show as exhaustion, repetition, resentment, or a talent that keeps peaking and then refusing to continue.

The first task is not to become a self but to become a worker. A worker has a schedule, a place, a standard, and a tolerance for bad versions. The self-knowledge that matters first is usually this: what can I do for an hour? What do I do when I am bored? What do I do when I am proud? What do I do when I am ashamed? What am I actually capable of making, not what am I capable of explaining?

This is why practice is not just training. Practice is a way of finding out. A writer who has written a hundred bad pages knows more about herself than a writer who has read a hundred books about the writing life. Not because the bad pages are true in some mystical sense, but because they are evidence. They show where the energy goes, where the attention collapses, where the voice becomes performative, where the subject becomes a costume.

People come to know themselves in several ordinary ways.

The most common is failure. Not dramatic failure, though that helps. Usually smaller failures: the project that did not finish, the performance that fell flat, the relationship that ended, the criticism that stung, the praise that felt wrong, the piece that got applause for the wrong reason. Failure is useful because it removes an assumption. A person may have assumed she wanted to be a novelist because she had always read. When the novel does not work, she may discover that what she wanted was not the novel but the feeling of being inside a long, complicated life. Or she may discover that she cannot sustain a plot, and that is a fact, not a betrayal.

The second way is comparison. A person learns about herself by seeing what she responds to and what she cannot stand. Not merely taste, which is broad, but the sharper kind: the work that makes her angry because it does what she secretly wants to do, the artist she admires because the artist has solved a problem she has not named, the genre she avoids because it requires a kind of honesty she has not trained. Taste is not decoration. It is a map of unmet needs and unmet obligations.

The third way is conversation. A person may be able to say what she believes about herself and still be wrong, because the belief is a story she tells to keep the world predictable. Another person can ask a question that breaks the story. “You say you want to write about your family. Why that family? Why now? What would it mean if you wrote about your friend instead?” The value is not in the answer. The value is in noticing that the answer was ready-made.

The fourth way is responsibility. It is hard to know yourself only as a feeling. You know more when you must answer for something: a student, a family member, a patient, a team, a deadline, a piece of work that has to be finished. Responsibility changes the shape of the self. It turns vague identity into a set of commitments. A person may discover she is not a “kind person” in the way she had imagined, or she may discover she is kinder than she thought, but only under certain conditions. Both findings are more useful than the old label.

The fifth way is time. Some self-knowledge is impossible in a single season. A person at twenty may be a person at thirty, but not in the way a sentence can say. The interests shift, the body changes, the old wounds either scar or reopen, the ambitions that seemed essential become embarrassing, and new ones appear that the younger self would not have recognized. This is why a fixed self-image is often a trap. It protects a person from change by making change feel like loss.

The sixth way is making things. This is the one the songwriter’s reply seems to protect. A person can say, “I am a musician,” and mean it, and still not know what her music is for. The music will tell her. If she keeps making songs about being misunderstood, she may be exploring a real subject, or she may be using the subject to avoid the harder one. If she keeps making beautiful, careful, safe work, the safety may be the point. If she keeps making chaotic work, the chaos may be the point, or it may be a way of not finishing. The work is not the self, but it is one of the few places where the self can be tested instead of narrated.

This is where self-knowledge becomes a craft problem. A creative person does not need a final self. She needs a working model of herself, and she needs to know when the model is failing.

A model fails when the person keeps choosing the same kind of subject and calling it a discovery. It fails when the person cannot say what is wrong with a piece of work except that it is not good enough. It fails when the person’s sense of what she wants is actually a sense of what she is allowed to want. It fails when the person confuses intensity with importance. It fails when the person cannot distinguish between a problem and a habit.

The practical question is not “Who am I?” but “What am I doing, and why does it keep doing that to me?”

A writer who always writes about rescue may be interested in rescue, or she may be avoiding the fact that she does not want to be rescued. A composer who always makes the music louder may be discovering sound, or she may be using volume because silence makes her feel exposed. A painter who always paints faces may be drawn to faces, or she may be afraid of abstraction because abstraction would require her to decide what the painting is doing without the comfort of recognition.

None of these diagnoses is certain. That is the point. Self-knowledge is not a verdict. It is a set of better questions.

The mistake is to expect the questions to end. People want a self that can be stated once: I am a romantic, I am a realist, I am a spiritual person, I am a political person, I am a perfectionist, I am a rebel. These words are not useless, but they are often too coarse. A person can be a rebel in one domain and a conformist in the one that matters. A person can be a perfectionist about form and reckless about content. A person can be political in her anger and private in her values. A person can be spiritual in her metaphors and material in her loyalties.

The more useful self-knowledge is comparative. Not “I am careful,” but “I am careful when the stakes are public and careless when the stakes are private.” Not “I am generous,” but “I am generous to people who make me feel young and stingy with people who make me feel old.” Not “I am brave,” but “I am brave in arguments and cowardly in commitments.” These are less flattering and more actionable.

This matters for creative work because the work is often a place where the self is exposed without being examined. A person can make a piece of work that is full of anger and still not know what the anger is for. She can make a piece full of tenderness and still not know whom the tenderness is trying to protect. She can make a piece that is technically impressive and emotionally empty, and the emptiness may be the most honest thing in it.

The danger is that a person can use the work to avoid the self. The work becomes a shield. The writer writes so much that she never has to say what she wants. The performer performs so well that she never has to be seen. The artist makes beautiful things and calls beauty the point, though the real point is that she does not know what to say plainly.

This does not mean self-knowledge should be pursued as a separate project, like a personality test with a creative supplement. It should be pursued inside the work and inside the life that supports the work. A person learns by finishing things, not only by beginning them. Beginning is often easier because it is still full of possibility. Finishing forces a choice. What stays in? What gets cut? What is the thing actually about? What will the person be willing to own?

A person also learns by receiving criticism. Not all criticism, but the kind that is specific enough to be tested. “It’s not good” is not knowledge. “The second scene loses the tension because the character stops wanting anything” is a claim. The person can argue with it, ignore it, or discover that it points to a pattern. Criticism is useful when it makes the person look at the work again with less attachment.

A person learns by watching what she does when no one is paying attention. This is where a lot of the real self shows up. The public work can be managed. The private hours are harder to manage. What does she read at two in the morning? What does she rewatch? What does she avoid? What does she rehearse? What does she pretend not to want? The private life is not a source of material in the cheap sense. It is a laboratory.

A person learns by aging. The self that wanted to be understood by a certain kind of person may no longer be the self that can be understood by that person without becoming small. The old wounds do not disappear, but they change their authority. A person may discover that what she called a need was actually a strategy for getting love, and the strategy has outlived its usefulness. Or she may discover that what she called a flaw was a capacity that had been punished into silence.

The songwriter’s answer, “you don’t need to know,” is best understood as a permission to begin. It does not mean the self is irrelevant. It means the self is not a prerequisite. The work can start before the self is legible. In fact, the work is often how the self becomes legible.

But the permission should not become a rule. A person who says, “I don’t need to know who I am,” may be protecting herself from a useful discomfort. She may be mistaking mystery for depth. She may be assuming that if she cannot say what she is, she must be infinite, and therefore not yet ready. That is a comforting idea, but it is not a method.

The method is smaller. Make the thing. See what it wants. Notice what you keep doing. Notice what you keep refusing. Ask what the work is for. Ask what you are afraid of when it is good. Ask what you would do if you were not trying to be interesting. Ask what you would do if you were not trying to be forgiven. Ask what you would make if the only audience were the people you already owe something to.

These questions do not produce a final identity. They produce better work and a less dishonest life. That is enough.

The deepest self-knowledge for a creative person is not a portrait. It is a set of limits that have been tested: what I can sustain, what I can refuse, what I can finish, what I can say, what I can bear to be seen doing, and what I am willing to lose in order to do the true thing rather than the impressive one.

prompt: Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?
response:
# Voting is a way to stop arguing

Voting is the only governance mechanism that works when people cannot agree and do not want to. It converts a dispute into a score. The minority can accept the result because it was produced by a rule they agreed to follow. This is a real achievement. It is also a poor fit for the questions that decentralized projects actually face.

Most governance questions in crypto are not about choosing between two clear options. They are about understanding a problem well enough to act on it. Should the protocol change its fee model, pause a migration, fund a research grant, respond to an exploit, adopt a new standard, or abandon a feature? These questions usually require technical judgment, historical context, and an account of consequences. A vote can say which option has more support. It cannot say which option is likely to work.

The problem is that voting separates the act of deciding from the act of understanding. A proposal is packaged into a title, a description, and sometimes a few links. The discussion happens in comments, Discord, X, and forums, but the vote is a thin event. People vote for positions, not for reasoning. The better argument does not necessarily win. The louder coalition does.

In a small group, voting is often the right tool. A five-person team does not need a referendum. It needs a conversation, a decision, and a record of who is responsible for what. In large decentralized communities, the problems are worse. Participation is low and skews toward people who are already organized or already paid. Whales can vote with their bags. Sybil attacks are cheap. Proposals can be gamed by timing, bundling, and narrative. The result looks democratic, but it is often just a snapshot of existing power.

Voting also makes disagreement feel finished. Once the vote passes, the losing side has a reason to say the process was fair. That is useful for routine matters, but it is dangerous for hard ones. A failed protocol design, a bad security decision, or a mispriced incentive is not resolved by majority rule. It is merely assigned to the majority. The community still has to live with the consequences.

The deeper issue is that decentralized projects need more than decisions. They need a process that produces shared understanding. A good governance system should make the reasons for a decision visible, test the assumptions, and leave the community able to explain what happened later. Voting does the opposite. It ends the process at the moment the community most needs to keep examining the problem.

## What voting is good for

Voting is not useless. It is good for a narrow class of questions.

- **Binary choices with known consequences.** Should the treasury approve a specific payment? Should the DAO ratify a legal entity? Should a grant of a stated amount be disbursed?
- **Questions where legitimacy matters more than optimality.** If the community needs to feel that it chose the path, voting can provide that.
- **Emergency decisions with a clear deadline.** If a bridge must be paused now, a vote may be the fastest way to record collective authorization.
- **Low-stakes or reversible decisions.** If the cost of being wrong is small, the cost of overthinking it may be larger.

These are real uses. But they are not the main uses. The main uses of governance in crypto are usually harder: deciding what to build next, how to allocate scarce capital, how to respond when something breaks, and how to change the rules that decide all of it.

For those questions, voting is usually the last step, not the main process.

## What is actually missing

Most crypto governance does not fail because it lacks a vote. It fails because it lacks a way to turn scattered knowledge into a shared decision.

A protocol has engineers, users, validators, integrators, researchers, attackers, and outsiders. Each group knows something different. The engineers know the code. The users know the product. The validators know the operational costs. The researchers know the theoretical risks. The attackers know the incentives. A vote asks all of them to choose one option. But the problem is not that they are choosing the wrong option. The problem is that no one has assembled their knowledge into a form the community can evaluate.

Good governance needs four things that voting does not provide by itself:

1. **A record of the actual dispute.** Not just the proposal, but the objections, the missing data, the competing models, and the reasons for taking one side.
2. **A way to test claims.** If someone says a change will improve security, the community needs a way to ask what evidence would support that, who can check it, and what would count as a refutation.
3. **A way to allocate attention.** Communities do not have infinite time. Governance needs to decide which questions are worth examining, which can wait, and which should be delegated to a smaller group.
4. **A way to close the loop.** After a decision is made, someone needs to say what happened, what was learned, and whether the decision should be reversed.

Without these, voting becomes a performance of participation.

## Alternatives that are not just voting with extra steps

The alternatives should be judged by what they add to the process, not by how they sound.

### Deliberation before the vote

The most obvious fix is to make the discussion part of the decision, not a prelude to it. A proposal should require a summary of the main objections, the evidence offered in response, and the unresolved questions. The vote should only happen after the community has seen the strongest case against the proposal.

This does not eliminate disagreement. It makes disagreement harder to hide. A vote for a proposal becomes a vote after the community has seen what the critics thought mattered.

### Structured disagreement

Some decisions are not settled by more voting. They are settled by making the disagreement explicit. Instead of forcing the community to choose between A and B, the governance process can ask:

- What would have to be true for A to be right?
- What would have to be true for B to be right?
- What evidence is missing?
- Who is in a position to provide it?
- What is the smallest experiment that would distinguish them?

This is useful when the community is not choosing a permanent rule but learning under uncertainty. The decision becomes: run the test, assign the work, set the stopping condition, and return with the results.

### Time-boxed mandates

A large community does not need to decide everything directly. It can grant a smaller group authority to act within limits. The mandate should be specific: what the group may do, what it may not do, how much it may spend, what it must report, and when the mandate expires.

This is closer to how real organizations work. A company does not hold a shareholder vote for every engineering decision. It gives managers authority, monitors results, and removes them when necessary. Decentralized projects can do the same, but they need to make the mandate public and revocable.

The danger is that mandates become permanent power. The fix is not more voting. It is better reporting, clearer failure conditions, and a realistic process for replacing the mandate.

### Reputation and responsibility

Voting treats all participants as interchangeable units. But governance is not only about counting preferences. It is about knowing who should be heard on a given question.

A user may be right about the product experience. A validator may be right about network operations. A protocol researcher may be right about a formal property. A past incident reporter may be right about a failure mode. A person who has spent months maintaining a component is usually better positioned to judge a change to that component than a person who holds a large amount of the token.

This does not mean governance should become a hierarchy of experts. It means the community needs a way to track who has been reliable on which questions. If someone repeatedly makes good security calls, their security objections should carry weight. If someone repeatedly misunderstands the product, their product complaints should be read with care.

The hard part is preventing reputation from becoming status. The best systems make reputation specific and revocable. It is not a rank. It is a record: this person has been right about these things, this person has been wrong about those, this person is responsible for this area, and this person has been removed from that role.

### Prediction markets for judgment

Some governance questions are predictions. Will a change increase adoption? Will a grant produce useful research? Will a new parameter reduce congestion? Will a migration succeed?

For these questions, prediction markets can be better than votes because they force people to attach confidence to their claims. A vote says someone supports an option. A market asks how much they are willing to stake on the outcome.

The market should not replace judgment. It should be used where the question can be scored later. If the outcome is clear and verifiable, the market can reveal what the community believes. If the outcome is vague, the market will mostly reveal what the community wants to believe.

### Adjudication for disputes

Not every disagreement should be resolved by consensus. Some should be resolved by a decision-maker with a limited authority.

This can work when the community agrees on the rules in advance. A dispute is submitted. The parties present their cases. A judge or panel decides. The decision is binding, but the process is constrained by the rules. The judge cannot create new policy. The judge cannot seize assets. The judge cannot change the protocol unless the rules allow it.

This is not democracy. It is closer to law. It is useful for questions where endless discussion would be worse than a bad but final answer: who gets a grant, whether a contract was breached, whether a committee acted within its mandate, whether a report was materially false.

The key is that adjudication works only when the community accepts the judge’s authority in advance. If the judge can be overruled by the loudest group, the system collapses. If the judge has no limits, the system becomes a dictatorship. The design problem is to make the authority narrow enough to be safe and broad enough to be useful.

### Reputable subgroups

Large communities cannot deliberate directly on every issue. They need smaller groups that can actually read the code, talk to the users, and make a recommendation.

The difference between a subgroup and a committee is not the name. It is the accountability. A subgroup should have a public mandate, a public record of its reasoning, and a public track record. If it makes a bad recommendation, the community should be able to see why: what information did it ignore, what assumption was wrong, what did it fail to test?

Subgroups are useful because they convert a large, slow, noisy process into a smaller, faster, more legible one. The community does not need to understand every technical detail. It needs to know what the subgroup concluded, what evidence it relied on, what objections it considered, and what the subgroup is willing to be held responsible for.

### Reverse voting and abstention

Some decisions are not choices between two good options. They are choices between doing something and not doing something. In those cases, the default should be inaction unless there is a reason to act.

Reverse voting can help. Instead of asking who wants the change, the system asks who is willing to block it. If no one blocks it, the change happens. If someone blocks it, the blocker must explain why and accept the process for resolving the objection.

This is not a general solution. It can be abused by a single holdout. But it is useful when the status quo is safe and the proposed change is risky. It shifts the burden from the proposer to the objector, which is often the right burden.

## A better default

Most decentralized communities do not need a new voting mechanism. They need a better process around the vote.

A practical default would look like this:

- **Small, reversible decisions** are made by the responsible subgroup and reported later.
- **Important but ordinary decisions** go through a short deliberation: proposal, main objections, evidence, and a time-boxed vote.
- **Uncertain but testable questions** are turned into experiments with explicit success and failure conditions.
- **Disputes with stakes** are sent to adjudication under agreed rules.
- **Structural changes** require a longer process: a public record of the dispute, a trial period where possible, and a vote only after the community knows what is being decided.
- **Mandates** are granted to small groups with limits, deadlines, and public reporting.
- **Reputation** is tracked by area, not as a general rank, and it is always revocable.

The vote remains, but it stops being the center of the system. It becomes one tool among several, used when the question is genuinely a choice and the community has already done the harder work of understanding the choice.

## The real test

A governance system should be judged by what happens after the decision, not by how democratic the decision looks.

Did the community understand why the decision was made? Did the people who opposed it feel that their objections were addressed, even if they lost? Did the responsible group have a clear mandate? Did the project learn from the result? Could the decision be reversed if the assumptions turned out to be wrong?

If the answer is yes, the system is working. If the answer is no, adding another vote will not fix it. More votes will only make the failure look more legitimate.

prompt: It's the day before the 2016 US election and the race looks close. I'm worried everyone will draw sweeping conclusions about the country from whichever way it falls. Write a short essay on how we should think about what the result will mean.
response:
We will call it a verdict, a referendum, or a verdict on the soul of the nation, depending on which side wins. A 2.8 percent margin in a 150 million-person electorate is not a verdict. It is a narrow slice of a much larger, noisier signal.

Treat the result the way a scientist treats a single trial. It is evidence, not proof. A margin that small could flip on a handful of counties, a bad night in Wisconsin, a TV ad, a snowstorm, or a scandal that breaks after the polls close. The 2000 and 2012 elections turned on far smaller margins than people remember, and neither one settled what the country “really” thought.

So do not read the result as a clean statement: Americans are X, or Americans prefer Y. Read it as a statement about a specific contest, under specific conditions, with specific voters showing up. It tells you something about the candidates, the parties’ coalitions, the issues that were most salient, the turnout patterns, and the states that happened to be close. It does not tell you what half the country believes, or what it will believe next month, or what it believes about the economy, immigration, or the president’s character.

The most honest question is not “What did the country say?” but “What did this race say?” And even that answer has limits. A close election can produce a large-looking mandate for one party’s agenda while also showing that the other party remains deeply competitive. It can mean that a candidate beat a rival rather than that the country embraced the candidate’s entire program. It can mean that a coalition won, not that the coalition is stable.

This is why the worst post-election reasoning is binary. One side will say, “The people have spoken,” as if a small margin in a two-person contest is a divine instruction. The other will say, “This is a fluke” or “This is a deep truth,” as if the result either means nothing or means everything. Both are wrong. The result means something. It means the winner was more electable, more appealing, or better positioned than the loser in this particular race. It does not settle the country’s values, and it does not end the argument.

A better rule is to separate three things: the result, the explanation, and the policy. The result is what happened. The explanation is why it happened, and explanations are contestable and often incomplete. The policy is what the winner should now try to do, and that should be judged on its own terms, not as a magical expression of the national will.

In a close race, the strongest lesson is humility. The country is not a single mind. It is a set of overlapping, contradictory, locally rooted preferences. A narrow result is a warning against overclaiming: against the winner who treats the margin as a license, and against the loser who treats it as a repudiation. The election will matter. It will also be far less definitive than the day’s headlines suggest.

prompt: Americans spend more on almonds than on all of election campaigns, which has always puzzled me. Write a post that explains how political money really works, who has figured out how to use it, and what that means for AI regulation.
response:
The almond statistic is true but the puzzle is based on a category error. Campaign finance money and business money do not do the same job, so their relative size says very little about which is more important.

**Campaign money is the visible layer.** It buys ads, mailers, phone banks, consultants, and data. It helps a candidate stay in the race and tells voters who is running. But the money that shapes policy usually does not flow through campaign committees. It flows through lobbying, industry associations, trade groups, think tanks, revolving-door hiring, legal pressure, and the quiet work of keeping a bill or rule from advancing. A company can spend far more on keeping an unfavorable law from passing than on electing any single politician.

The reason is simple: campaigns are short. A race lasts months. A rule, tax break, or regulatory carve-out can last for years. If your product is regulated, the regulatory process is often more valuable to you than the election. That is why many firms treat lobbying and regulatory affairs as core business functions, not political hobbies.

**Who has figured this out?** The firms that are good at it are usually not the loudest. They are the ones with long time horizons and concentrated stakes.

- Pharmaceutical companies have spent decades shaping drug pricing, patent law, and reimbursement policy.
- Fintech and payments companies understand that the difference between a rule that says “you may do this” and one that says “you must do this” can define a market.
- Defense contractors know that procurement rules, standards, and export controls can matter as much as elections.
- Energy companies have spent generations shaping permitting, environmental law, and grid policy.
- Big tech has become unusually skilled at this because its business model depends on default rules: what is allowed by default, what can be stored, what can be sold, what can be automated, who is liable when it fails.

The best players do not just write press releases. They staff regulatory agencies before and after employment. They fund studies that become the technical record. They join standards committees where the real rules are drafted. They hire former regulators. They make the regulated version of a law look more reasonable than the unregulated version. They know that most policy is not decided in a single dramatic vote. It is decided in implementation.

**That is exactly why AI regulation is different from most consumer products.**

If the government regulates a toaster, the main questions are safety and performance. If it regulates an AI system, the questions are much broader: who is responsible when the system fails, what data may be used, how much a company must disclose, how models may be evaluated, whether a government may compel access, how small rivals can compete, and whether the technology can be used in ways that create new kinds of harm.

This makes AI regulation a high-stakes rules game. The company that can make its preferred framework look like neutral technical policy can gain an enormous advantage. For example:

- A rule that says “AI systems must be explainable” can help incumbents with large compliance teams and hurt small innovators that move quickly.
- A rule that says “AI companies must retain logs for a year” may look like safety, but it can also change the economics of cloud, privacy, and liability.
- A rule that treats certain AI uses as a special category can create a licensing system that favors established firms.
- A rule that limits liability for automated decisions can protect platforms, but it can also delay accountability for users.
- A rule that bans certain uses can create a compliance moat for companies that already have governance structures.

The interesting fights will not be whether AI should be regulated. It will be who gets to define the categories. “AI system,” “high-risk use,” “automated decision,” “model,” “deployment,” “safety testing,” “red teaming,” “explainability,” “acceptable risk” — these are not neutral technical terms. They are policy choices wearing technical clothes.

**The people who understand this are not necessarily the most moral or the least self-interested.** They are the ones who understand that the state is a rules maker, and that rules are a form of market design. A company that can shape the rule may gain more than a company that simply builds a better product, because the rule changes who can enter, who must disclose, who can be sued, and what customers are allowed to assume.

That does not mean every regulation is capture. Some regulation is necessary because AI systems can cause real harm: discrimination in hiring or credit, dangerous medical or legal advice, manipulation of vulnerable users, unsafe control of physical systems, and large-scale abuse of automation. The goal should not be to prevent regulation. The goal should be to prevent one set of private interests from writing the rulebook while calling it public policy.

The best safeguards are boring but important:

- Rules should be written around public harms, not around the convenience of particular firms.
- Technical standards should be developed in public or at least subject to meaningful scrutiny.
- Regulatory agencies need real technical expertise, not just political appointments.
- Companies should have to disclose material risks, not just promise responsible AI.
- Liability should follow the actor with the power to prevent the harm.
- Enforcement should be credible, because a rule without enforcement is a slogan.
- The public should be able to see who is trying to shape the rule and what they are proposing.

The deeper point is that AI is not just another product category. It changes the cost of persuasion, surveillance, fraud, labor displacement, and centralized control. Whoever writes the default rules will influence the shape of the economy for decades.

So the almond comparison misses the real question. It is not that Americans spend too little on elections. It is that most policy money is spent after the election, in the places where ordinary citizens are least likely to look. The firms that understand this have an advantage not because they are smarter than voters, but because they have more to gain from the next regulation and more time to work on it.

The same logic now applies to AI. The important battle is not whether a future government will notice AI. It is whether the rules will be designed to reduce public harm, or whether they will be designed to protect a particular set of companies that happen to be good at writing them.
